articles.title: Philippines, UAE go after Filipino visa scammers
articles.summary: The Philippines and UAE are collaborating to pursue visa scammers who duped hundreds of OFWs. The two countries also roll out new digital recruitment systems.

blocks.text: ASSURANCE. Migrant Workers Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac tells Filipino household service workers during a get-together in Dubai on November 7, 2026, that there are legal services and funds available to them.
Jojo Dass/Rappler
The Philippines and UAE are collaborating to pursue visa scammers who duped hundreds of OFWs. The two countries also roll out new digital recruitment systems.

DUBAI, UAE – The Philippines’ Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) is working with the United Arab Emirates’ Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratization (MOHRE) to go after the Filipinos who allegedly victimized fellow Filipinos seeking freelance visas.

“We have coordination with the host government in running after the scammers, protecting victimized visa scams as well as cooperation with respect to addressing and finding those who prey upon OFWs,” DMW Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac told overseas Filipino workers (OFWs) in Dubai on November 7.

Cacdac was in Dubai until November 8 for the fourth Serbisyo Caravan of government agencies to provide one-stop services for OFWs, and for the Salamat Kabayan early Christmas celebration for household service workers.

Rappler earlier reported that two Filipinos — Junie Sorsano, a prominent Dubai-based content creator for over a decade, and Ryan Ronel Baco — allegedly duped some 400 overseas Filipino workers of AED 3.6 million (around P62 million) in visa facilitation.
The victims were mostly domestic helpers, caregivers, and retail sales staff, who sought freelance visas to legally pursue independent, self-sponsored employment.

blocks.caption: Dubai visa scam leaves hundreds of OFWs in financial, legal woes

blocks.text: Cacdac said he had raised the issue during a meeting with MOHRE head Dr. Abdulrahman Abdulmannan Al Awar.
“We have stronger cooperation now,” Cacdac said, noting this was his fourth meeting with Al Awar this year.

“If the alleged visa scammers have already fled UAE and are hiding in the Philippines, we will also talk to the DOJ, to Secretary [Fredderick] Vida about this matter and determine what charges can be filed against them,” he added.
He highlighted that victims can access MWO’s legal services and action fund.
“Rest assured, we have the legal services of our legal retainer that will help victims and in coordination with MOHRE on this issue. We may also tap the action fund on this,” the DMW secretary said.
He urged OFWs to consult the MWO to avoid scams.

Cacdac also signed an agreement with DataFlow Group to pilot the Digital Recruitment and Employer Accreditation Management (DREAM) System, an online platform allowing UAE employers, principals, and recruitment agencies to submit documents and pay fees digitally.
Designed to cut processing time and costs, the system complements MWO Dubai’s Online Employment Contract Verification System (OECVS), which has verified over 100,000 contracts since July 2025.

“Our 20 to 30 people at MWO will not anymore be sitting behind desks doing clerical or documentation work because these can now be done through the digitalized system, which means more of our people will be out there talking to the Filipino community, going to places where the Filipinos usually congregate visit hospitals, visit prisons to deploy legal services,” Cacdac explained.
Cacdac also discussed the upcoming Manila meeting of the Abu Dhabi Dialogue (ADD), which the Philippines will chair in 2027.

Established in 2008 as a voluntary consultative forum and currently chaired by Oman, ADD member states include the UAE, Philippines, Afghanistan, Bahrain, Bangladesh, India, Indonesia, Kuwait, Malaysia, Nepal, Pakistan, and Qatar.
The 9th edition (2026–2027) will focus on Artificial Intelligence and digitalization.

Cacdac also visited Pinas Cargo, a logistics firm shipping care boxes to the Philippines, meeting with founder and CEO Marlyn Castro. (READ: Dubai OFWs pay it forward with scholarships for Filipinos back home) – Rappler.com

articles.title: Palace: Apollo Quiboloy extradition 'long overdue'
articles.summary: The issuance of an extradition arrest warrant for Kingdom of Jesus Christ (KOJC) founder Apollo Quiboloy to face criminal charges in the United States is already "long overdue," Malacañang said…

blocks.text: Published November 13, 2026 6:43pm

The issuance of an extradition arrest warrant for Kingdom of Jesus Christ (KOJC) founder Apollo Quiboloy to face criminal charges in the United States is already "long overdue," Malacañang said Friday.

Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said the extradition warrant of arrest and hold departure orders are part of legal procedure, following Manila's receipt of the US government's request to extradite Quiboloy.
She added that the court's issuance merely coincided with the arrival of US President Donald Trump to the Philippines for the 46th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit next week.
"Hindi. Nagkataon lang siguro dahil alam na natin noon pa itong pag-request at voluminous ang documents," Castro said.
(No. It's just a coincidence because we already knew about this request and the documents were voluminous.)
"Kaya medyo natagalan din ang pag-aaral. So long overdue na ito. Maraming nang binasa para makagawa ng petition," she added.
(That's why it took a while to study, so this is long overdue. A lot of documents read to come up with a petition.)
The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) announced last August that it has received the extradition request from the US.
The Makati Regional Trial Court issued an extradition arrest warrant and hold-departure order for Quiboloy and two of his co-accused, the Department of Justice (DOJ) said Friday.

"The court issued an Extradition Warrant of Arrest against the foregoing individuals, after finding probable cause that: (a) each extraditee is the person named in the corresponding foreign arrest warrant and indictment, (b) that the offenses charged are extraditable offenses, and (c) that each extraditee committed the offense or offenses charged," it said in a statement.
"At the same time, said court likewise issued a Hold Departure Order against each extraditee, to prevent any attempt by each of them to depart from the Philippines," it added.
Castro also said President Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr. is letting the DOJ handle Quiboloy's case.
"Even before, sinabi naman ito ay ipinauubaya niya sa DOJ. So, alam naman niya ang nagiging proseso," Castro said.
(Even before, Marcos said he would leave it to the DOJ. So, he knows the process.)
Also on Friday, the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) said it is ready to assist in the extradition of Quiboloy, in coordination with the DOJ and other law enforcement agencies.

The NBI explained that the law enforcement agency holding custody of Quiboloy will be responsible for presenting him in court, noting that the extradition will undergo a process and require a hearing. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: EU leaders gather for first ever AI summit
articles.summary: The summit comes as worries about the artificial intelligence's global impact mount and Europe seeks a role in its development and regulation.

image.caption: The meeting is taking place in Dublin's Convention Center, which is also hosting the European Political Community summit this weekImage: Brian Lincoln/JNA/picture alliance

blocks.text: European Union leaders are meeting in Dublin on Friday at the first ever summit on artificial intelligence (AI). The meeting comes at a critical moment, as the bloc seeks a unified policy on the rapidly evolving technology.

"Given the rapid pace of AI development, ​I ‌believe that a first dedicated discussion, at leaders' level, is now needed on the opportunities presented by AI, as well as on its transformative effect on our economies and societies," European Council ‌President Antonio Costa wrote in a letter to EU leaders last week.
The meeting is taking place in Dublin's Convention Center, which was also the meting place of the European Political Community summit this week.
Scrutiny over AI and its leaders grow
French AI company Mistral's CEO Arthur Mensch, as well as Nobel-prize winner and researcher Geoffrey Hinton, widely known as the "godfather of AI," are expected to speak to EU leaders at the summit.
The summit will take place a time of mounting worries about the emerging technology, which promises to transform ‌industries, labor markets and societies.
It also comes in the wake of a series of incidents involving rogue AI agents in recent months and the wider discussion about how the technology could harm humanity.

Tech leaders behind the technology have also fallen under scrutiny. As recently as this week,Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was forced to resign after it was revealed that he had been in a relationship with a Chinese spy and a direct report in his company.
Finding Europe's role in the AI revolution
During the summit, a discussion about where Europe fits in within the AI movement is expected.

Leaders face questions on how to unlock AI's potential, how to catch up with China and the United States in the race for the technology, but also how to protect against the risks it poses to individuals and businesses.

The governments of Estonia and Finland wrote in a letter ahead of the summit that Europe must "establish EU-level arrangements for responding to serious AI incidents," calling for "developing advanced AI and governing it responsibly."
Meanwhile, Mistral has pushed back on calls to slow down AI development, urging Europe to push ahead.

Torreon clarified that he does not represent Quiboloy in the extradition proceedings, noting that his duties are limited to the religious leader's pending criminal cases before the Pasig and Quezon City courts.
He confirmed that Quiboloy has already been notified of the extradition petition, which the Department of Justice (DOJ) filed on Monday on behalf of the United States government.

He emphasized that they will answer the allegations against Quiboloy in court, where the matter belongs, rather than in the court of public opinion.

Earlier on Monday, the DOJ confirmed that the Makati Regional Trial Court had issued an extradition arrest warrant and a hold departure order against Quiboloy, who is currently detained at the Pasig City Jail.

Regarding the pending criminal cases against the Davao-based religious leader, Torreon said his client will continue to face the charges and urged the public not to make any assumptions about the issue yet.

articles.title: Microsoft outage hits hospitals, GPs, schools and police across UK
articles.summary: NHS experiencing ‘serious’ and widespread disruption and people are told of possible delays in receiving prescriptions

blocks.text: Hospitals, GPs and police forces across the UK have been hit by the global Microsoft outage, as key services battle to get systems back online.

Police forces across the country reported that their systems had been affected, while NHS sources said the healthcare system was experiencing “widespread” and “serious” disruption, with staff reporting being unable to access email and IT systems they use to deliver healthcare.
Patients getting their prescriptions were also warned of possible delays, while schools and universities were unable to access emails.
There were also reports that ambulance services had been affected by the outage.

The problems began late on Thursday afternoon and users have been unable to access many of Microsoft’s most popular services. Thousands worldwide reported they were unable to send and receive emails through Outlook.

The Microsoft executive vice-president Charles Lamanna said the outages did not appear to be the result of a cyber-attack. On Friday morning the firm said it was seeing “early signs of stabilisation”.

NHS staff arriving at work on Friday morning reported being unable to access email, affecting their ability to deliver healthcare in hospitals and surgeries, amid warnings that the outage would be highly disruptive through the day.

In some cases, staff said they were able to use their phones to access Microsoft Teams, which is heavily relied upon in the healthcare sector, but meetings were having to be cancelled across the board.
Some NHS organisations took to social media to apologise, urging patients not to email and to use the telephone to contact them instead.

Rachel Harrison, the GMB national secretary, said: “The Microsoft data outage is having a serious impact across ambulance and NHS trusts. Luckily emergency and life-threatening callouts appear to be unaffected.”

Pharmacy sources told the Guardian they were also unable to access email, and said the Microsoft outage was affecting their ability to communicate with some GP surgeries about prescriptions. This was having a “significant” impact on patient waiting times for medicines, they said.

A National Pharmacy Association spokesperson said: “We are aware of the disruption impacting pharmacies today, including access to NHS email systems, due to national issues with Microsoft. This affects a pharmacy’s ability to communicate with GP practices and some patients.
“Please bear with your pharmacy teams today, where waits may be longer than normal and there may be delays to some prescriptions.”

Meanwhile, engineers from the government were working with Microsoft to assess the impact of the outage, according to a minister, while the Welsh government said it was putting contingency plans in place.

Luke Pollard, the minister for defence readiness and industry, told Times Radio: “Government engineers and the systems are working with Microsoft at the moment. I would expect that to be able to be detailed throughout the day. But as more people come online with their working days shortly, I think there’ll be sadly more people frustrated with the system.”
Pollard said the Microsoft outage demonstrated the need for “greater resilience” against technology failures.

He told the Today programme on BBC Radio 4: “My appetite for disruption when it comes to using my phone is virtually zero. I imagine that’s the case for every one of your listeners, that people want it to work all the time, every time, and we’re seeing more disruption from those tech companies. That’s partly because we’ve become more dependent on technology.”

The Metropolitan, Northampton, Hertfordshire, South Wales, Dyfed-Powys and Dorset police forces all reported that their systems had been affected. Access to Microsoft products used by MPs was also down.

A parliamentary spokesperson said: “We are aware of the global issue affecting Microsoft email services, which is impacting users of the parliamentary network. We are working with Microsoft to resolve the matter as quickly as possible.”

articles.title: What if paying bills turned into a psychological horror game?
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – When the theme for the Filipino Horror Game Jam 2026 dropped, Angelo Barrera and the team at Mithika Games figured they’d end up making something with ghosts or local folklore.…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – When the theme for the Filipino Horror Game Jam 2026 dropped, Angelo Barrera and the team at Mithika Games figured they’d end up making something with ghosts or local folklore. Then somebody pitched an idea as a half-joke: what about household bills?

Electric bills, rent, and grocery receipts don’t exactly sound like classic horror fare on paper. But as the team kept kicking the concept around, a much heavier question sank in: what if the real nightmare isn’t the bills themselves, but the person stuck paying them?

That spark became Breadwinner, a psychological horror title centered on a Filipino panganay (eldest child) trying to stretch a single paycheck across endless family expenses. Players spend their commute choosing what gets covered, from rent and electricity to meds for a parent or school fees for a younger sibling, before heading home to face the inevitable fallout of those choices.

Barrera, an eight-year industry veteran who has worked as a programmer, designer, and producer, mentioned that the idea took shape while looking for an angle on the jam’s “real-life horror” theme that wouldn’t get lost in the crowd.

Early on, they toyed with scenarios like floods, muggings, or stalkers. While scary, Barrera felt those situations lacked a universal, daily resonance. Someone might assume they’ll never get mugged, but having your monthly expenses outpace your bank balance is an anxiety almost everyone recognizes.

This went from family dynamics to the financial pressure on lower-income households, particularly what Barrera calls toxic sides of family culture. In many homes, the eldest breadwinner ends up supporting people far beyond their immediate self. A paycheck that could comfortably support one person suddenly has to keep an entire household afloat.
RELATED STORY: Block 123: Pinoy Street Rumble brings nostalgia to MOBA
Making a game out of the bills

The pieces for Breadwinner didn’t start out in one game. Initially, the team had separate prototypes: one focusing on the walk home, another on a jeepney ride, and a third set entirely inside the family house. On day two of the game jam, Barrera decided to stitch them into a single narrative flow.

The result is a brief, focused journey through a single day in the protagonist’s shoes, where your financial choices directly alter the vibe and narrative progression. Instead of relying on jump scares or monsters, Breadwinner mines terror from that quiet, suffocating dread of watching your money run out while your responsibilities mount.

Honestly, the team wasn’t even sure if the game would hit when they turned it in. Barrera remembers wondering if they’d pushed the boundary too far, especially since it looked so different from standard horror jam entries.

Then streamers picked it up, and comment sections across Facebook, Instagram, YouTube, and TikTok blew up. Barrera said they were caught off guard by how quickly players picked up on tiny details and subtle themes they had tucked into the design.
Many players felt like the game was telling their exact life story, while others admitted the depiction of familial guilt hit way too close to home.

Mithika Games had initially worried the story might be too hyper-specific to the Philippines to resonate elsewhere. But surprisingly, Barrera started getting messages from players in Latin America saying the exact same dynamic exists in their culture.
“It’s Filipino-flavored,” he noted. The slang or local references might change depending on where you are, but the core story remains universally human.

That reaction highlights why Breadwinner lands so well outside its home region. While the panganay experience carries distinct local nuances, the grinding tension between family duties and a limited income isn’t bound by geography. The game doesn’t need to dilute its cultural identity for foreign audiences to understand the weight on the protagonist’s shoulders.
A two-week project gets a second life

Originally, Mithika Games viewed Breadwinner as a quick game jam project to finish, ship, and forget. Everyone on the team works a full-time job, so game dev is something they tackle on nights and weekends. The whole thing was thrown together in about two weeks without any master plan for a full release.

The overwhelming response flipped those plans on their head. Encouraged by the feedback, the team put together version 0.2, adding features and narrative beats that got cut from the original build. Barrera says they now see real potential to expand Breadwinner into a full-fledged narrative experience with richer gameplay mechanics.

Plans under consideration include expanding the commute route into a fully explorable neighborhood and giving players a closer look at the main character’s workplace. Barrera emphasized that the team is taking its time to flesh these ideas out properly rather than calling it done.

Voice acting has come up in discussions too, though the branching story makes voice recording tricky while the script is still evolving. Since players can choose between playing as a kuya (older brother) or ate (older sister), every narrative branch needs to be voiced twice.

A Steam launch is definitely on the radar, but Barrera feels the game isn’t meaty enough yet to ask people for money. They aren’t interested in rushing out a cash-grab just because they’ve caught a wave of hype. Instead, they’re looking at games like Until Then, another breakout Filipino narrative game, as a standard for storytelling depth and overall polish.

Barrera says the focus right now is quietly building out story paths, tweaking gameplay mechanics, and listening to community feedback. Mithika Games is also open to bringing in production partners to help bring the full project across the finish line.

Beyond Breadwinner, Mithika Games has diverse interests. Barrera pointed to Tata, a project created in collaboration with the Cultural Center of the Philippines to showcase regional arts and heritage. The studio intends to keep experimenting across genres while holding onto their quality standards.

On a personal level, Barrera dreams of making a sci-fi MMO centered on player choice and community dynamics. Growing up on StarCraft, Red Alert, and Dota, he always assumed his landmark project would be a massive commercial sci-fi game. A game about budgeting bills was never on his original radar.

Yet here they are, building on a project that started with a joke about monthly expenses. What began as a throwaway entry for a game jam has given Mithika Games a story worth telling at full scale. They’re still figuring out the exact contours of the expanded version but they are definitely on the right track.

At its heart, the game is relatable on so many levels from that monthly salary, a stack of bills, and a family depending on one person to make it all work. In more ways than one it really is scary stuff to think about.

items: 24m agoUK-EU deal will lead to 'growing pressure' for parliament to scrutinise legislation, committee warns

blocks.text: UK-EU deal will lead to 'growing pressure' for parliament to scrutinise legislation, committee warns
Hello and welcome to the UK politics live blog.

There will be a “growing pressure” for parliament to scrutinise EU legislation under new deals on food and emissions to be sealed ahead of the UK’s summit with the bloc next week, a Lords’ committee has warned.

Prime minister Andy Burnham is due to meet EU leaders in Brussels next week and sign agreements that he says could raise GDP by 0.4%. This includes a sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) deal on food and farming, as well as one on emissions trading and another for a youth mobility scheme.

A deal is also thought to include a health security agreement to help address shortages of drugs such as antibiotics and ADHD medication, which have got worse since Brexit, according to a draft text seen by the I newspaper.

It will mark a significant shift in the Britain’s post-Brexit relationship with the EU as they will require dynamic alignment, the process of matching laws to the bloc’s evolving legislation, the House of Lords European Affairs Committee said in a new report.
The committee of peers says this will mean parliament needs to set up a “robust, consistent and adequately resourced cross-departmental system” to manage the UK’s dynamic alignment commitments.
The committee chairman, Jock Stirrup, said:

double quotation markAlthough important details remain to be determined of the legal and institutional form that dynamic alignment will take, its introduction will mark a major change to the nature of the UK-EU relationship as it exists under the Trade and Cooperation Agreement. As the UK aligns with more EU law, parliament will face growing pressure to scrutinise significant volumes of EU legislation.
The food and farming deal alone could generate at least 780 pieces of in-scope EU law every year, the committee heard.
Meanwhile, the I reports that the government is close to securing a deal with Europe to help tackle post-Brexit medicine shortages, including antibiotics, ADHD medication and epilepsy drugs.
Experts on post-Brexit health policy have reportedly described the deal as “significant'” and a “good first step” in addressing shortages that have hit both sides in recent years.
It comes as prime minister Andy Burnham said he believes a “win-win” deal could be done with the EU that could be “more like the Brexit that people thought they were voting for in 2016”.
The prime minister was meeting fellow leaders at the European Political Community summit in Dublin, ahead of the summit next week, where he hopes to bring Britain closer to Europe.
Burnham said:
double quotation markI believe there is a good deal to be done that could be a win-win for Britain and Europe. The deal is not done, and there’ll be some long nights ahead in the next seven days.
In other developments:

items: Some young people with disabilities will lose their personal independence payments and will have to apply instead to a local fund for short-term expenses and equipment, Alan Milburn’s review will recommend.

articles.title: What we know about the global Microsoft outage
articles.summary: Microsoft has said the outage was not caused by a cyber-security incident, but efforts to fix the issues have so far been largely unsuccessful.
articles.byline: Helen Davidson, Jessica Lamb, Helen Sullivan

blocks.text: Watch: What we know about the Microsoft global outage overnight
ByHelen DavidsonJessica Lamb and Helen Sullivan
A major global Microsoft outage has caused problems, or in some cases disabled entire services, including emails and artificial intelligence products.
Microsoft has said the outage was not caused by a cyber-security incident, but efforts to fix the issues have so far been largely unsuccessful.
Here's what we know about the services affected and what went wrong.
What happened?
Microsoft 365 Services, including Teams, Outlook and Microsoft's artificial intelligence software Copilot, have been affected by "connectivity problems".
Customers are reporting varying levels of access - many have not been able to send or receive emails, view certain files or details on their calendar apps.
Some users have been able to use Teams and are using messaging and online meeting functions without issues.
How many people have been affected?
More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps according to Microsoft's website.
The full scale of the outage has not been confirmed, but monitoring website Downdetector had 140,000 people from 74 countries report issues with Outlook on Thursday evening.
The real figure affected is likely much higher because Downdetector relies primarily on users self-reporting.
Microsoft 365 is also used by companies worldwide and is expected to have a knock-on effect to other services.
Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic have both reported problems as a result of the outage.
ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which has caused some tools to not work as expected.
Government agencies and services, including the Singaporean government and Australia's spy agency, have also said they have been affected.
Across the UK, GP surgeries, pharmacies, police and schools have been affected by the outage.

Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains, while several large police forces are urging members of the public to call if they want to make a report.
What has Microsoft said?
Microsoft has ruled out a cyber-attack and attributed the ongoing outage to "elevated load" on its infrastructure.
The term refers to when servers are handling a much higher volume of stress than they usually do.
In the case of the Microsoft outage, a large number of servers became "unexpectedly unavailable", the company said, which sent added traffic to remaining servers, straining these.
On Friday morning, Microsoft said it was seeing "early signs of stabilisation", but service capacity has "not yet returned to normal levels".
In an earlier statement, the tech giant had said that its attempted fixes were "not taking as expected".
What have experts said?
Australian cyber-security expert Troy Hunt told the BBC the outage could have far-reaching consequences.
"Microsoft is a massive part of the internet backbone and reminds us how critical email still is.

"Not only does this outage affect many people's ability to work but also things like the ability to communicate about appointments, purchase things that need verification, create or access accounts and services," he said.
Paul Spain from New Zealand-based advisory firm Gorilla Technology said that with e-mails and services offline, companies have practically "lost a business day", which is "frustrating" users".

articles.title: FACT CHECK: Old Remulla video misused to falsely claim Dela Rosa has no ICC warrant
articles.summary: A January 2026 interview clip released months before the ICC unsealed the warrant recirculated on social media and was falsely presented as a current update on Dela Rosa’s arrest

blocks.text: Claim: Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) Secretary Jonvic Remulla said there is no arrest warrant against Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa.
Why we fact-checked this: A reel posted on November 6 by the Facebook page “Pobre Nga Uyamot” shows an interview clip of Remulla with the overlaid text, “Klaro walang warrant (Clearly no warrant).”
Additional overlaid text read: “Walang kaso si Bato sa Pinas! Pag lumaban, mamatay pulis order sa taas ma-blame! High risk! Law of the land pa rin.”
(Bato has no case in the Philippines! If he fights back, police will die and whoever gave the order will be blamed! High risk! The law of the land still applies.)

In the clip, Remulla says: “Si Bato, ano hahanapin namin? ‘Di ba, alam naming nasa Davao siya. Pero wala naman kaming warrant of arrest. Wala. So bakit namin hahanapin? Ba’t namin aarestuhin? Kung gusto niya, siya [ang] mag-citizen’s arrest.”

(Why will we search for Bato? We know he’s in Davao, but we don’t have an arrest warrant. None. So why would we search for him? Why would we arrest him? If he wants to, let him make a citizen’s arrest.)
As of writing, the video has 2.5 million views, 15,000 reactions, 2,300 comments, and 3,400 shares.
The facts: The clip is old and was misleadingly presented as a current update on Dela Rosa’s status as a subject of an International Criminal Court (ICC) arrest warrant.

The clip was from Remulla’s January 27, 2026 interview on ANC, during which he addressed former senator Antonio Trillanes IV’s suggestion to search for Dela Rosa, who at the time had not been attending Senate sessions amid rumors of an ICC warrant against him.

Remulla then made the remark shown in the Facebook reel, adding that he would personally go to Davao to fetch Dela Rosa. He also suggested that Trillanes could carry out a citizen’s arrest if such a warrant existed.

At the time Remulla said this, the ICC warrant had not been made public. The ICC’s records show it was issued as secret on November 6, 2025, and unsealed only on May 11, 2026, several months after the interview from which the clip was taken.
Dela Rosa is accused of murder for crimes against humanity involving at least 32 killings between July 2016 and April 2018 under the bloody drug war of former president Rodrigo Duterte.

What happened after January: In May, the Supreme Court denied Dela Rosa’s request for a temporary restraining order seeking to block the ICC warrant. Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida then said a valid ICC arrest warrant exists and is now enforceable, allowing the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) and the Philippine National Police (PNP) to effect the senator’s arrest.
Dela Rosa went into hiding shortly after the warrant was issued and is now the subject of a P50-million bounty. (READ: Bato dela Rosa’s escape: Timeline, analyses, opinions from experts)
Manhunt for Dela Rosa: On October 23, Remulla described Dela Rosa as “armed and dangerous.” He also warned that an attempt to arrest the senator by force could result in a “bloodbath.”

Dela Rosa’s camp continues to dispute how the warrant can be enforced. His lawyers argue that no local court has issued an arrest warrant and that the bounty cannot replace domestic judicial procedures that they said were necessary before the senator could be arrested.

Authorities have received at least 500 tips about Dela Rosa’s whereabouts, PNP chief General Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said on November 9. The NBI has said it hopes to arrest the senator before the year ends. – Cyril Bocar/Rappler.com

Efren Cyril Bocar is a journalist from Llorente, Eastern Samar who graduated with a degree in English Language Studies at the Visayas State University. Cyril is also a graduate of the Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: Philippine Navy to deploy vessels to secure 2026 ASEAN Summit
articles.summary: The Philippine Navy will deploy majority of its vessels under the Naval Defense Command (NDC) to ensure maritime security during the upcoming ASEAN Summit, its spokesperson said Friday.

blocks.text: Published November 13, 2026 5:40pm
The Philippine Navy will deploy majority of its vessels under the Naval Defense Command (NDC) to ensure maritime security during the upcoming ASEAN Summit, its spokesperson said Friday.
Navy spokesperson Captain Marrisa Martinez said the deployment would cover Manila Bay, its maritime approaches, and other strategically significant maritime areas.
"Almost all the ships of the Philippine Navy will be employed for this initiative or for this purpose, which is the ASEAN," Martinez told reporters in an ambush interview.
Among the naval assets to be deployed are the newly acquired offshore patrol vessels BRP Raja Sulaiman and BRP Raja Lakandula.
Martinez said priority patrol areas would include the sea approaches to Manila Bay.
The Navy will also deploy personnel from the Philippine Marine Corps, Naval Special Operations Command, Naval Special Warfare Force, as well as air capabilities.
Martinez assured the public that the ASEAN-related deployment would not affect the Navy's regular operations across the country.
She said vessels operating in the West Philippine Sea would continue their patrols and maritime domain awareness activities, particularly given the security situation in the area.

The Navy's security operations will also continue even after the summit concludes, potentially extending for a week or longer to ensure the safety of delegates who remain in the country, Martinez said. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Humanitarian situation in Gaza worsens amid political deadlock
articles.summary: In war-battered Gaza, heavy rain flooded and damaged thousands of tents. Several people died. Could pressure by Trump's Board of Peace on Israel and Hamas help to ease the humanitarian crisis amid…

image.caption: Torrential rain has exposed the dire humanitarian situation of Gaza's war-battered population amid a political deadlock between Hamas and Israel Image: Abdel Kareem Hana/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: This autumn's heavy rain and falling temperatures are exacerbating the humanitarian situation for civilians in Gaza. Torrential rainfall over the weekend killed at least six people, including children, according to UNICEF. Local authorities said at least 70,000 tents were flooded and more than 200,000 people affected.
"Over the past two days, we have been trying to stabilize our tent with sand and rubble to keep water from seeping inside," Rawan Al-Omari, a mother of two, told DW on the phone.

She and her children share a tent west of Jabalia in northern Gaza. "The entire area around us has turned into mud, so even leaving the tent has become difficult," the 33-year-old said. "Everything is exhausting."
The rain also soaked the tent and everything 45-year-old Radi Amin and his three children own.

"For three consecutive days, we have been trying to dry our clothes while my children were shivering in the cold," he told DW. "Only on Wednesday, with the sun finally out and warm enough, our belongings started to dry."
Amin said that "the heavy rain served as a stark reminder of our truly dire state."

Aid teams meanwhile have started to clear blocked sewer lines and stormwater basins at 60 locations, benefiting an estimated 30,000 families, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported on Wednesday.

However, OCHA's humanitarian partners also warned that there is not enough space to relocate people living in flooded areas or war-damaged buildings. "Israeli authorities are restricting Palestinian access anywhere behind the so-called 'Yellow Line,' which means that most of Gaza's land remains off limit," OCHA said.

Following the Hamas terror attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023, the ensuing war in Gaza has destroyed most of Gaza's infrastructure and housing. More than 74,600 people were killed in the Gaza Strip, according to figures from Gaza's Health Ministry. Israel controls about two-thirds of the territory, which is marked by a military demarcation line, the so-called Yellow Line.

Hamas continues to exercise governing authority in much of the remaining territory close to the Mediterranean Sea, where most of Gaza's roughly 2 million residents live. Most of them have been displaced several times and live in tents, camps for displaced people or in houses that are deemed unsafe. Hamas is classified as a terrorist organization by Germany, the EU, the United States and others.

blocks.caption: Despite the nominal ceasefire from October 2025, Israel keeps targeting alleged Hamas members in Gaza, like here at the Nasser Medical Complex Image: Ramzi Abu Amer/JNA/ZUMA/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Reconstruction stalls amid Hamas-Israel deadlock over disarmament and Israeli presence in Gaza

As part of the US-brokered ceasefire in October 2025, US President Donald Trump established the Board of Peace (BoP) committee to oversee the ceasefire's implementation as well as Gaza's postwar governance and reconstruction. According to a joint assessment by the World Bank, United Nations and European Union published in April 2026,Gaza's recovery and reconstruction will require an estimated $71.4 billion (€64.2 billion) over the next decade.

However, little progress has been made as negotiators have been failing to agree on terms for Hamas to disarm and for Israel to withdraw its troops from the territory. Despite the ceasefire, Israel continues to carry out airstrikes on Gaza. On Thursday, Israel carried out a strike on Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis against alleged Hamas members.
For Nathan Brown, a professor of political science and international affairs at George Washington University in the US, the current rainfall exemplifies the deadlock of Trump's peace plan for Gaza.

"The failure of the Board of Peace to advance reconstruction, or even secure reliable relief, is fundamentally due to Israeli objections based on the insistence that Hamas has to completely disarm first," he told DW.
Until the recent elections in Israel, the Board of Peace showed little interest in challenging that view, Brown added: "Now it is willing to go public, though not in very confrontational terms."

On Monday, the Board of Peace issued a statement saying that Israel's steps to improve the humanitarian situation ahead of the coming winter remain insufficient. "We call on the leadership of the current Government of Israel to act immediately to authorize and facilitate the entry of all necessary winterization and humanitarian supplies."

Israel's Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT) said the same day that among other equipment, 12 sewage vacuum trucks for the International Committee of the Red Cross arrived in Gaza and that 91,000 tents and more than 8,200 trucks carrying tarpaulins, blankets and winter clothing had entered Gaza in recent months.

In its statement, the Board of Peace also called on Hamas to abide by commitments under the ceasefire, including laying down its weapons and transferring governing authority. Hamas promptly rejected the criticism in a statement and accused Israel of obstructing implementation of the peace plan and withholding urgently needed humanitarian supplies.

The United Nations as well as numerous international agencies have accused Israel of systematically preventing the import of prefabricated shelters into Gaza. The UN said around 150,000 tents were outside Gaza and ready to be dispatched, pending the necessary approvals, a claim Israel rejects.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is serving as caretaker prime minister while a new government is being formed following the October 27 elections, denied that Israel was responsible for the worsening conditions and blamed Hamas instead.
He warned that "as long as Hamas remains in power, it will use every dual-use item entering Gaza to entrench its terror regime and expand its military arsenal."

blocks.caption: Most of Gaza's population lives in shelters, displacement camps or houses that are deemed unsafeImage: Omar Al-Qattaa/AFP

blocks.text: Residents bear the brunt of man-made humanitarian crisis
For Gaza's population, this deadlock amid the approaching winter spells ongoing hardship.

"Children and families are facing devastating conditions, with around 1.2 million people, including more than 560,000 children, living in critical or catastrophic shelter conditions," Ahmad Alhendawi, regional director of the aid organization Save the Children, told DW.
The amount of available winter clothing remains critically insufficient in Gaza, he added.
Gaza's children bear lasting scars three years into war

"As available supplies cover less than 1% of needs, hundreds of thousands of children face the winter without adequate clothing, blankets or heating, leaving them exposed to hypothermia and respiratory illnesses," Alhendawi said.

Furthermore, Nestor Owomuhangi, the UN Population Fund's (UNFPA) representative to Palestine, told DW that around 400,000 people in Gaza continue to live in areas at high risk of flooding, including an estimated 10,000 pregnant women.

"For women and girls already enduring displacement and hunger, the rain threatens their health, safety and dignity," he told DW, adding that "with around 180 babies born every day, mothers and newborns urgently need dry, warm shelter."

articles.title: PH says Code of Conduct talks at 70%, but key provisions need clarification
articles.summary: The negotiations on the proposed Code of Conduct (COC) in the South China Sea are at the clarification stage, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said Friday.

blocks.text: Published November 13, 2026 5:22pm
The negotiations on the proposed Code of Conduct (COC) in the South China Sea are at the clarification stage, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said Friday.

"Our negotiators are at that point where they need to make some clarifications on some of the elements contained in the agreement," Foreign Affairs Assistant Secretary Dominic Xavier Imperial, spokesperson for ASEAN Affairs, said in a press briefing.
Currently, the negotiations are at 70%, with points in the agreement that need to be "refined," the DFA said.

"On the description of what 70%, 30% means, that is actually just a representation of how the progress is going. I did not mean to describe it as the number of paragraphs that were agreed upon," Imperial explained.

"While there are challenges, I would also like to point out that there's a commitment among the parties to be able to finalize whatever they need to finalize and to come to an agreement on some of these issues that they are continuously discussing," he added.
In GMA's Unang Balita interview, Imperial said Manila also wants to ensure that the proposed agreement would not prejudice the rights of third parties or countries that are not part of the COC.
“Gusto rin po natin na yung mga karapatan po ng third parties or yung ibang bansa na hindi part nito ay hindi rin po sila maaagrabyado dito sa agreement na ito,” he said.
(We also want the rights of third parties or other countries that are not part of this agreement not to be aggrieved in this agreement.)
Malacañang said it is still hopeful that the COC would be signed before the Philippines' ASEAN chairmanship ends.
"Bawat araw dapat may pag-asa (we should have hope every day)," Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said.

"Sa ngayon, hindi rin natin masasabi kung talagang hindi ito magkakaroon ng konklusyon sa 49th ASEAN Summit dahil ang gusto pa rin ng Pangulo ay masapinal sa panahon na ang Pilipinas ang ASEAN chair," she added.
(As of now, we cannot say if the COC will be concluded during the 49th ASEAN Summit because President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. wants to finalize it during the Philippines’ chairmanship.) —LDF, GMA News

Editor’s Note: This story was originally published on May 4, 2026, and republished with updates on November 13, 2026.
MANILA, Philippines – All eyes are on the Philippines as it takes on the role of chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in 2026.
This places Manila at the forefront of coordinating priorities across Southeast Asia’s leading multilateral bloc, guiding discussions on regional cooperation, stability, and integration.

Established in 1967, ASEAN was formed to promote regional peace, political stability, and economic cooperation among Southeast Asian countries. The Philippines is one of the five founding members, along with Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand.

articles.title: We tested 6 popular apps to see what data they collect and share. Here’s what we found
articles.summary: Marketplace tested six of the most popular Android and iOS apps in Canada — Tim Hortons, PC Optimum, Weather Network, Facebook, Amazon and YouTube — to find out what data they collect and where it…
articles.byline: Bobby Hristova, Kathleen Coughlin, Rosa Marchitelli

image.caption: Marketplace tested six of the most popular Android and iOS apps in Canada – Tim Hortons, PC Optimum, the Weather Network, Facebook, Amazon and YouTube – to find out what data they collect and where it’s shared. (CBC)

blocks.text: Whether you are buying a coffee, groceries, checking the weather or unwinding with an online video, there’s a free mobile app for just about everything.
But a Marketplace investigation shows the cost of this convenience is your privacy – and the data you’re sharing goes far beyond what you might realize.

Marketplace tested six of the most popular Android and iOS apps in Canada — Tim Hortons, PC Optimum, the Weather Network, Facebook, Amazon and YouTube — to find out what data they collect and where it goes.

To do so, Joel Reardon, an associate professor in the department of computer science, and his team at the University of Calgary scanned the network traffic of the apps on an Android device. Privo, an organization that evaluates apps to ensure they comply with U.S. child privacy laws, also did a scan of the apps on iOS, Apple’s operating system.

While doing scans to see the network traffic of mobile apps on Android, some apps appeared to be sending information to outside companies around the world. The network scan above shows the activity from all the apps on someone’s phone, not necessarily the apps Marketplace tested. (CBC)
In their user policies, the apps we tested explicitly disclose that they collect or share certain data and that when you use the app, you accept their terms.
But Reardon and Celeste Rollason, an independent analyst who used to work with Privo, are concerned some apps collect more than they need and are sharing what they learn with others around the world.
That data ranges from your name and email address to your exact whereabouts.
“To me, this is not the internet we wanted. This is not the internet we deserve. It's turned into a monstrous data collection surveillance system,” Reardon said.
Here’s what we learned about each app we tested, and what you can do to protect your data.
Tim Hortons
(CBC)
The scan showed that the Tim Hortons app appeared to be sending data to third-party companies as soon as you launch it.

Reardon said one overseas third-party company built into the app appeared to be receiving enough information to create the equivalent of a digital fingerprint for each device, so it can be identified in the future.
“This was beyond the pale,” he said.
Some of those details include:

items: The name given to the device (for example, Bob’s iPhone).
An identifier unique to the device.
A list of many of the sensors on the device.
The details of the device’s camera (for example, the size of your lens).
The names of the ringtones and alarm sounds used.
The names of Wi-Fi routers near you, which Reardon said can be used to determine your location.

blocks.text: Rollason said the third party brands itself as a fraud protection service. She noted the amount of data collected “seems quite excessive” to validate the purchase of a cup of coffee.
Marketplace isn’t identifying any of the third-party companies or their locations because accountability rests with the app developer.

In a statement, Tim Hortons’ director of communications Michael Oliveira said this third party only collects this information for “fraud prevention, account protection, and payment abuse prevention, not for marketing or advertising … or to work around guests’ choices regarding those activities.”
Oliveira said the information collected can help detect if a never-before-seen device is being used on a customer’s account or if a “threat actor” is pretending to be a customer.
He also said the third party is not allowed to sell the data and that Tim Hortons does not sell users’ personal information to third-party companies or data brokers.
PC Optimum

The test showed the PC Optimum app appeared to be sending 10 outside companies information about which products users are searching for — even if the product was sensitive like a search for prenatal vitamins.
One third-party company appeared to be receiving a user’s latitude and longitude and an identifier unique to the device.
The scan also showed the app sending different details to an overseas third-party including:

items: The first name of the user.
Their unredacted email address.
Their PC Optimum member number.
An identifier unique to the device.
How the user interacts with the app, like when they open the app and what they do in the app.

blocks.text: Reardon and Rollason said the data collection seemed to be more than what was necessary for the app to work properly. Based on their experience, they say they didn’t understand why the app needed 10 outside companies to know what users were searching for.
In a statement, Loblaw, the company behind PC Optimum, said the company has never sold personal information and continually reviews and strengthens its systems to protect people.
It said the information collected through Loblaw apps supports everyday features for customers such as shopping online and finding nearby stores.
The Weather Network
The scan showed that when users allowed the Weather Network app access to their location, it appeared to be sending a third-party company those details for targeted advertising, including:

items: A user's precise latitude and longitude.
The user’s local weather conditions.
The device’s advertising ID (unique to each device).

blocks.text: Reardon said it could allow the app to send you advertisements based on where you are or “so you could get ads for a rainy day.”
He also noted it creates a “location history, because all of [the data sent] are bridged by this one thing that doesn't change — this device identifier.”
Rollason said understanding a user’s behaviours is key to advertisers.
“Are you using your phone more when it's raining or you're in the house, perhaps, versus going out on a nice day?” she said.

Pelmorex, the parent company of the Weather Network, said in a statement that the Weather Network does not sell any user data to third parties and data brokers. It said the app only uses location data when a user allows it and uses that data to provide the local weather and show relevant ads. It also said users can access the weather without giving the app their location.
Facebook

The scan showed when users give the Facebook app access to their camera roll to post one image, the app appeared to collect the metadata of other images and videos on the device that were not uploaded.
Metadata contains details like the name of the file, the date and time it was taken and the camera settings.
For whatever image or video is actually posted to Facebook, the scan appeared to show the app also collected the latitude and longitude of where the image was taken.
The app also tracked what users do while using Facebook, including every scroll and how long you linger on something.
Reardon and Rollason noted Facebook didn’t appear to share any data with third-party companies during the scan.

Meta, the parent company of Facebook, had no comment on Marketplace’s findings; however, its privacy policy does state it collects this data. The policy also says “we don't sell any of your information to anyone.”
Amazon
The scan showed Amazon appeared to be collecting what users searched for, even if the product was sensitive, along with the device’s advertising ID.
It didn’t show Amazon sending data to any third-party companies during the scan.
“This is to be expected with these very large companies because they have the resources to have their own ad network,” Reardon said.
Amazon said in a statement it never sells customers’ personal data. It also said it designs products and services to “protect their privacy and to put them in control of their experience."
YouTube
The scan didn’t show YouTube sending data to any third-party companies at the time of the test. The data appeared to only be going to the U.S.
Marketplace also tested if YouTube would follow the rules of its parent company, Google, and not play targeted advertising while a user was watching children’s content.
The test found no targeted ads while watching a children’s video.
Google said in a statement it doesn’t sell personal information.
‘You lack total control’
Ann Cavoukian, the former privacy commissioner of Ontario, said Canada’s current privacy laws aren’t strong enough, and the country's privacy commissioners also need to step up.
Speaking generally, she also said companies should be prioritizing people’s privacy by only collecting what they need and deleting data when they don’t need it anymore.
“You lack total control,” Cavoukian said. “It can be used in a variety of unorganized ways. It can come back to haunt you.”
Ann Cavoukian served as the privacy commissioner of Ontario from 1997 to 2014. (CBC)
The Office of the Federal Privacy Commissioner of Canada declined an interview, but a spokesperson said Marketplace’s findings raise “a number of concerns.”

Speaking generally, the office of Canada’s AI Minister Evan Solomon said in a statement that Canadians need privacy protections that “keep pace with changing technology and the ways companies collect, use and share their data.”

His office also noted the government introduced Bill C-36 to give people more control over their information and to force companies to be more transparent and accountable about how they handle people's data. The bill is still before the House of Commons and has received praise and criticism from privacy experts.
How can you protect your data?
Cavoukian said people should ask companies what data is being collected, why it’s being collected and ask that it be deleted as soon as the company doesn’t need it anymore.

Reardon and Rollason said there’s little you can do to stop the transmission of data because apps on your device, and the third parties in those apps, may be sending or collecting information even when your device is out of reach.
They said deleting apps if you’re not using them and only keeping what you need is the best protection.

articles.title: They called her 'Mommy': Vulnerable senior dies after 2 strangers take over her life
articles.summary: Two men moved into an elderly Toronto woman's home and began claiming to be like her sons. She quickly gave them powers of attorney and signed a will, leaving them everything. Then she died.
articles.byline: Krista Hessey, Linda Guerriero, Ioanna Roumeliotis

image.caption: Elton John Rambarrat, left, and Daniel Gopie moved into Dorelia Licorish’s Toronto home and began calling her ‘Mommy.’ She signed a will leaving them everything, then she died. (llustration: Daniel Rofusz/CBC; Photos: TikTok/Daniel Ram, Ousama Farag/CBC, Submitted by Carolyn Garner)

blocks.text: Dorelia Licorish didn't know where she was. Her confusion came after she was asked a simple question by a Toronto judge presiding over a video court hearing last May.
"Are you in Guyana right now?"
Licorish, an 86-year-old Toronto resident who was in the South American country at the time, turned to the two men with her.
"I'm supposed to say yes?"
"Yes," one of them responded.
A provincial agency had gone to court to get legal guardianship over Licorish, arguing she was mentally incapable and the men were taking advantage of her financially.
Back in Canada, members of her family had been searching for Licorish. They called police after they hadn't been able to reach her for weeks and her house looked abandoned.

Less than six months after that call, Licorish died in hospital from an infected bedsore so deep her pelvic bone was exposed. The two men with her in Guyana are living in her Toronto home. Police have laid no charges.
Licorish’s nieces, Susanne Perch, left, and Andrea Phillips-Beckles, right, are seeking answers from police about what happened to their aunt. (Krista Hessey/CBC)

An investigation by CBC's the fifth estate into Licorish's death reveals that even when government agencies and law enforcement are alerted to a case of suspected elder abuse, they can fail to protect the most vulnerable seniors.
Licorish's family believe she was neglected by the men who had moved in as tenants before declaring themselves her caregivers.
"I would like to get justice for her because [the police] didn't take anything seriously at all," said Andrea Phillips-Beckles, Licorish's niece.

items: Watch the full documentary, "The called her 'Mommy,'" from the fifth estate on YouTube or CBC-TV on Friday at 9 p.m.

blocks.text: Mistreatment of older adults is on the rise, experts say, as Canada becomes a "super-aged" country this year, with one in five people aged 65 or older.

While rates of elder abuse are not tracked nationally, a 2022 study by University of Toronto researchers found one in 10 Canadians over age 65 experiences some form of elder abuse — physical, financial or sexual — every year, and racialized and cognitively impaired older adults are at higher risk.

"Dorelia's story is one that's being played out in so many places, among so many individuals each and every day in our country, and this issue is only growing bigger," said Dr. Samir Sinha, director of geriatrics at Sinai Health System and University Health Network in Toronto.
"What's preventing this from happening to you?"
An undated photo of Licorish. (Krista Hessey/CBC)
Beloved auntie

Licorish immigrated to Canada from Barbados in the early 1960s. She was sharp-witted and fiercely independent, her family and friends said. She did not have any children of her own, but after her sister died, raised Phillips-Beckles.
"She was one vibrant, vibrant woman," Phillips-Beckles said.
Licorish worked as a nurse at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health on Queen Street West in Toronto for decades before retiring.
Christiana Egi, Licorish's former nursing colleague and close friend of 35 years, told the fifth estate she noticed Licorish was displaying memory problems as early as 2018.
Remembering a much-loved family member
In early 2024, Licorish told Egi that a married couple, Daniel Gopie and Elton John Rambarrat, had moved into her basement and were helping her around the house.
"I was like, 'I hope this is for real, that something doesn't happen.'"
The first red flags for Licorish's family came in June 2024. Licorish's landline had been disconnected and a second cousin received word the new tenants had said the house was now in their name.
The cousin showed up at Licorish's home on Lawrence Avenue East with police, but Licorish got angry and asked them to leave.
Daniel Gopie, left, Licorish and Elton John Rambarrat in an undated photo. (Submitted by Daniel Gopie)

A month later, she gave Rambarrat and Gopie powers of attorney over her property and personal care — giving them control of her finances and health should she be deemed incapable. Then she signed a will leaving all her assets to them, including her million-dollar Toronto home.

When Phillips-Beckles went to the home in August 2024, she says Licorish didn't immediately recognize her and the men never left her aunt's side. One of the men told her Licorish's will is "bulletproof."
"He started calling her 'Mommy,' and then she said, 'These are my sons from God.' I said, 'No, they're sons from the devil,'" Phillips-Beckles said.
Legal documents in question
In September 2024, Ontario's Office of the Public Guardian and Trustee (OPGT) began looking into the relationship between Licorish and her tenants after receiving a tip from a real estate lawyer.
The OPGT is a provincial agency tasked with safeguarding the interests of mentally incapable Ontarians.
The lawyer told the agency he had been asked to add Rambarrat and Gopie to the title of Licorish's property. He refused after Licorish could not recall the men's names.

In a 120-page affidavit filed in Ontario Court of Justice, the OPGT detailed what allegedly happened after Rambarrat and Gopie moved in. The men said they had met Licorish at her church and she allowed them to live in the basement rent-free in exchange for helping her with shopping and chores.

They began going with Licorish to appointments with her longtime family doctor, court records show. The doctor told the OPGT that after an appointment in September 2024, she asked Licorish about the men and the powers of attorney document they had shown her, Licorish was "very surprised" and didn't remember signing it.
An undated photo of Gopie, left, Licorish and Rambarrat. (Submitted by Daniel Gopie)

Her family doctor wrote she had "concerns with Ms. Licorish's memory" and had booked a mini-mental status exam. However, Rambarrat cancelled the appointment. In medical notes from August 2025, doctors wrote Licorish had a history of dementia but it is unclear when it was first diagnosed.
In an interview with the fifth estate, the men said Licorish did not have dementia and was capable of granting them powers of attorney and creating a will that named them sole beneficiaries.
"The lawyer did the will. She did think it was fine and we didn't see it as a problem; it's something [Licorish] wanted to do," Rambarrat said.
The lawyer, Veena Pohani, told OPGT that while the three had "an unconventional relationship," she did not see signs of abuse and Licorish appeared happy.
Pohani declined to be interviewed for this story, citing client-solicitor privilege.
Rambarrat says lawyer Veena Pohani created the powers of attorney documents and will for Licorish. (veenapohani.com)

While a dementia diagnosis does not necessarily mean someone is incapable, lawyers have a duty to ensure clients have the mental capacity to understand the legal decisions they are making and that they are not being pressured by outside forces, according to the Ontario Law Society.
Pohani told the OPGT Licorish was capable of making these decisions, although no information is included about how she determined that.
Allegations of financial abuse

Banking records submitted in court show a dramatic change in Licorish's spending around the time the men entered her life. Thousands of dollars in ATM cash withdrawals and near-weekly alcohol purchases quickly depleted her modest pension and drove her account into overdraft.

Rambarrat and Gopie were added to Licorish's accounts in early October 2024. They cashed out some of her investments and withdrew money from her line of credit a few weeks before they took Licorish to their home country of Guyana for the first time.
Undated photos of Licorish with Gopie and Rambarrat in Guyana. (Submitted by Daniel Gopie)
Bank staff wrote to OPGT that Licorish told them she "trusts them fully" and the transactions were completed with her consent.
However, about six weeks later, Licorish told OPGT investigators that she was not aware of withdrawals in the thousands.
Rambarrat and Gopie deny using Licorish's money for their own purposes and say they used it for home repairs.
However, when asked by OPGT investigators, they could not provide a receipt.
Family tries to intervene
Over 18 months, Licorish's family members made multiple calls to Toronto police, voicing concerns about the men's relationship with their elderly relative.
Body camera recordings and records obtained through the Freedom of Information Act show police treated multiple reports as "family disputes."
The fifth estate also learned police went to Licorish's house in March 2024, the same month the men allegedly moved in, and noticed she had cognitive issues.

items: Rising number of cases of senior abuse and neglect point to needed changes, says B.C. seniors advocate
Family violence against seniors reaches record high in Canada: StatsCan

blocks.text: Court records also reveal Gopie, who became Licorish's main caregiver, pleaded guilty to two assault charges in 2013 and 2018, unrelated to Licorish. Yet, police took no action to intervene.
Retired Durham police detective Martin Franssen, who specialized in suspected cases of elder abuse and reviewed the OPGT court file, says Licorish's case is "textbook."
He says Gopie's criminal history and Licorish's vulnerable mental state should have alerted officers to look into the situation more.
"This is the future of Canada — based on the changing age demographics — and we have to change our ways."
OPGT goes to court, Licorish goes to Guyana
In October 2024, the OPGT filed a notice in court to remove Rambarrat and Gopie as Licorish's powers of attorney for property and for the agency to take over her financial affairs.
However, seven months passed before OPGT submitted evidence.
By then, the men had taken Licorish to Guyana for a second time. All three attended a virtual court hearing to assign Licorish a lawyer who would be tasked with discerning her wishes.
In the audio recording of the hearing, obtained by the fifth estate, the OPGT's lawyer said the agency went to court "hastily" and did more investigative work after speaking to Pohani.
The lot in New Amsterdam, Guyana, where sources say Rambarrat and Gopie intend to build a house. (Krista Hessey/CBC)
The men told the judge they were in Guyana because they are building a house. They said they brought Licorish with them because they were her caregivers and it wasn't safe for her to be left alone.
The men spoke for Licorish until the judge asked if there was anything she wanted to say.
"I don't want them to leave me," she replied weakly.

Franssen says it is common in predatory relationships involving older adults for the perpetrator to quickly make the victim feel dependent upon them, making it less likely that they will report the abuse.
"If cognition comes into play … they may not even realize it's being done, but they will believe, in a lot of cases I've seen and dealt with, that they have that reliance on that individual."
The fifth estate spoke to several residents who saw and interacted with Licorish while she was in Guyana. Fearing retaliation, CBC News agreed not to identify them.

Multiple sources questioned how well Licorish was being cared for because Gopie would drink heavily, sometimes becoming intoxicated with Licorish. They said the three of them stayed in a dilapidated home where several other people connected to Rambarrat also lived.
Sources say the men and Licorish stayed at this house for weeks alongside several other members of Rambarrat’s family. (Krista Hessey/CBC)
During the trip, Licorish grew too weak to leave the house independently and would be left alone for hours, several sources said.
The men deny this, saying she was on vacation and well-cared for. They say she only visited the rundown home during the day and slept elsewhere.

The fifth estate has learned that when Licorish returned to Canada in July 2025, the lawyer assigned to her at the court hearing was unable to obtain instructions, though there was no explanation as to why.
"We have a system that, as designed, can't act quickly enough," Sinha said. "We don't have the luxury of time in these cases."
Licorish's final months

Upon returning from Guyana, Licorish's mental and physical health had declined, Licorish's friends and family said. She became bedridden after a brief hospitalization in August for a swollen knee and began receiving visits from personal support workers and nurses.

Partial records from the province's home-care agency, Ontario Health atHome, obtained by the fifth estate show Licorish had a pressure injury on her tailbone on Oct. 5, 2025. Nursing notes say the men were not "willing and able" to care for the wound.
The Victorian Order of Nurses, a non-profit nursing agency, was authorized to send someone to tend to the bedsore every three days.

A nurse reported to Ontario Health atHome Rambarrat had assisted him with turning Licorish because she would not allow the male nurse to touch her and he advised Rambarrat to turn Licorish frequently.
That same nurse said on Nov. 5 he requested a specialist to come to look at the wound because it was getting bigger and deeper. However, it's unclear if that occurred.
Licorish was unresponsive when she arrived at Scarborough General Hospital on Nov. 7, 2025. (Submitted by Susanne Perch)
On Nov. 7, 2025, Licorish was rushed to Scarborough General Hospital after a nurse found her unresponsive, medical records show.

She had gone into septic shock, a reaction to an infected Stage 4 bedsore, the most severe rating, that was oozing brown liquid and had a foul smell. Doctors also noted "profound dehydration" and high blood sugar levels.
When asked why he or Gopie did not take Licorish to the hospital sooner, Rambarrat said they deferred to the health-care professionals caring for Licorish.
Both S.R.T.-Med-Staff, the agency sending PSWs to care for Licorish daily, and the Victorian Order of Nurses did not respond to detailed questions, citing privacy laws.
The men, as Licorish's attorneys for personal care, had a legal duty of care to her, retired police detective Franssen said.
"Why didn't you pick up [and call] 911? Why did you need a health-care professional to walk in that day and turn to you and say, 'I suggest you call 911?'"
Licorish died on Nov. 21, 2025, 10 days after the men agreed for her to be moved to palliative care.
Sinha says her death was preventable.
"If she arrived at the hospital sooner, she may still be alive."
Because of her passing, the OPGT's case in court was dismissed.
Police close the case

Licorish's family only found out she was in hospital after a cousin driving by her house saw an ambulance out front. When they became aware of Licorish's condition, they called Toronto police again. This time, they alleged the men neglected Licorish and begged police to investigate.
In May, six months after Licorish's death, Toronto police detectives informed the family they had closed the case.
Toronto police declined interview requests, saying in a statement they conducted a thorough review of the circumstances surrounding Licorish's care, finances and death.

"The investigation included the examination of extensive medical, home care and other records, consultation with multiple parties involved in her care.... Following that investigation, no evidence was identified to support the laying of criminal charges," a media spokesperson wrote.

Multiple members of Licorish's extended family called Toronto Police Service's 43 Division about Rambarrat and Gopie's relationship with their elderly aunt. They accuse the police of not taking their concerns seriously. (Ousama Farag/CBC)
Family members are in the process of contesting Licorish's will, arguing she wasn't mentally capable at the time of signing.
Rambarrat and Gopie say Licorish's family did not care for her and they are entitled to her house.
"I'm obligated to get something," Gopie said in an interview. "Does nobody come and clean her piss? Clean her shit? Do anything for her?"
Phillips-Beckles has a binder of files and contacts she's been collecting as she tries to piece together what happened to her aunt.
"I can't wrap my head around it at all, that she's gone and how she went," she said. "She shouldn't have gone that way."
