articles.title: Countries vulnerable to climate disaster push for faster, easier access to finance at COP31
articles.summary: Developing countries want to make finance for climate adaptation and disaster relief a top priority at the COP31 summit in Turkey in light of the recent devastating floods in Nepal — a tragedy that…

image.caption: A house damaged by the catastrophic flooding of the Trishuli River in Nepal, pictured Sept. 7. The country is facing billions of dollars in damages from the disaster that could push it further into debt. (Niranjan Shrestha/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Science·New

Developing countries want to make finance for climate adaptation and disaster relief a top priority at the COP31 summit in Turkey in light of the recent devastating floods in Nepal — a tragedy that has laid bare the inadequacy of current programs, experts say.
Disaster and adaptation programs underfunded and slow to access, experts say
A group of African countries succeeded on Monday to put financial commitments on the agenda of the UN climate negotiations in Antalya, which run through Nov. 20.

They say they're seeking a measure of justice at the talks, as smaller, more vulnerable nations suffer the impact of climate change despite their relatively low emissions — and action is urgently needed as the UN now expects the world to overshoot the 1.5 C global warming target set by the 2015 Paris Agreement.

Several finance-related proposals are on the table, including measures like a "debt pause clause" that could help countries in the aftermath of climate disasters, and more funding to help compensate countries that suffer damage to their infrastructure, culture and economy.

items: UN countries agree on legal obligation to address climate change

blocks.text: Developing countries, who need loans and grants to fund climate-related measures, also want a clearer and faster process for spending the billions of dollars that have already been pledged by richer donor nations like Canada.
Nepal gets UN damage fund's first payout
Sagar Dhakal, a member of Nepal’s delegation to the summit, said the "whole world" recently saw what climate change means to his country in the Himalayas.

“Within 10 minutes, we have lost roughly more than 7,000 people,” said Dhakal, referring to the devastating flash floods caused by a collapsed glacier that swept down the Trishuli River north of Kathmandu in August.
More than 1,450 people have been confirmed dead and almost another 5,300 remain missing due to the floods, which destroyed towns and cost billions in damages.

In response last month, the UN’s Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage — created three years ago to compensate developing countries for climate-related losses — made its first payout, earmarking $21.6 million US for Nepal.
But that sum only shows how underfunded the program is, says Sasha Jattansingh, loss and damage expert at Climate Analytics, a Caribbean research organization.
Why you can’t predict a disaster like Nepal’s flood | About That
“This first step shows the fund can act quickly and be responsive. However, $21.6 million covers less than one per cent of the actual loss and damage estimated for Nepal,” Jattansingh said.

Nepal is one of 119 countries that have applied for money from the fund, requesting a total of about $2.8 billion US. Donor countries have pledged about $822 million US to the fund so far, but have paid in roughly half of that.
LISTEN | Nepal's flood and climate change:
What on Earth?26:23The disaster in Nepal as a ‘wake-up call from Mother Nature’
Harjeet Singh, a climate finance campaigner based in India, is running a campaign called Fill the Fund to push donor countries, including Canada, to pledge and pay more.
“It's like we've got a fire station, but not enough water to put out the fire,” said Singh, who also believes the UN's loss and damage fund needs to respond faster.

He told CBC’s What On Earth it took about seven weeks for the fund to hold a board meeting and decide to earmark the money for Nepal. The money has still not been paid out, Singh adds — that’s a further process involving applications for specific projects.
Climate finance campaigner Harjeet Singh at a rally during a UN climate summit in Dubai in December 2023. (Amr Alfiky/Reuters)
Call for faster funding approval
There’s also a push to speed up other forms of climate finance at COP31.

Representatives of vulnerable countries, such as low-income and small island nations, want an easier process for accessing funding for adaptation and mitigation projects, which they say can be tedious and technical — a difficult lift for countries with smaller government bureaucracies.

Singh pointed out that Nepal applied to the UN’s Green Climate Fund (GCF) — which finances climate-related projects in developing countries and is backed by about $87 billion US — to fund a flood-protection project about eight years ago, and it took seven years for approval.
That’s clearly too slow to help countries like Nepal prepare for just the kind of flooding it suffered, he says.
“They could not even start acting on that project and they were hit by this disaster,” Singh said.
Negotiations at COP31 will aim to put pressure on the GCF, donor countries and other funders to make it much faster and easier for developing countries to access that money.
An aerial photo taken Aug. 26 shows some of the devastation caused by the flash floods in Nepal. (Navesh Chitrakar/Reuters)
Nepal’s experience is also showing the growing need for debt relief, experts say.
Developing countries are forced to borrow money to help adapt to climate change and rebuild after disasters.
That’s what Nepal had to do after a devastating earthquake in 2015 left thousands dead and hundreds of thousands homeless across the country.
From 2015 to 2023, Nepal's debt to other countries and multilateral lenders went from about $4 billion US to over $10 billion US, in part to fund post-quake relief and development.
In 2027, Nepal will owe about $400 million US to service its loans to the World Bank and Asian Development Bank — money that should be used for rebuilding instead, experts say.

items: Canada's credibility on the line at COP31 as it defends fossil fuel expansion while trumpeting clean energy

blocks.text: The country is a perfect example of a developing nation that is going deeper and deeper into debt because of the frequency of climate disasters, said Ritu Bharadwaj, a climate finance expert at the International Institute for Environment and Development in London.
“Nepal has been in the state of constant rebuilding,” she said.

While proposals to temporarily pause the debt of vulnerable countries is important, what’s more helpful, Bharadwaj says, is to “assess how much debt has been accumulated because of climatic disasters and, instead of servicing the debt, allow them to use [that money] for reconstruction.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Inayat Singh covers the environment and climate change at CBC News. He is based in Toronto and has previously reported from Winnipeg. Email: inayat.singh@cbc.ca

articles.title: Ex Ottawa Uber driver admits to giving 12-year-old girl 'secret admirer' candy, prowling house after delivery
articles.summary: A 45-year-old former Uber Eats delivery driver has pleaded guilty to harassing a 12-year-old girl with "secret admirer" messages and candy, as well as prowling her home at night, after he met her…

image.caption: An Uber sokesperson said the former driver's behaviour was 'unacceptable and has no place on the Uber platform.' The company said it removed the man's access to the Uber app as soon as it learned of the incidents. (CBC)

blocks.text: Ottawa·New

A 45-year-old former Uber Eats delivery driver has pleaded guilty to harassing a 12-year-old girl with "secret admirer" messages and candy, as well as prowling her home at night, after he met her while dropping off an order she had placed.
Adam Daniels of Ottawa turned himself in after recognizing himself on social media

Adam Daniels sat hunched forward and looking down at the floor in the glass-walled prisoner's box of an Ottawa courtroom on Tuesday, as a Crown prosecutor read out an agreed statement of facts against him.

The 12-year-old girl was having a sleepover with a friend on Aug. 4, the Crown said, when at 2 a.m. they placed an order for Wendy's desserts called Frosties. Daniels was working for Uber Eats that night and made the delivery to the girl's home in Kanata.
At her door, Daniels told the 12-year-old she appeared "very mature," the Crown said. (The girl cannot be identified due to a routine publication ban.)

At 4 a.m. that same morning, the girl noticed a paper bag had been left at the front door. It was addressed to her from a "secret admirer." Her mother thought a friend of the girl might be playing a prank on her and installed a security camera the next day, the Crown told court.
'I f--ked up,' Daniels told brother

On Aug. 16, another brown paper bag was discovered at the front door — this one containing $20, more candy and Daniels's phone number. When the girl's mother checked the new security camera's footage, the girl immediately recognized the man who dropped off the bag as the Uber driver who had delivered the Frosties the night of the sleepover, the Crown told court.

The girl's mother contacted Ottawa police and told the story to CTV News to warn the public. Meanwhile, the 12-year-old girl felt unsafe at the home she shared with her mother and opted to move in with her father, the Crown said.

Court heard Tuesday that Daniels recognized himself in surveillance footage on social media, called his estranged brother about it and told him, "I f--ked up." Thinking he was wanted on a warrant, he turned himself in to police and was arrested Oct. 2.

"This behaviour is unacceptable and has no place on the Uber platform," an Uber spokesperson told CBC in an email Thursday. "We take reports like this extremely seriously, and as soon as it was reported, the delivery person's access to the app was removed."
After Daniels pleaded guilty Tuesday, his defence lawyer requested a pre-sentence report, a document written by a probation officer to give the judge more information about Daniels.
Psychiatric assessment ordered
Ontario Court Justice Norm Boxall granted the request for the report, and asked counsel whether a psychiatric assessment and/or sexual behaviour assessment might be warranted to learn more.
"He's 45 years old, she's 12, he's leaving these notes," Boxall said. "There's something not working."
The defence lawyer told the judge that Daniels had spent time in rehab for drug addiction prior to being arrested. She said she didn't want to ask for a sexual behaviour assessment for her client.
In the end, Boxall ordered a psychiatric assessment in addition to the pre-sentence report.
"You can't change what's happened, but we want to know what happened so it doesn't happen again," Boxall said, addressing Daniels directly.
"OK, I understand," Daniels replied.
Daniels remains in jail after his Tuesday guilty pleas and is next set to appear in court in the new year. His defence lawyer declined to identify herself and declined to comment.

articles.title: Your genes could change your prescription. So why aren't doctors testing?
articles.summary: One in four people has been prescribed a drug for which their genetics could affect treatment, according to a recent study. Genetic testing could help doctors choose safer, more effective drugs, but…

image.caption: Genetic differences can affect how patients respond to common medications, including drugs used to treat heartburn and high cholesterol. Researchers say DNA testing could help doctors tailor prescriptions to individual patients. (Yves Herman/Reuters)

blocks.text: Health

One in four people has been prescribed a drug for which their genetics could affect treatment, according to a recent study. Genetic testing could help doctors choose safer, more effective drugs, but cost and other barriers currently limit its routine use in Canada, researchers say.
New study finds nearly 1 in 4 participants had taken medication potentially affected by their genes
One of the clues your doctor may be missing when prescribing medication is in your DNA.

A study published Wednesday in Science Translational Medicine found that nearly one in four participants had been prescribed a medication that could have required a different drug or dose based on their genetics.
The study, led by researchers at the University of Pittsburgh, examined 16 genes that affect how the body responds to medications.
DNA samples from 98,590 people in the National Institutes of Health's All of Us Research Program were analyzed and linked to participants' medical records when available.

Each carried at least one relevant genetic variation that could affect how their body responds to certain medications, with a typical participant carrying nine. Among those with both genetic and clinical data, 24.4 per cent had been prescribed at least one medication that, based on their genes, guidelines suggest should have been replaced with another drug or given a different dose.
However, the study did not determine whether patients experienced side effects or whether their medications were less effective because of their genetic makeup.

The study's senior author, Dr. Philip Empey, an associate professor at the University of Pittsburgh school of pharmacy, says knowing a patient's genetic profile could help reduce the trial and error of medicine.
"I think anything we can do to better predict the first time, what the best medicines should be, what the best dose should be, the more we can reduce that trial and error," he said.

A pharmacist sorts medications at a pharmacy in Vancouver in October 2022. Genetic variations can affect how patients respond to certain medications, potentially requiring doctors to adjust the dose or prescribe an alternative drug. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)
Finding the right medication

Omeprazole and pantoprazole for acid reflux and atorvastatin for cholesterol were among the most common medications prescribed to participants with genetic profiles that could call for changes in treatment.
Empey says some genetic variations can increase the risk of muscle problems when patients take statins like atorvastatin, which are used to reduce the risk of heart attack or stroke.
This knowledge could help doctors choose another drug or to adjust treatment.

"It allows the clinicians to make better decisions, to say, 'Well, maybe not that cholesterol medicine. Maybe we start slower. Maybe there's a maximum dose. Maybe we watch for specific toxicities more aggressively,'" Empey said.
For some medications, the consequences can be more serious.

For example, experts interviewed by CBC News say genetic testing can help identify patients who are unlikely to respond well to clopidogrel (Plavix), a drug used to prevent blood clots after cardiac stenting, allowing doctors to treat them with a different medication.

Dr. James Kennedy is head of the Tanenbaum Centre for Pharmacogenetics at Toronto's Centre for Addiction and Mental Health. He says genetic testing can help doctors choose medications, but other factors, including diet, lifestyle and medications a patient is already taking, must also be considered. (CBC)
A blueprint, not a guarantee

The study's results were not surprising, says Dr. James Kennedy, head of the Tanenbaum Centre for Pharmacogenetics at Toronto's Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (CAMH), but he was particularly impressed by its genetic diversity and representation of people of African ancestry.
Kennedy says his team has provided genetic testing for approximately 11,000 patients, many of whom had already tried two or three antidepressants without satisfactory results.
About eight to 10 per cent of people break down certain commonly prescribed antidepressants unusually slowly, allowing the medication to accumulate and potentially cause side-effects, he says.
Kennedy says genetic testing is especially useful for patients who may have already struggled with several medications.

However, DNA testing alone will not predict how a patient will respond to a given medication, he said. Other medications the patient is taking, whether they smoke and their diet must also be taken into consideration.
"We say, 'OK, here's your blueprint, here's some tendencies you have, and now here's a discussion of all the other things you have to consider before you make a final decision,'" he said.

A 2023 European clinical trial cited in the study found that genetic testing before prescribing certain medications reduced adverse drug reactions. But making such testing routine in Canada remains a challenge.

A researcher at the University of Calgary holds a diagnostic kit used to identify genetic variations in February 2024. While such testing could help doctors tailor medications to individual patients, cost and practical challenges have limited its widespread use in Canada. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)
Why Canada isn't testing everyone

Toronto cardiologist Dr. Jacob Udell says the study was impressive, particularly given the genetic diversity of its participants, but few clinicians in Canada or the U.S. routinely screen patients for genetic variations to understand how they might metabolize medications.
"It's certainly not on the front-line clinicians' radar to do this," he said.

Udell says that for many conditions, a doctor can prescribe a medication, monitor the patient's response and make adjustments as necessary, usually without serious consequences. That approach can be more practical than routinely screening patients for genetic variations.
He also questions whether widespread testing should be a priority when Canada's health-care system is struggling to provide more basic services.
"We're just trying to get everyone a family doctor," he said.
In addition to the costs of the tests, Udell says clinicians would need access to the results of genetic tests and the expertise to interpret them.
Empey agreed that making genetic testing routine would require significant investment in training, infrastructure and new systems to share results between health-care providers.
"The science is strong for many medicines. The question about implementation then becomes more economic, more process-oriented and more education-oriented," he said.
For now, Empey says patients can ask their doctor or pharmacist whether genetic testing would be useful and share any results with them.
Udell warned that private testing may become more common for patients who can afford to pay for it, "but that won't help those who can't afford the testing."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Eric Michael Johnson is a senior writer and editor based in Vancouver. Before joining CBC, he was an award-winning science writer and editor. He holds a PhD in the history of science from the University of British Columbia. He can be reached at eric.johnson@cbc.ca.
With files from Christine Birak and Amina Zafar

articles.title: Leaders meet in Dublin amid search for lead EU negotiator for peace talks with Russia - Europe live
articles.summary:
Ukraine and Russia have agreed to expand next round of negotiations to include European countries

in Dublin

EU leaders will continue talks on their diplomatic and…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 9m agoEurope needs to be included in Ukraine talks 'to safeguard our interests,' EU's von der Leyen says
40m agoEU leaders meet in Dublin to talk Ukraine, AI

blocks.text: Estonian prime minister Kristen Michal has warned that Ukraine faces “winter … like hell again,” with Russia “bombing everything” as he urged European leaders to double down on their backing for Kyiv.

blocks.caption: Estonian PM Kristen Michal speaking to the media ahead of a meeting of the EU Council at the Convention Centre Dublin. Photograph: Liam McBurney/PA

blocks.text: “Putin has to change his goals because the war, aggression, and killing of women, children, and civilians would stop right now if he gave an order.”
He added:
“The European plan for a while [has been] quite simple: help Ukraine push Russia and so should it be.”
Michal warned that Putin’s attempt to discuss the broader European security architecture before agreeing to end the war is “a mental trap” by Russia’s Putin.

“Does anybody really think that Europe is a threat to Russia? This is not sane talk to be honest. So, I would say that our red line is quite clear: we should have peace, on Ukraine’s terms, and after that everything can be talked, but not before and not at the same time.”
The Estonian PM also said that if the EU needs to send its negotiators, the European Council president António Costa and EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas are “the persons to do it”.
Europe needs to be included in Ukraine talks 'to safeguard our interests,' EU's von der Leyen says

European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen insisted it is “self-explanatory” that Europe should be included in the peace talks on Ukraine “to safeguard our interests, but also to support Ukraine.”

blocks.caption: European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen speaks to the media on the day of an informal EU leaders' meeting focused on artificial intelligence in Dublin, Ireland. Photograph: Natalia Campos/Reuters

blocks.text: “We will come forward as a commission with a proposal for the financing of the Ukrainian needs in 2027, and with the 22nd sanctions package before the next European Council,” she said.
von der Leyen also said today’s talks would focus on “the risks … but also the opportunities’ associated with the rise of AI.

blocks.caption: Jennifer Rankin

blocks.text: Jennifer Rankin
in Dublin
EU leaders will continue talks on their diplomatic and financial support for Ukraine today, after Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged them to “pay attention” to Vladimir Putin’s demands on security.

blocks.caption: Meeting on Ukraine on the sidelines of the Dublin summit. Photograph: dts News Agency Germany/Shutterstock

blocks.text: European leaders meeting in Dublin on Thursday rejected calls that there was any need to recreate a European security architecture, while restating that Russia needed to stop attacking Ukraine.
European Council president António Costa summed it up:
“There is no need to reinvent the wheel. Europe had a functioning European security architecture until it was first, gradually undermined, and ultimately destroyed by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.”
Speaking to reporters the UK prime minister Andy Burnham said Europe “in the wider sense” i.e not just the EU, would decide on its own arrangements.

“In terms of the wider point, there was a very strong feeling that you know, Russian demands to put the question of European security architecture or European security arrangements into this negotiation – that is not up for negotiation... It is for Europe to decide its own arrangements. Europe and Europe alone. And again, I am talking in the wider sense when I say that.”

Around 40 countries, most of the attendees of the European Political Community summit on Thursday, signed a declaration drafted by France declaring that European states “bear a primary responsibility and are assuming greater responsibility for the security of Europe”.

EU leaders are continuing talks in Dublin on Friday, focusing on AI. But following interventions from Giorgia Meloni and Friedrich Merz, they will also discuss Europe’s role in international peace talks and the question of future financial support for Ukraine.
EU leaders meet in Dublin to talk Ukraine, AI

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa
EU leaders are meeting in Dublin today for discussions on Ukraine and AI, among others, as they continue their search for a lead EU negotiator in any peace talks with Russia.

blocks.caption: President of France Emmanuel Macron looks on during the Ukraine security meeting at the European Political Community in Dublin. Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/Reuters

blocks.text: Their discussions are becoming increasingly urgent, after Ukraine and Russia have agreed to expand the next round of peace negotiations to include European countries, US envoy Jared Kushner said last night after meeting Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Dublin.

blocks.caption: Ukraine's president Volodymyr Zelenskyy flanked by US envoys, president Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and businessman Steve Witkoff. Photograph: Paul Faith/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “This will allow us to address the broader postwar European security arrangements alongside the territorial issues between Ukraine and Russia,” Kushner ​said ​later on X.
But, as he somewhat mockingly said on Wednesday,
“If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiations.”
Ouch.
Let’s see what comes out of these discussions, with the leaders also expected to talk about AI.
Elsewhere, I am still keeping an eye on the Dutch government crisis as Rob Jetten works hard to avoid the collapse of his minority cabinet.
It’s Friday, 13 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

The budget committee in the Bundestag worked into the night to sign off on next year's spending plans. These include levels of new debt only eclipsed once, at the height of the COVID pandemic. DW has more.

blocks.text: What you need to know

items: Lawmakers on the Bundestag budget committee worked into the night on late revisions to the 2027 budget
It includes the second-highest amount of borrowing in modern German history
The only budget richer in new debt was 2021's, at the height of the COVID pandemic
New insolvency figures for August, more than 2,000 companies applied for protection

blocks.text: Follow our collection of news and analysis on stories from or relating to Germany on Friday, November 13.
November 13, 2026
Budget committee concludes marathon session on 2027 spending plans

Politicians in the Bundestag budget committee burned the proverbial candle at heading into Friday morning, trying to finalize details of the federal government's spending plans for 2027 before the year's end.

The session took more than 15 hours, and already politicians are talking about areas where they still see room for further improvement or alteration — but the document does at least stand in such a form where it can take effect without too many complications.
Including all spending plans, in the core budget and from the so-called "special funds" for infrastructure and military modernization, new debt constitutes around a third of total spending plans.
In total, the plan is to take out new debt worth just over €210 billion ($233 billion), while taking in a little less than €400 billion in taxes.

That's the second-highest level of new debt in the post-war history of the Federal Republic of Germany. Even at the height of the COVID pandemic in 2021, new debt was only slightly higher, at €215.4 billion.
We'll break down more of the details and cover some of the reactions in later posts.

articles.title: Storm Charles causes floods and flight cancellations across southern Europe
articles.summary:
Heavy rain and strong winds have also caused disruption across British Columbia, Canada, over the last week

Storm Charles has brought destructive weather to the Iberian peninusla this week,…
articles.byline: Ed Walton and Alice Nightingale-Smith for MetDesk

blocks.text: Storm Charles has brought destructive weather to the Iberian peninusla this week, particularly in Portugal and the far south of Spain. Heavy rain and strong south-westerly winds arrived first in the Portuguese island of Madeira, before the system headed towards the mainland on 11 November. A wind gust of 84.5mph (136 km/h) was recorded at Funchal airport, alongside rainfall totals reaching 355mm in 12 hours. Lisbon saw 183 flights cancelled on Wednesday, around a third of its normal daily traffic, while Madrid Barajas airport had 155 cancellations.

After causing widespread flooding in Spain and Portugal, the system moved on a north-easterly track through southern France and then towards northern Italy. This resulted in significant flooding in parts of Cannes, some of which caused rock falls and led to the closure of roads along the French Riviera. The Italian weather service issued a red rainfall warning, its highest level, for the area extending from Tuscany to Venezia. Further heavy rain is expected to fall in Italy and the Balkans over the next few days, with the latest forecast models indicating an additional 100mm could accumulate widely, while totals close to 200mm are likely in more mountainous areas.

blocks.caption: Waves crash into a fort near Estoril as Storm Charles hits mainland Portugal. Photograph: Zed Jameson/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Successive rounds of heavy rain and strong winds have caused flooding, landslides and disruption across British Columbia, Canada through the last week or so.

Between Monday and Friday last week, severe rainfall and strong winds left more than 400,000 customers without power in British Columbia. These unsettled conditions continued into the weekend, with further heavy rain leaving 135,000 customers without power, alongside downed trees, flooded roads and landslides. Strong winds were also recorded on Sunday, with a gust of 72.1mph (116 km/h) on Herbert Island and a gust of 60mph (96 km/h) at Victoria international airport.

Heavy rain warnings were then issued on Wednesday for British Columbia’s Vancouver Island and southern coastal areas as multiple stations recorded rainfall totals in excess of 100mm. Additionally, the River Forecast Centre issued flood warnings on Wednesday across the south coast with heavy rain and high streamflow continuing to bring an increased risk of flash flooding and landslides.

A further area of low pressure is expected to bring torrential rain and strong winds across this same region over the weekend. More than 100mm is likely across central and southern parts of Vancouver Island on Saturday, with gusts in excess of 60mph likely too.

articles.title: OCTA Research rejects bias claims over Leni-Sara surveys, cites Duterte's lead
articles.summary: OCTA Research has rejected claims that its hypothetical 2028 election surveys were rigged to favor Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo.

blocks.text: November 13, 2026 | 4:48pm
Combination photo shows Vice President Sara Duterte and Naga City Mayor Leni Robredon
Inday Sara Duterte via Facebook and AFP

MANILA, Philippines — OCTA Research defended the methodology and findings of its hypothetical 2028 election surveys on Friday, November 13, amid criticism that they were rigged to favor Naga City Mayor Leni Robredo.
The polling firm said its head-to-head and tandem matchups measure different voter preferences from surveys that present respondents with longer lists of potential candidates.
"These questions measure different things and produce different numbers. Trends can be read reliably only within a single survey series," OCTA said in a statement.
It also rejected suggestions of political bias, noting that Vice President Sara Duterte had led every hypothetical head-to-head matchup OCTA conducted in 2026.

What the surveys show. OCTA said its surveys showed no statistically significant decline in Robredo's support, which moved from 35% in March to 34% in July and 33% in its September 28 to October 4 survey.
The changes fell within its national margin of error of ±3 percentage points and did not establish a downward trend, it said.
By contrast, Duterte's share fell from 46% to 40%, a change OCTA said it had previously reported.
Suggesting a parallel survey with similar findings, OCTA cited Pulse Asia figures showing Robredo's share rising from about 13% in February and March 2026 to 26% in September.
In doing so, the polling firm cautioned against directly comparing the two organizations' results because of differences in their survey designs.
"The column compares figures from different survey firms, taken at different times and with different questions," OCTA Research said. "The column's own sources do not support its conclusion."

The firm pointed out that its surveys measured hypothetical election scenarios, not actual candidacies or declared political tickets. Its reports also disclosed Robredo's statements that she would not run in 2028.
Political bias?

To counter allegations of political bias, OCTA pointed to its latest surveys showing President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.'s trust and performance ratings falling to their lowest levels in the firm's series.
"A firm serving any camp would not publish these results. OCTA serves neither the administration nor Mayor Robredo. OCTA serves no camp," it said.
OCTA maintained that its Tugon ng Masa surveys were not commissioned by political groups and were released as a public service.

It also cited its election polling record, saying its final pre-election survey in 2022 closely reflected the results, while its April 2025 survey included all 12 eventual Senate winners among its probable winners.
Response to criticism. The statement followed a November 11 newspaper column alleging that OCTA's surveys were flawed and favored Robredo.
OCTA said the columnist had compared polls conducted at different times and using different methods without identifying specific errors in its sampling, fieldwork or data.
"Cherry-picking is not analysis," the firm said.
OCTA said it issued the statement partly because the column was being circulated online in what it described as an effort to discredit its work.
"We always encourage scrutiny by our media partners. But we ask that it be fair and accurate," it said.
The firm urged the public to examine published reports and technical details when assessing the validity of survey findings.

articles.title: Huang exit, US scrutiny imperil $3 billion in Chinese AI projects reliant on Nvidia
articles.summary: The projects reveal the scale of continuing demand for Nvidia hardware even as Washington seeks to curb Beijing's access to the technology powering the global AI boom

blocks.text: NVIDIA AND CHINA. The Nvidia logo and Chinese flag are seen in this illustration taken August 27, 2025.
Dado Ruvic/Reuters
The projects reveal the scale of continuing demand for Nvidia hardware even as Washington seeks to curb Beijing's access to the technology powering the global AI boom

items: Nvidia claims US export controls have excluded it from China's AI data-center market, yet over $3 billion in Chinese projects utilizing its restricted processors have been identified.

A review found that Nvidia technology is still deeply embedded in various Chinese sectors, including local government ventures and universities, despite the company's market share in China dropping to zero.
The ongoing demand for Nvidia's technology raises concerns for Washington, as export controls tighten and scrutiny increases following the resignation of Nvidia's co-founder amid a scandal.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

BEIJING, China – Nvidia has said US export controls have effectively shut it out of China’s AI data-center market, but a Reuters review has identified more than $3 billion in Chinese computing projects built around the American chipmaker’s restricted processors.

The projects, stretching from China’s wealthy coastal technology hubs to remote western provinces, reveal the scale of continuing demand for Nvidia hardware even as Washington seeks to curb Beijing’s access to the technology powering the global artificial-intelligence boom.

The Reuters review examined more than 150 Chinese procurement notices, investment plans, construction contracts and corporate disclosures, identifying projects and equipment agreements with a combined reported value exceeding 23 billion yuan ($3.2 billion).

The findings paint a detailed picture of how deeply Nvidia technology remains embedded in China’s AI expansion. They reveal the company’s technology reaches well beyond China’s largest tech firms, into local government-backed ventures, universities and regional computing centres.

The estimate includes planned investments and signed contracts as well as completed installations. It covers buildings, power systems and other infrastructure, and does not reflect spending on Nvidia chips alone.
China’s commerce ministry and Nvidia did not immedietely respond to Reuters request for comment.

The findings come a day after Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive amid a scandal over his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman suspected by US authorities of intelligence ties to Beijing.

Huang, a vocal advocate of easing export restrictions, said last year Nvidia’s market share in China had fallen from 95% to zero. The company has also excluded China data-center computing revenue from its forecasts, citing regulatory uncertainty.

That does not mean Chinese demand has disappeared. While Nvidia’s statements address its own ability to compete and sell directly in China, the documents Reuters reviewed show Chinese customers continuing to plan purchases and, in some cases, operating restricted processors.

Sunny Cheung, an analyst at the Washington-based Jamestown Foundation, said Reuters’ findings reinforce his own view on enforcement: “Washington must stop focusing solely on who buys the chips on the surface and start examining who ultimately uses the computing power—and for what purpose.”

Across China, developers and institutions are advancing billions of dollars in AI data-centre projects designed around restricted Nvidia H100, H200, and H800 processors. These range from massive regional computing hubs to retrofitted commercial sites — such as a facility in northwestern Gansu province that was expected to install thousands of Nvidia chips before year-end, though it remains unclear if those processors ever arrived.

While some facilities are already operational or under construction, operators are exposed to potential delays, supply disruptions, or costly redesigns around domestic chips as export controls tighten.
Huang’s departure could deepen these vulnerabilities by weakening Nvidia’s lobbying leverage as US lawmakers press for tighter controls.
Washington began restricting Nvidia’s advanced AI processors in 2022 and subsequently tightened controls on modified chips developed for China, including the H800.
In January, the Trump administration moved to review H200 export licences for eligible Chinese customers individually, subject to conditions.

Nvidia’s August filing said it was effectively excluded from China’s data-center computing market. But an IDC report cited by Reuters in October estimated Nvidia still accounted for 34% of Chinese AI-accelerator shipments in the first half of 2026.
The figures measure different things and do not establish how the restricted hardware identified in the Reuters investigation reached Chinese users.
The scrutiny has intensified since Huang’s resignation on Thursday, following allegations involving Alice Huang, a former executive associated with Singapore-based Nvidia cloud partner Megaspeed.

Megaspeed has denied illegally diverting Nvidia chips to China. Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation, saying it had no reason to believe company secrets or US national security were compromised. There has been no public finding that Jensen Huang violated export-control laws.
The Chinese projects identified by Reuters have not been linked to Megaspeed or the allegations involving Huang. – Rappler.com

MANILA, Philippines – The Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) on Wednesday, November 10, announced that it received reports of a data breach involving its Local Government Unit Support System-Barangay Information Management System (LGUSS-BIMS).

The system tracks resident profiles; manages issuances, such as ordinances, resolutions, certificates; disaster preparedness plans; gender and development plans and budgets; and reports for national agencies.

In an advisory, the department said that the potential data breach contains Records of Barangay Inhabitants (RBI). These records include household demographics, such as the residents’ names, civil status, occupation, address, contact details, and classifications (person with disability, overseas Filipino worker, or solo parent).

The DILG has also coordinated with the National Privacy Commission (NPC) and initiated precautionary measures to protect data and strengthen its security system. It has also begun its investigation and will take appropriate action based on findings.
Users have received an email from the DILG about the breach, advising them to report any suspicious activity observed related to the misuse of personal information.
Several government agencies and institutions have recently reported data breaches.

St. Luke’s Medical Center revealed unauthorized access to its mobile application, which is managed by a third-party service provider. The incident includes personal information of patients and employees.

According to an email forwarded to Rappler, the compromised pieces of information include the name, hospital patient number, birth date, civil status, gender, address, email, contact number, dependents, citizenship, and nationality.
Ten other government agencies reported leaks, according to the NPC:

items: Presidential Commission on Good Government
Department of Information and Communications Technology
Department of Labor and Employment, through its Bureau of Local Employment
Bureau of Internal Revenue
Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation
Department of Justice, through its Office for Alternative Dispute Resolution
Securities and Exchange Commission
Philippine Coast Guard
Department of Trade and Industry
Department of Science and Technology-Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology

blocks.text: Under the Data Privacy Act of 2012, government agencies or institutions that hold personal information should immediately inform the NPC and the affected individuals if their personal information has been compromised. They are also held accountable for the information they hold, including records processed by third parties. – Rappler.com

articles.title: NBI says it's ready to assist in extradition of Apollo Quiboloy
articles.summary: The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) is ready to assist in the extradition of Kingdom of Jesus Christ (KOJC) founder Apollo Quiboloy, the bureau"s director, Atty. Melvin Matibag said Friday.

blocks.text: Published November 13, 2026 4:38pm
The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) is ready to assist in the extradition of Kingdom of Jesus Christ (KOJC) founder Apollo Quiboloy, the bureau’s director, Atty. Melvin Matibag said Friday.
Earlier Friday, the Makati Regional Trial Court (RTC) issued an extradition arrest warrant and a hold departure order against Quiboloy and two of his co-accused, according to the DOJ.
“We are ready to assist depending on our coordination with other law enforcement agencies, more importantly, with the Department of Justice (DOJ),” Matibag told reporters.

Matibag explained that the law enforcement agency holding custody of Quiboloy will be responsible for presenting him in court, noting that the extradition will undergo a process and require a hearing.

“So ‘yung law enforcement who is in care of the person, sila ‘yung mag-present niyan sa court for the hearing— that’s based on the petition filed by the DOJ because of the request of the US Government,” he explained.

(The law enforcement agency that has custody of the individual will be the one to present them in court for the hearing. That is based on the petition filed by the DOJ on behalf of the US government.)
The Davao-based religious leader is currently detained at the Pasig City Jail.

He was arrested in September 2024 on charges of violating Republic Act 7610, or the Special Protection of Children Against Abuse, Exploitation, and Discrimination Act. He also faces a non-bailable qualified human trafficking charge under Section 4(a) of Republic Act 9208, as amended, before a Pasig court.
On Monday, the DOJ filed an extradition petition against Quiboloy, Teresita Tolibas Dandan, and Helen Panilag before the Makati RTC on behalf of the US government.
The charges cited in the petition include international human trafficking, sex trafficking, conspiracy, and bulk cash smuggling.
Matibag refused to give an estimated timeline for Quiboloy’s extradition, emphasizing that the matter is under the court's jurisdiction.
“We don’t know; depende sa korte (it will depend on the court). I don't like to speculate, and I don't want to be the one saying it because it’s under the jurisdiction of the court,” he said.
As for Quiboloy’s co-accused, Matibag said they have yet to verify Dandan and Panilag's status. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Czechia braces for massive protest against cuts to public media
articles.summary: A fast-tracked bill to cut public media funding has sparked strikes, rallies and fears for the independence of public broadcasting in Czechia. A massive protest is planned for Prague on Sunday.

image.caption: 'Strike — For a free press, free media' Many in Czechia fear that the government's plans to change the way public media is funded will undermine the independence of Czech Television and Czech RadioImage: Katerina Sulova/CTK Photo/IMAGO

blocks.text: Hundreds of thousands of people are expected to rally in Prague this weekend to protest the Czech government's bid to ram a bill to reform public media funding through parliament in a surprise overnight session in October.
The right-populist coalition headed by Prime Minister Andrej Babis fast-tracked the first of three readings of the legislation, which culminated in a vote of approval at 4:36 a.m. on October 24.
The bill has already provoked numerous demonstrations and strikes across the country, but Sunday's gathering in the capital's Letna park is likely to be by far the largest to date.
What's in the bill?

Under the government's proposal, the license fee model that currently funds Czech Television (CT) and Czech Radio (CRo) would be scrapped, and the broadcasters would be funded directly from the state budget.

The three parties in the coalition — Babis's centrist ANO, the far-right SPD, and radical conservative Motorists, whose voter bases tend to be less affluent — insist that the license fee is an unfair tax.

blocks.caption: Crowds protested outside parliament while inside, the government pushed through the first reading of the controversial media funding bill on the night of October 23/24Image: Michal Kamaryt/CTK Photo/IMAGO

blocks.text: The parties argue that the new arrangement, which would see funding for CT and CRo cut by around 15% in the first year, would make the two more efficient. They also point out that several other European Union states have made similar changes.
What are the objections to the bill?
Critics have angrily dismissed these justifications.

Opposition parties, civil society organizations and international watchdogs accuse the government of seeking to undermine the independence of the broadcasters, whose critical reporting has long irked ANO and the SPD in particular.
Analysts point out that while models in other EU states include guarantees of long-term financial stability and editorial independence, the Czech government proposal offers neither.
CT and CRo have warned that the reduced budget included in the bill will mean programming- and staff cuts.

When the first publication of the proposed bill was met with protests over the summer, Vaclav Stetka of the European New School of Digital Studies told DW that such "dramatic budget cuts represent an act of cultural vandalism."
There has also been condemnation of the restriction of the parliamentary debate amid the fast-tracking of the bill.

blocks.caption: The protests continued in the days after the late-night vote in parliamentImage: Michael Heitmann/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: "The confrontational approach, the attempts to limit parliamentary debate and the government's rhetoric towards journalists and critics have all contributed to the public backlash," Otto Eibl, political scientist at Masaryk University in Czechia's second city Brno, told DW.
What has happened since the bill was fast-tracked?
The backlash was immediate. Crowds picketed parliament through the night as the government pushed through the first reading of the bill.

Since then, multiple rallies have taken place in cities and towns across the country. Many of these protests were led by students and joined by unions, Churches and representatives of educational and cultural institutions.
CT and CRo staff called a strike in early November, disrupting the country's TV and radio schedules.
Sunday's protest is set to up the ante.
It will take place two days before the anniversary of the start of the Velvet Revolution, which ultimately brought down communism in what was then Czechoslovakia in 1989.

The civil society group Million Moments for Democracy, which is organizing Sunday's rally, brought an estimated 300,000 onto the streets to protest during Babis's first term as prime minister in 2019 and more than 200,000 earlier this year.
Why has the reaction been so strong?

The government's sudden bid to push through the proposal reflects impatience to deliver on a core pledge made ahead of the October 2025 election, as well as the longstanding ambition of the prime minister, who was stymied in his attempt to engineer control of CT's governing council during his first term in power in 2017–21.

blocks.caption: 'For you, not for politicians' — Public broadcasters are seen by many in Czechia as cornerstones of democracyImage: Eva Korinkova/REUTERS

blocks.text: Vaclav Stetka notes that repeated assaults on public media by Czech governments past and present reflect a particular political culture across Europe's post-communist states.
"The political elite has never accepted the independence of public media," he asserted.
In Czechia, however, the public broadcasters have earned special status as cornerstones of democracy.

That standing was forged in what became known as the "Czech TV crisis" of 2000–01, when an occupation of CT's studios by staff and mass protests forced the government of the day to back down on a bid to wrest control.
"The fight over the public service media has become a symbol of the defense of liberal democratic values and institutions," Eibl said.
How has the government reacted?

As anger has swelled, the government has sought to calm the situation. Babis has said that a new proposal, which would see public media funding moved off budget and editorial independence guaranteed, would be drawn up and made available for a full and open debate.

blocks.caption: During the November 3 strike at Czech Television, hosts read the news in front of a darkened newsroomImage: Eva Korinkova/REUTERS

blocks.text: However, critics remain unimpressed, noting a lack of any detail and the fact that other members of the government appear determined to remain on course.
Million Moments for Democracy has insisted the pressure must continue.
"Words are worth nothing," the group said. "While people stand up for independent media, the government continues to act as if it owns the country."
What are the potential risks for the government?
With little sign that the opposition will dissipate, the government faces a choice.
It has the parliamentary majority it needs to push the bill through and defeat any likely vetoes from the upper house Senate and President Petr Pavel.
But this could come at a cost.

Polls suggest political support for the government has been weakened and could diminish further if the protests expand to include growing frustrations over the cost of living and housing, as happened recently with student-led protests in France and other European countries.
"The real risk for the government is that the media issue becomes a lightning rod for broader dissatisfaction," said Martin Vokalek of the Prague-based EUROPEUM Institute for European Policy.
Could things turn violent?
Babis is aware of the danger.

blocks.caption: Public opposition to the government's plans for Czech public media are nothing new: this demonstration outside Czech Television in June called for the dismissal of Culture Minister Oto Klempir and expressed support for the country's public mediaImage: Ondrej Deml/CTK/picture alliance

blocks.text: The PM announced that he will not attend the Velvet Revolution anniversary celebrations on November 17, which are hugely symbolic, in the hope that his absence might "calm the tense situation."
However, there's little concern that the Czech protests could descend into violence.
Analysts note that the anger in Czechia remains tightly focused on the public media proposal and continues to be expressed in a similar way to the seismic events of the country's modern history.

"I would not expect French-style scenes," Vokalek told DW, noting that the same "large, peaceful and civic Czech protest culture," which gave the Velvet Revolution and 1993's Velvet Divorce from Slovakia their name, is still strong.

articles.title: After suffering its worst election result, what's next for the ANC — and for South Africa?
articles.summary: A crushing local election result across the country has left South Africa's ruling ANC searching for answers. Experts say the vote reflects public frustration with service delivery failures —…

image.caption: A new era: Coalition governments are no longer the exception in South African politicsImage: Themba Hadebe/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: South Africa's governing African National Congress (ANC) party is forced to confront its worst electoral setback to date after securing under 31% of the vote in the country's significant local government elections; party leaders themselves have described the result as "catastrophic."

This outcome marks a steep decline for the party that had once led South Africa's liberation struggle; the party that had dominated the country's political landscape since the end of apartheid in 1994.

The result reflects growing public frustration about the ANC's lack of performance in key areas such as skyrocketing unemployment, poor service delivery, local governance failures and years of graft and corruption — sometimes at the highest levels of government.
So what comes next for the ANC — and for South Africa?

blocks.caption: After years of dominating the political scene, the ANC's future now looks increasingly unstableImage: Leandre Steenberg/Matrix Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Voters express growing frustration and despair

Tasnim Essop, a researcher at the Society, Work and Politics Institute (SWOP) at the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, says it is time for the party to undertake some serious introspection. She believes that the ANC has to confront a long list of difficult questions about governance, leadership and accountability.

"You're talking about issues like water, electricity, housing, public services at the basic municipal level. And those kinds of things have been key issues. And ... research has shown that unemployment is also a big part of what drives people to vote in certain ways" she told DW.
Essop also highlights the fact that the outcome of the vote didn't happen overnight, and that it rather reflects a slow erosion of public confidence in the erstwhile ruling party over a long period.
South Africa election hit by disinformation surge

DW correspondent Dianne Hawker-Kalubi, who reported from various polling stations during the election, agrees with that observation, stressing that many of the voters she had spoken to expressed "a lot of frustration, a lot of concern about basic services not being delivered" for years.
Mokhiri Phooko, a Cape Town resident, said that "people are losing hope" across the country after over three years of the political landscape being dominated by late President Nelson Mandela's party:
"You promised us jobs, why [are] you not keeping up the end of your bargain right," she told Reuters, stressing that "(t)he unemployment rate went up drastically" in the past few years.
A shifting role for the ANC

The ANC itself meanwhile has acknowledged that things have to change: In a statement, the party announced that its National Executive Committee would convene a special meeting to deal with the "serious political responsibility to listen to the people, confront its shortcomings and provide leadership."

Furthermore, the party also has to prepare a framework for upcoming coalition negotiations at the same time — many times involving some of its biggest rivals, as was the case after the 2024 general elections.

blocks.caption: Helen Zille, chairwoman of the DA, has agreed to coalition talks with the ANC beforeImage: DW

blocks.text: The election results therefore signal a broader shift in South African politics, with voter support increasingly spread across multiple parties rather than being concentrated behind a single dominant force.

While nationally, the ANC remained the country's largest party, opposition parties made significant gains; the Democratic Alliance (DA) managed to strengthen its position across several major urban centers.

Meanwhile the uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party, launched by former President Jacob Zuma in late 2023, performed rather strongly in the KwaZulu-Natal provice despite entering the political arena so recently.
At the local level, smaller civic organizations and community-based movements also recorded notable successes.
'Vote fluidity' enters South African politics
Essop describes this trend as a growing sense of "vote fluidity," with voters increasingly willing to move their support between parties instead of remaining loyal to a single political organization.

Some observers have already linked this drift to the idea of South Africans are moving beyond liberation-era loyalties; however, Essop opines: "I would be cautious to say that liberation politics are dead and gone," as many political parties continue to draw ther legitimacy and support from the country's liberation history — even if they no longer operate under the ANC banner.
Essop argues that the political shift does not signify a wholesale rejection of that liberation narrative itself, but rather a growing demand for effective governance and leadership.
A critical test for the ANC

For the ANC, the challenge now is rebuilding trust, with South African President Cyril Ramaphosa saying that the results are a challenge not just for his party but for all political parties to come together and perform better for citizens.
In a statement, Ramaphosa said that "[t]hose who have been elected to councils now need to prove themselves worthy of the trust placed in them by the South African people."

blocks.caption: The election results also represent a growing lack in confidence in Preseident Cyril Ramaphosa's leadershipImage: Ignacio Lopez Isasmendi/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: While the ANC still remains South Africa's largest political party, its latest setbacks at the polls underscore how much the country's political landscape is no longer what it was when apartheid ended.
The era of undisputed ANC loyalty and dominance appears to be over as voters are showing a greater willingness to support alternative parties and punish those they believe have fallen short.
Whether the ANC can reverse this decline will depend largely on how convincingly it can deliver not only improved public services, but effective change throughout.

articles.title: Cebu experts urge gov’t to comply with WHO air quality standards
articles.summary: Experts from UP Cebu, in collaboration with Clean Air Asia, are set to deploy new sensor technology to support air quality monitoring in the province

blocks.text: NETWORK. Health professionals, scientists, and environmental advocates launch the Cebu Clean Air Network (Cebu CAN) at the University of the Philippines Cebu on November 13, 2026, calling for stronger measures to address air pollution and protect public health.
Jacqueline Hernandez/Rappler
Experts from UP Cebu, in collaboration with Clean Air Asia, are set to deploy new sensor technology to support air quality monitoring in the province

CEBU, Philippines – Environmentalists and health and science experts launched the Cebu Clean Air Network (Cebu CAN) on Friday, November 13, to urge the government to take immediate action towards meeting the World Health Organization (WHO) Global Air Quality Guidelines.

Francis Joseph dela Cruz, Institute for Climate and Sustainable Cities (ICSC) Partnerships and Advocacy advisor and AktivAsia Co-founder, told Rappler in an interview that the network specifically chose Cebu for the launch due to developments in the province’s struggle for clean air.

“Cebu is a major economic center and it’s here that we find evidence of air pollution. We know where it’s coming from because research showed that 70% of it comes from mobile sources, which means transport and the rest, stationary — coal plants,” Dela Cruz said.

In April, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources–Environmental Management Bureau in Central Visayas (DENR-EMB 7) reported “very unhealthy” levels of air quality index (AQI) due to a lack of wind movement and accumulation of vehicle and industrial air pollutants.
“Data from the Talisay City Station confirms a significant and concerning rise in fine particulate matter (PM2.5),” said a DENR-EMB air quality advisory in April.
Cebu also experienced strong haze due to volcanic activity from the Kanlaon Volcano in July and forest fires from Indonesia in September.

The WHO air quality guidelines set an average annual limit of no more than 5 micrograms per cubic meter for concentrations of PM2.5 or particulate matter smaller than 2.5 micrometers — these are particulate matter small enough to travel deep into the lungs and even enter the blood stream.
According to Cebu CAN, the country’s current annual guidelines for PM2.5, set in 2020, remain five times higher than the limit recommended by the WHO.
Dela Cruz explained that the impact of unhealthy air quality can be seen in disrupted economic activity and hampered use of public resources.

“If you have an unhealthy citizenry, then the money that they earn, rather than go to what they need, goes to medication and if they cannot work, it gives them more problems. If they go to a public health center, the center will have to allocate more resources for patients,” the clean air advocate said.
According to a 2021 study by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air and the ICSC, air pollution costs the country an estimated P4.5 trillion a year in economic costs.

blocks.caption: PLEDGE. Cebu CAN member organizations Clean Air Asia, the UP Cebu Center for Environmental Informatics, 350 Pilipinas, CAP-Cebu Chapter, Health Alliance for Climate and Clean Air Philippines, Philippine Movement for Climate Justice, AktivAsia, Health Care Without Harm, Greenpeace Cebu, and Amnest…

blocks.text: For Jonnifer Sinogaya, center head of the University of the Philippines in Cebu Center for Environmental Informatics, there’s a need to address gaps in the reliability of the monitoring of the province’s air quality index.

“During the haze, there was only one source of data, which was from the station in Talisay City so if there is now a network, more stations to deploy, you can get more reliable data and that will supplement those from the DENR-EMB,” Sinogaya said.
With the launch of the Cebu CAN, the University of the Philippines Cebu (UP Cebu), in a memorandum of agreement with Clean Air Asia, is set to deploy new air quality sensors in the province.

Apart from data gathering, Dela Cruz shared that local governance could also take part in improving Cebu’s air quality by reviewing the province’s reliance on energy sources like coal that emit harmful pollutants.

At present, Cebu contributes a majority of the energy from coal in the Visayas grid. The Cebu island sub-grid consists of coal (82.03%), diesel (12.94%), solar (4.93%), and hydroelectric (0.1%) power plants.
The province is also host to the coal-fired power plants that have been on forced and unplanned outages in recent months.

Dela Cruz suggested that the electrification of transport packaged with a transition to the use of renewable energy would provide the province an advantage in addressing gaps in its energy and air quality demands.

“So that’s the first step, looking at how you can transform modes of mobility and transportation. If we can afford it, switching to electric vehicles will address mobile sources of pollution,” the clean air advocate said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Customs chief takes BCDA helm amid controversial Pax Silica
articles.summary: The change comes as BCDA prepares long-term arrangements for Camp John Hay’s key facilities and as the Marcos administration readies the Pax Silica framework deal with the US

blocks.text: BOC. Bureau of Customs Commissioner Ariel Nepomuceno speaks before the start of the bidding of seven luxury vehicles confiscated from the Discaya family, on November 20, 2025.
Rappler
The change comes as BCDA prepares long-term arrangements for Camp John Hay’s key facilities and as the Marcos administration readies the Pax Silica framework deal with the US

items: Ariel Nepomuceno has been appointed as the new president and CEO of the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA), taking over from Joshua Bingcang.

Nepomuceno will oversee two major projects: Camp John Hay in Baguio and the Pax Silica industrial hub in New Clark City, which has faced scrutiny regarding environmental impacts and local consultations.

The leadership change comes as BCDA prepares long-term management plans for Camp John Hay and continues discussions on the Pax Silica project, with concerns about national sovereignty and compliance with Philippine laws.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

BAGUIO CITY, Philippines – A leadership shake-up is putting a new man in charge of two major government development projects, including Camp John Hay in Baguio and the controversial US-backed Pax Silica initiative at New Clark City, Tarlac.

Bureau of Customs Commissioner Ariel Nepomuceno has been appointed president and chief executive officer of the Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA), replacing Joshua Bingcang, who is moving to the Philippine Economic Zone Authority (PEZA).
Nepomuceno confirmed his transfer on Wednesday, November 11, the same day President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed his appointment, which took immediate effect.

The change comes as BCDA prepares long-term management arrangements for Camp John Hay’s golf course and hotel facilities, following the completion of an updated master development plan for the former American military reservation.

Under Bingcang, BCDA pursued plans to attract private investors to manage and improve the facilities after regaining control of disputed properties from former developer Camp John Hay Development Corporation in January 2025, following a Supreme Court ruling. (READ: Camp John Hay: A 3-decade saga of turf wars, court drama, and a new beginning)
The agency also extended interim management arrangements for the golf course through 2026 while preparing for a long-term concession.

blocks.caption: MVP’s Landco eyes 25-year Camp John Hay Golf lease

blocks.text: Beyond Baguio, Nepomuceno inherits the proposed 4,000-acre Pax Silica industrial hub in New Clark City, Tarlac, part of a US-led initiative aimed at strengthening supply chains for semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, and technologies supporting artificial intelligence.

The proposal has faced scrutiny over its potential environmental impact, land rights, and consultation with affected communities, including indigenous peoples. (READ: [In This Economy] Pax Silica: What’s the Philippines’ trump card?)

Capas Mayor Roseller Rodriguez questioned the lack of prior consultation with local officials and sought greater disclosure of the project’s scope and potential effects. In August, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources confirmed that it had not received or processed an environmental impact assessment application for Pax Silica.

BCDA, however, has maintained that the proposed development would occupy designated buildable areas, would not displace Indigenous communities, and would comply with Philippine environmental laws. (READ: Pax Silica: BCDA’s claims and the counterarguments)

Questions over national sovereignty also surfaced during a House hearing on Wednesday, November 11, when lawmakers raised concerns about a proposed joint-governance arrangement with the United States.
Bingcang assured legislators that Philippine laws would prevail, stressing that negotiations on the project’s legal framework were still ongoing, with no confirmed signing date.
Following the announcement of his transfer to PEZA, Bingcang said Pax Silica remained a national government initiative.

Nepomuceno now takes over BCDA with both projects at critical planning stages. The agency has yet to announce whether the leadership change will affect Camp John Hay’s proposed management contracts or the timetable for the Pax Silica agreement. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Australian cricket's sandpapergate is back - and it cuts deep in a 'nation of good sports'
articles.summary: Claims the entire Australian team knew of the 2018 sandpaper cheating plot are dividing the cricket world.

blocks.text: As Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins spent more than an hour being grilled by reporters over one of sport's biggest cheating scandals, the tension in the hall was occasionally pierced by muffled cheers.
Outside, a crucial match in the top tier of domestic cricket was getting under way. Cummins was clear he'd rather we all be talking about that.

But inside the nets at Cricket Central in Sydney, he faced more than a dozen TV cameras and a gaggle of journalists several times as large. His goal: to put rumours of his involvement in "sandpapergate" to rest.
"I don't want to talk about this again after today," he said. "Even if it takes all day... I'll stay here until we have no more questions."
A book by his friend and former teammate Usman Khawaja has renewed scrutiny on a 2018 plot to tamper with the ball using sandpaper in Australia's third Test match against South Africa in Cape Town.
Three players admitted they were involved at the time and were handed lengthy bans, but in a memoir released last week, Khawaja said the entire Australian team knew about the sandpaper scheme.

His claims have plunged the Australian cricket world into chaos, thrown speculation over key figures from that Test - including star bowler Cummins who has since risen to hold what many joke is Australia's most important job - and reopened wounds for fans.
Josh, 28, told the BBC he thought everyone had moved on: "It's just a bit crazy that it's all blown up again... I think it is a bit ridiculous, after eight years."
"I'm a bit bored of it," another spectator at the New South Wales vs South Australia Sheffield Shield match said.

Among fans, there's frustration that Khawaja has chosen to come forward now, almost a decade on and at the start of an exciting summer, and year, of cricket. Though there's an argument there'd never be a good time for Khawaja, who retired from international cricket in January, to make these allegations.
There's worry about the impact on the men's team's performance this summer, after a lacklustre showing in South Africa last month - its first Test matches there since the 2018 incident.

And there's a sense of injustice that Australia can't seem to escape the scandal, given - according to many players themselves - how common boundary-bending on ball tampering apparently was in that era.
"It's a bit of a stitch up," 21-year-old James said.
"Every country has done it... if it wasn't us, it was probably going to be someone else."
Khawaja's memoir is also causing rancour among current and former players and coaches.
In it, he said he had wanted the team to take collective responsibility for the tampering after batsman Cameron Bancroft was caught with the sandpaper on field.
"I said: 'Take this as a team. We did this as a team. We knew what was going on, and we have to take it as a team'."
However Khawaja has since said he didn't want to start a "witch hunt" and has refused to answer questions on exactly who he claims knew of the scheme, and what they knew.
David Warner, who received the most severe punishment of the Cape Town trio, said Khawaja had written the truth and that Cummins' press conference denying the claims "threw him under the bus".

Steve Smith, the captain at the time who was also suspended, has been travelling overseas and is yet to say anything publicly about the claims in the book. Bancroft is also staying silent for now despite previously suggesting the bowlers knew.
But half of Australia's living cricket royalty and a slew of former coaches - some of whom have been accused of wrongdoing too - have thrown in their two cents.
And Cricket Australia is under pressure from some to reopen its investigation into sandpapergate - something chief executive Todd Greenberg has already ruled out.
Prof David Rowe of the University of Western Sydney told the BBC the saga was still so painful for many players and fans as the country sees itself as "a nation of good sports".
"The idea of being a good sport is two things. One is being good at sport, so you actually win. But the other side is that you do it honourably and fairly," he said.
"Many Australians would see themselves as above all that. That is: cheating is what other teams get up to... not the nation of good sports."
He said the revelation was a "nasty shock" which brought the country "collective shame" which lingers today.
He says he doubts that the cricket scene would be able to move on without a fresh response from the governing body, Cricket Australia.
"One of the best ways to fuel conspiracy theories and keep sandpapergate going is to essentially say 'there's no more to see here' - especially when that comes from the authorities," Rowe said.
Asked about a fresh investigation, Cummins said it was a matter for Cricket Australia.

Over the marathon press conference - which one reporter suggested was the longest in Australian sporting history - Cummins was cautious, pausing often to consider his responses and to make sure they answered the questions being asked of him.

But he was also frank - using strong words to reject what he said were "vague" claims by Khawaja and admitting he was frustrated a friend had put him in this position. "Friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations... That's something I've been grappling with the last couple of days."

As the reporters ran out of steam, Cummins said it was "annoying" that sandpapergate scandal was still a distraction for Australian cricket. He gestured outside to the Sheffield Shield match and mentioned Friday's one-day international against England in Perth, from which he and other key players are being rested.
"It's been eight years... Hopefully today we put a line through it and we're done and we can all move on to much more fun topics, like actual cricket."
Few people think he'll get his wish.
"It's going to be hard to move on, given that there's two sides of the story and it doesn't look like either side is going to back down," James said.
"I don't know what the outcome will be."
