Reading aloud from a piece of paper in front of her, Graham called the vote to end debate on St John’s nomination by mistaking the abbreviation for saint in her name, with the one for street. “The question is,” Graham said, “is it the sense of the Senate that debate on the nomination of Anna Street John of Louisiana to be United States judge for the fifth circuit shall be brought to a close?”
The Alliance for Justice (AFJ), a progressive judicial advocacy group, strongly opposed all three nominees.

Cook, who worked as a volunteer attorney in the 2000 Bush v Gore legal battle, is described by the AFJ as “a lifelong conservative who has consistently aligned himself with extremist ideologies in pursuit of more political power” whose “track record demonstrates a commitment to corporate interests and the spread of conservative ideology — not justice.”

Domenico, who is described by the AFJ as a potential supreme court nominee, was nominated to the US district court in Colorado by Trump in 2019. This year, Trump picked him to serve on the US court of appeals for the 10th circuit in Denver.

In January, when Trump nominated Anna St John to serve as a federal judge for the US district court for the Eastern District of Louisiana, the AFJ wrote that she “has spent her legal career silencing women, attacking LGBTQ+ rights, and cutting off corporate accountability for everyday people.” Before being confirmed to that role, and then nominated to a federal appeals court in New Orleans, St John led the Hamilton Legal Law Institute, which the AFJ calls “a far-right extremist organization that routinely files lawsuits to attack civil rights, undermine consumer protections, eliminate gender equality, and deny basic human rights”.

In her confirmation hearing for her elevation the the appeals court in August, St John refused to say that Trump lost the 2020 election and refrained from characterizing the January 6 2021 Capitol riot as an insurrection.

Democrats from across the country have gathered at the What’s Next conference in Denver to discuss what the party should do moving forward – now that they’ve secured majorities in the US House and Senate, and won control of the governor’s offices in a majority of states.

The conference, hosted by the group Majority Democrats, is bustling with excitement. In the outdoor space, there’s a six-piece jazz band playing upbeat variations of Americana songs, flanked by a colorful food truck.
The main stage event will be livestreamed, starting at 2:30 Mountain Time.
In the further annals of Donald Trump not changing a thing since last week’s midterm election defeat, he also mused earlier today on Truth Social: “Will the Seditious Six ever be prosecuted?”
“What they did was a great violation to our Country and its Constitution!” the president added.

It’s a reference to six Democratic lawmakers who last year published a video reminding members of the military and intelligence community that they can refuse illegal orders, amid concerns that Trump would attempt to use them against his political adversaries.
Here’s what senator Mark Kelly had to say about Trump’s latest threat:

double quotation markThe American people delivered a massive rejection of Donald Trump’s chaos and corruption last week. Now he’s again threatening to prosecute people who stand up to him because he’s afraid of being held accountable. Donald Trump has tried and failed to intimidate me for a year now. His threats won’t stop me from doing my job.

Immediately after Republicans suffered a drubbing in last week’s midterms, Donald Trump made some comments indicating he’d considering working with the incoming Democratic majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives.

Just about everything he’s done since – from appointing immigration hardliner Stephen Miller his chief of staff to threatening one of the top Democratic investigators – indicates he’s not looking to change much at all. Further evidence arrived this afternoon in the form of a Truth Social post, where the president says he’d like to work with Chuck Schumer on fighting corruption – but only in states led by Democrats.

“Billions of Dollars are being stolen on an hourly basis. Hopefully his words will ring true! It will be an honor to work with him on this very big Democrat problem that, when solved, will literally balance the Budget of the U.S.” the president writes.

Little he writes in that sentence appears to be true. There are 8,760 hours in a year, and the Government Accountability Office estimated in 2024 that between $233 bn to $521 bn are lost to fraud annually – so certainly not billions “on an hourly basis,” as Trump wrote. Meanwhile, there are unanswered questions around how Trump has gone about increasing his wealth since he’s been president:

Democrats may have ridden voter concerns over the war with Iran to their largest congressional majority in years in last week’s midterm elections, but Donald Trump today announced that the US is no longer bothering to find peace with its Middle Eastern adversary. Here’s more, from the Guardian’s Andrew Roth:

Donald Trump has said that the US is no longer seeking a deal to end the war with Iran and ordered JD Vance, who had spearheaded recent efforts to restart negotiations with Iran, to focus on domestic politics instead.

In a post to his social media site on Thursday, Trump said he was redirecting the vice-president to focus his “complete and total attention on the Massive Corruption and Crime taking place in Democrat run Cities and States throughout the U.S”.

Vance had reportedly been talking to intermediaries in Iran and Qatar about restarting negotiations to end the war, which began in February when the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran. Iran responded by closing access to the strait of Hormuz, which led to a steep increase for the cost of fuel around the globe.
But on Thursday Trump appeared to shut down the negotiations, redirecting Vance to focus on domestic issues and downplaying the need for a final deal.
“We don’t need a deal with Iran,” Trump wrote. “Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”
We reported earlier that Ukraine’s president has said that Starlink, the satellite internet service it relies to counter Russian drone attacks, has slowed down, hampering its defenses.

Democrats are already expected to investigate a number of the activities of Elon Musk, who controls Starlink, and whether the service is being deliberately throttled for Ukraine could be on their list. While many of these inquiries are sure to be strictly partisan affairs, Michael McCaul, an outgoing House Republican who supports defending Ukraine against Russia, just signaled his support for this particular line of questioning, writing the following on X:

double quotation markI am deeply concerned by reports that Ukraine’s access to Starshield has once again been restricted. These capabilities play a critical role in Ukraine’s defense against Putin’s relentless missile and drone attacks, which target civilian homes, parks, hospitals, and energy infrastructure. With peace negotiations on the horizon, maintaining Ukraine’s momentum and leverage is more important than ever. I urge a full investigation into why these disruptions have now occurred twice and call for measures be put in place to ensure it does not happen again.

Donald Trump’s health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, is facing potential legal trouble after a Democratic senator opened an inquiry into whether the lied to Congress, citing reporting by the Guardian. Here’s more, from the Guardian’s Michelle R Smith:

A top Democratic senator has launched an investigation into evidence that Robert F Kennedy Jr “unlawfully lied” in his 2025 confirmation hearings to become the US health secretary, citing a report by the Guardian.

Ron Wyden of Oregon, the incoming chair of the powerful Senate finance committee, is seeking extensive records from Children’s Health Defense (CHD), the non-profit anti-vaccine group Kennedy has used as a vehicle to fuel his political rise, including all documents related to a 2019 trip Kennedy took to Samoa.

“We are beginning an investigation into evidence that Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F Kennedy, Jr unlawfully lied to Congress on multiple occasions,” Wyden said in a letter to the group that was sent on Wednesday and obtained by the Guardian. The letter was also signed by Angela Alsobrooks, a Democratic senator from Maryland.

In the letter, the two lawmakers cited reporting by the Guardian that indicated Kennedy lied about his reasons for going to Samoa in 2019, a trip that occurred just months before a measles outbreak killed 83 people in the Pacific island nation, mostly children under age five.

The trip, which Kennedy made as the chair and chief legal counsel of CHD, became one of the most criticized events in his career before he entered government. Critics, including Samoan officials, have said Kennedy’s presence emboldened anti-vaccine activists in Samoa, worsening a vaccination crisis. Kennedy has denied the allegations, saying he never gave any public statement about vaccines or discouraged Samoans from getting vaccinated.
The Trump administration faces an investigation of its scheme to take a 15% cut from any Nvidia chip sales going to China, as part of a deal to secure export licenses for the semiconductors.

Under the scheme, Nvidia chips made in Taiwan could be sold to Chinese companies if they were imported to the US first for a security review. This also made them subject to a 25% tariff under section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, which was aimed at dealing with imports that threaten national security. The commerce secretary could then grant an export licence to sell the chips to China.

Two Democratic senators are now demanding Trump officials retain all records relating to the scheme as the fallout from now former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy continues to grow.

Senate finance committee ranking member Ron Wyden and House ways and means committee ranking member Richard E. Neal said they were beginning to investigate following reports of the affair – which led to Huang’s resignation on Thursday. One focus of the investigation appear to be report that both commerce secretary Howard Lutnick and Donald Trump were briefed about the relationship but granted export approvals anyway.
In a statement, Wyden and Neal said:

double quotation markThe Trump administration’s ostensible attempt to mask an unconstitutional export tax as a national security tariff action – benefitting both Nvidia and the Chinese government – raises serious concerns within our committees’ jurisdiction over matters relating to taxation and tariffs. Congress wrote Section 232 to give the president a tool to take action against imports he has determined to pose a national security threat; Trump’s use of the statute appears to have done the opposite, undermining US national security and putting Americans at risk.
Trump's commerce secretary faces being dragged into fallout from Nvidia scandal

Senior White ⁠House officials are discussing whether commerce secretary Howard Lutnick should be pushed out ⁠in the wake ⁠of ​the spy scandal surrounding Nvidia’s now former CEO Jensen Huang, two people familiar ⁠with the situation told Reuters on Thursday.
Here’s more from the Reuters report:

double quotation markA growing number of lawmakers criticized Lutnick over ⁠the administration’s refusal to add dozens of Chinese ​companies to a key ‌US trade blacklist, ‌and over whether the government was properly overseeing ‌Nvidia’s exports to China. Criticism of Lutnick’s actions predates Thursday’s resignation of Nvidia’s Huang, who announced he would step down as CEO of the leading AI chipmaker after revelations of an affair with ‌Alice Huang, whom US authorities suspect of spying for Beijing. But the charge ​that Lutnick has not done enough to restrict AI chip shipments to China has bubbled up as the fallout of Jensen Huang’s actions grows. The ⁠White House did not immediately respond to a ​request ​for comment on Lutnick’s future. A ​White House official said of criticism ​of Lutnick ‌that President Donald ​Trump “maintains ​complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position.“

blocks.caption: Marina Dunbar

blocks.text: Marina Dunbar

Here’s a bit more on the story of Pete Hegseth awarding a medal to the soldier who reprimanded him and his aides for breaking the silence around the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington cemetery on Veterans Day.

A Pentagon official confirmed to CNN that Hegseth hosted members of the 3rd infantry regiment, known as the Old Guard, at the Pentagon “where he proudly awarded Specialist Iglesias the Joint Service Commendation Medal for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the unknown Soldier on November 11, 2026”.

Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell addressed the incident in a statement: “The secretary and the entire department have always honored – and will always honor – the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe.

The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington national cemetery is one of the most sacred war memorials in the country, marking the final resting place of an unknown soldier who was killed in the first world war.

Soldiers from the Old Guard have maintained a round-the-clock watch over the tomb since 1948. Part of their responsibility includes enforcing strict standards of silence and respect, and correcting visitors whose behavior disrupts the solemn atmosphere.

The Joint Service Commendation Medal is awarded to members of the US armed forces who distinguish themselves by “meritorious achievement or service while serving in any specified activity”, according to the air force’s personnel center.
When will the Alaska Senate race be called?
With Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom’s election confirmed yesterday, there is just one Senate race outstanding: Mary Peltola’s bid to oust Alaska’s incumbent Republican senator, Dan Sullivan.

Alaska typically takes a long time to count its ballots, due to the complicated logistics of elections in a massive state that’s home to many communities inaccessible by road. Thus far, things are looking good for Peltola: she is in the lead over Sullivan, with 86% of ballots counted, according to the Associated Press.

We may know the final result in the next few days. According to Alaska’s division of elections, tomorrow is the deadline for them to receive absentee ballots mailed in the US, while next Wednesday is the date they have targeted to receive overseas absentee ballots. On that day, they also plan to review races to see if any candidates have not reached 50%, and, if not, run ranked-choice tabulation.
Should Peltola win, Democrats will have won 56 seats in the US Senate, their largest majority since the 111th Congress that began in 2009 and ended at the start of 2011.

Speaking of things Democrats want to investigate, Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Starlink, the satellite internet service his armed forces rely on to counter Russian drones, is once again unusably slow.

“We have detected speed restrictions on Starshield on our Ukrainian territory – in the temporarily occupied parts of Ukraine. The speed limit is back at 161 kilometers per hour – that’s 100 miles per hour,” Zelenskyy wrote on X earlier today.

“This directly affects our ability to intercept Russian jet-powered ‘shahed’ drones. These drones come from those areas, and because of the speed restrictions, we simply cannot catch up with them in time.”

Starlink is a project of Elon Musk, who Democrats will undoubtedly haul before Congress next year over an array of matters, including his leadership of the Department of Government Efficiency initiative that made widespread cuts to federal staffing and funding. Expect the Starlink throttling to come up at some point as well.
Here’s the latest on the conflict in Ukraine:
Top Senate Democrat Schumer calls for investigation into Nvidia scandal

The Senate’s Democratic minority leader, Chuck Schumer, has called for an investigation both into former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s ties to an alleged Chinese spy, and the Trump administration’s handling of the matter.

The White House reportedly knew about Huang’s involvement with a woman said to be linked to Chinese intelligence, but still let him accompany Donald Trump on an official visit to China. Here’s what Schumer – who may be the Senate majority leader in about two months – had to say about all that:

double quotation markDespite Jensen Huang’s resignation, Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk. The Trump administration must also answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Were government officials told not to investigate because of Trump’s relationship with Mr. Huang? What did Trump know when he personally invited Mr. Huang aboard Air Force One? Americans deserve to know that those at the highest levels of power are putting America first, not their bottom line or their personal friendships.
The Democratic House minority leader, Hakeem Jeffries, is in line to become speaker when his party takes the majority in the chamber next year.

But it won’t be without controversy. Democrats have faced calls from activists and constituents to find another candidate, and a Change.org petition (started by someone who gets paid for such efforts) has received more than 1.15m signatures.

blocks.caption: Hakeem Jeffries at his press conference in the Capitol today. Photograph: Jim Watson/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Asked about these tensions at his press conference, Jeffries issued a lengthy recap of his accomplishments while leading the party in the House during their soon-to-conclude period in the minority. He ended with:

double quotation markThe record speaks for itself. But that doesn’t mean it’s not important to talk to every single member of the House Democratic Caucus family about what the future looks like and how we can build upon this record where everyone doubted our ability to aggressively fight back and continue to bring about the type of bold, dramatic, and decisive change that the American people deserve.
Which is a pretty good sign that Jeffries has no intention of going anywhere next year but the speaker’s office.
For what it’s worth, Donald Trump thinks Apple CEO Tim Cook should take over as head of Nvidia.

“NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!” the president wrote on Truth Social.
Top House Democrat calls for classified briefing on Nvidia scandal
The Democratic House minority leader Hakeem Jeffries just said lawmakers should receive a classified briefing on the scandal surrounding chipmaker Nvidia.

The company is seen as among America’s most important, because it makes advanced chips that are powering the AI boom. Recently, it was revealed that its CEO, Jensen Huang, had an affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy, leading to his resignation today.

“We need a classified briefing made available to members of Congress as it relates to the Nvidia situation and to the extent that our national security has been compromised,” Jeffries said at his ongoing press conference. “The American people deserve answers, and we’re going to work to make sure that happens.”
Here’s more about Huang’s resignation:
The Democratic House minority leader, Hakeem Jeffries, began his press conference today with a few words about the mass shooting in Washington DC.

“Our prayers and our thoughts certainly go out to anyone who has been victimized or hurt by this tragedy, all of the family members and loved ones,” said Jeffries, who is set to become speaker next year, when Democrats take the majority in the House.

“Our thanks go out to the Capitol Police, as well as of course the Metropolitan DC Police Department, and all of our law enforcement professionals [who] continue to work incredibly hard to keep the American people safe, and we’re grateful for their service, encourage their bravery, and their work.”
Here’s the latest on the shooting in the Logan Circle neighborhood:

articles.title: Widespread outages reported across Microsoft apps
articles.summary: A widespread outage hit Microsoft platforms including Outlook on Thursday, with many users encountering trouble using their email accounts and other errors across the tech giant's suite of apps.

image.caption: Tens of thousands of Microsoft users reported issues with email and other apps Thursday in a widespread outage. (Dado Ruvic/Illustration/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New
A widespread outage hit Microsoft platforms including Outlook on Thursday, with many users encountering trouble using their email accounts and other errors across the tech giant's suite of apps.
Nearly 130,000 users reported problems on Downtracker at its peak around midday

Nearly 130,000 users on outage tracker Downdetector reported problems accessing Outlook just after 1 p.m. ET. New reports have since fallen from that peak, but many said they couldn't send and receive emails, or had trouble loading their inboxes altogether.
Thousands also reported issues with Microsoft's workplace messaging app Teams, as well as its AI assistant Copilot and wider Microsoft 365 services.
Microsoft said it was investigating disruptions, notably related to its email and Teams applications.
In updates posted on social media, Microsoft said it was aware of users "experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas."

We're investigating reports of users experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas. More details can be found in the Microsoft 365 admin center under EX1550543.—MSFT365Status

Microsoft later explained that a portion of its infrastructure was "experiencing elevated load," which it said was "likely contributing to the connectivity errors." The company determined a number of servers were "unexpectedly unavailable" due to a problem that caused them to fail during automated checks.
CBC News has reached out to Microsoft for details about how users in Canada are affected.
Microsoft did not immediately provide more information around what might be causing the failure, but said it was testing a fix.
Microsoft's Visitor Centre in Redmond, Wa. The company said 'elevated load' was likely the cause of connectivity errors users encountered. (Lindsey Wasson/The Associated Press)
"We're aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact," the Microsoft 365 Status account wrote on X.
Earlier in the day, the company said it had "successfully restored" problems related to Microsoft Teams in North America, although some users continued to report connectivity issues.

articles.title: Original Star Wars returning to theatres for 50th anniversary
articles.summary: If you missed the chance to see Star Wars in the theatre in 1977 — or weren't yet born — you'll get another chance on Feb. 19, when Disney re-releases both the original film and a 70-millimetre Imax…

image.caption: Director George Lucas speaks with Anthony Daniels, in costume as C-3PO, during shooting of 1977's Star Wars. Disney will re-release the film next year to mark its 50th anniversary, along with a documentary about its production and a new entrant in the franchise, Star Wars: Starfighter. (Walt Disney

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

If you missed the chance to see Star Wars in the theatre in 1977 — or weren't yet born — you'll get another chance on Feb. 19, when Disney re-releases both the original film and a 70-millimetre Imax version to mark its 50th anniversary.
Disney also marking the year with 2nd season of Ahsoka and the new movie Star Wars: Starfighter
Missed the initial release of Star Wars in 1977? Maybe you thought it looked weird, didn't want to line up for tickets, or — if you're under 50 — you just weren't born yet.
You'll get another chance on Feb. 19, when Disney re-releases both the original film and a 70-millimetre Imax version to mark its anniversary.

"It is incredibly special to mark the 50th anniversary by returning the original version of Star Wars to theatres so audiences can experience this part of film history on the big screen," said Lynwen Brennan, co-president of Lucasfilm, in a press release.

This won't be the first time Star Wars — now also known as Star Wars: A New Hope — has returned to theatres. For its 20th anniversary, in 1997, creator George Lucas rereleased it with a number of changes, including some CGI touchups, additional scenes and — infamously — the villainous Greedo shooting at Han Solo first in the Mos Eisley Cantina scene.
Disney — which bought the franchise and Lucasfilm in 2012 — says the upcoming release will be a "restored version" of the 1977 film.
The franchise has been under the leadership of Brennan and Dave Filoni since Kathleen Kennedy stepped down in January.

The re-release is part of a slate of projects for 2027, which will also include a new season of the live-action series Ahsoka, a documentary on the making of A New Hope, and the theatrical release of Star Wars: Starfighter.
Ryan Gosling, left, and Shawn Levy speak on stage at Comic-Con in San Diego, Calif., on July 25, 2026. Levy will direct Gosling in next year's new Star Wars film. (Amy Sussman/Getty Images)
The new movie will hit theatres on May 28 and feature a pair of Canadians.

Ryan Gosling (The Fall Guy, Blade Runner 2049) will star as a cynical rogue (sound familiar?) who has a mysterious past and is thrust into a galactic adventure, working under Montreal-born director Shawn Levy, best known for Big Fat Liar, Night at the Museum and, most recently, Deadpool & Wolverine.
The film will take place five years after the events of 2019's The Rise of Skywalker, according to Lucasfilm.

It will be the first Star Wars film in theatres since last year's The Mandalorian and Grogu, which broke the drought since Rise of Skywalker but grossed just $345.8 US million worldwide, making it the franchise's lowest grossing live-action film ever.

The franchise has recently had better luck on the small screen and will release the second season of Ahsoka on Disney+ on Jan. 20, bringing back both Rosario Dawson as the titular former jedi and Hayden Christensen as Anakin Skywalker.
It will pick up where the first season left off, as Ahsoka chases down Grand Admiral Thrawn, a former leader of the Empire who has once again declared war on the Rebel Alliance.
The show will also feature Rory McCann as the recast antagonist Baylan Skol, following the death of Ray Stevenson in 2023.
The documentary The Hero Awakens will be released on Disney+ on May 4 — also known as Star Wars Day.

From filmmaker R.J. Cutler, best known for documentaries such as 1993's The War Room and The September Issue it will, according to a press release, feature never-seen-before archival footage and audio from the making of the 1977 film.
A new poster for 1977's Star Wars by artist Matt Ferguson marks its return to theatres in 2027. (Walt Disney Studios)
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Philip Drost is a network senior writer for CBC News based in Fredericton. You can reach him at philip.drost@cbc.ca.

articles.title: China rules out hosting Cop33 climate summit in 2028
articles.summary:
Decision disappoints experts hoping for world’s biggest emitter to take global lead on climate crisis

China has ruled out hosting the Cop33 UN climate summit in 2028 after months of…

blocks.text: China has ruled out hosting the Cop33 UN climate summit in 2028 after months of deliberations, leaving the field open for other Asian countries to hold it, the Guardian understands.

The decision will disappoint many countries and climate experts, who had hoped the world’s biggest emitter would take the lead on the global stage, as the US under Donald Trump has vacated all forms of international cooperation on the climate.

Al Gore, the former US vice-president, was among those left disheartened by the decision. “I would be very much in favour of that idea [of China hosting the summit],” he told the Guardian. “It’s too bad.”

China is in the midst of an economic transformation, from being heavily dependent on coal to becoming an “electro state”. John Kerry, the former US secretary of state, told the Guardian that China was leaving the rest of the world behind in forging and using the low-carbon technologies of the future.

Renewable energy generation capacity has now outstripped coal in China, and its greenhouse gas emissions appear to have declined slightly this year. Sales of electric vehicles in the country have also taken off, making up nearly two-thirds of the market last month, and China’s clean energy industries drove more than 90% of the country’s investment growth last year.
The rules of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) mean an Asian country should host in 2028.

blocks.caption: A robot shows off its moves at the China Pavilion on the sidelines of Cop31 in Turkey this week. Photograph: Rasit Aydogan/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Gareth Redmond-King, the international lead at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit thinktank, said China’s position as an industrial powerhouse would have made it a formidable contender to hold the summit.

“It would undoubtedly be significant for the world’s biggest emitter and second-biggest economy to host a climate Cop,” he said. “They’re leading the world on investment, manufacture and deployment of clean energy tech, and their emissions have started to tick down. As a leadership story, China hosting Cop33 would be a big deal.”

It is not clear why China has decided against hosting the conference, but several experts that spoke to the Guardian suggested that the US electoral cycle was likely to have been a factor. The next US presidential election will take place on 7 November 2028, and Cop33 is scheduled for 6 to 17 November that year.

After the strong showing by Democrats in the recent midterm elections, in which voter concern over the climate crisis was thought to be a factor, the Democrats will be hoping to elect a climate-friendly president in 2028. But even if they succeed, Trump will still be in office until the following January.
The US president rejects climate science and withdrew the US from the Paris agreement, and is also withdrawing from its parent treaty, the 1992 UNFCCC.
after newsletter promotion

China seeks to be seen as a leader among developing countries, but has been wary of stepping into the gap left by the US. Under the Democratic presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama, the US and China enjoyed a close partnership on climate issues, setting joint targets on reducing methane and developing clean technology.

Cop33 will be an important meeting because it will include the “global stocktake” – a mechanism under the 2015 Paris climate agreement that examines countries’ progress on cutting emissions in line with the goal of limiting global temperature rises to 1.5C. That limit is now certain to be surpassed, but experts say countries should now try to minimise the temperature “overshoot”, to avoid worse ravages from extreme weather.

India’s government considered offering to host Cop33 for several months earlier this year, but also decided against it. India’s coal use has been increasing, even as the country exceeds its own renewable energy targets.

The Guardian understands that other countries mulling a bid to host Cop33 include Uzbekistan, South Korea, Indonesia and Thailand. No decision on a host is likely to be made at this year’s Cop31 meeting, which is ongoing in Turkey, with the Turkish and Australian governments jointly presiding over the summit.

articles.title: EU leaders tussle over whom to send to Ukraine, Russia peace talks
articles.summary: A seat at the table for Europe now appears likely following comments by a US envoy who just held talks with Putin. But who will take that seat remains unclear.

image.caption: Who could Europe send to peace talks to stand by Ukraine's side?Image: Olivier Hoslet/REUTERS

blocks.text: European leaders are under pressure to put forward a name to represent them in Ukraine peace talks after US envoy Steve Witkoff told reporters that the Europeans will be present at the next meetings.

When asked by DW during the European Political Community summit in Dublin why Europe should only get one seat at the table while the US gets two, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas responded with a wry, ironic laugh ― clearly a sign of the frustration felt by European leaders about being sidelined thus far.

The summit of 47 European leaders in Dublin comes in the wake of a diplomatic tour by two Donald Trump administration advisers, the president's son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, to talks in Abu Dhabi, followed by a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.
The pair then hot-footed their way to Dublin to debrief Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelekenskyy.
Zelenskyy and Kushner also said Thursday that Europeans would be at the table for the next talks with Russia on ending the war.

blocks.caption: Steve Witkoff (center) and Jared Kushner (right) received a friendly welcome from the Russian president in MoscowImage: Vyacheslav Prokofiev/Sputnik/REUTERS

blocks.text: Kallas is one of the figures tipped as most likely to represent the EU in any future talks to end Russia's war against Ukraine, alongside EU Council President Antonio Costa. As yet, the EU hasn’t been able to land on one central figure to send ― many of the national leaders want to be present themselves.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz insisted Europe will be present.
"At the table must be sitting Ukraine, must be sitting the Europeans, must be sitting the Americans, and naturally Russia," he told reporters in Dublin.
But he, like many other leaders, played down the idea of appointing a special envoy for the talks.

blocks.caption: EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas is one of the people who could potentially represent the bloc at talksImage: Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP

blocks.text: A divided Europe
Zelenskyy is insistent on European involvement in the peace talks.

"Not directly yet, and not yet when the Russians are at the table," he told the other leaders during the Dublin meetings. "But Europeans are already involved. And we need to make sure that Europe becomes a regular part of these negotiations."

Europe’s division over exactly who should be present has caused a public battle to erupt. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote an excoriating letter to Costa last week, bemoaning the lack of unity.
"By projecting the image of a Europe that is in disarray, we are merely serving the interests of those who want this war to continue," wrote Meloni.
European leaders had even seemed divided over their level of frustration about the situation.

Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Jansa said in Dublin that it was creating a "bad mood" among leaders, however Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs disputed those comments saying, "I don’t feel that."
Europe seeks role in Ukraine peace talks
European security at stake

The palpable fear among the leaders in Dublin is that the US will accept Russia's demands that Europe changes the way it structures its own security, mainly through the NATO military alliance, in exchange for a seat at the table.
Putin said a commitment that Ukraine will never join NATO and even the potential rolling back of the alliance to remove new joiners Finland and Sweden, could be among his demands.

"What do we hear from them [Europeans]?" asked Putin during the meeting with Kushner and Witkoff in Moscow. "That once a peace agreement is signed, they will immediately deploy troops in Ukraine. This is a legitimate target for us, so the war will resume immediately."
This is exactly the kind of rhetoric the European leaders say they are most wary of, especially those in Russia’s direct neighborhood.
"Right now, we are in the [Russian] trap," said Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal. "If something is a threat to you, will you discuss your defense with the threat [itself]?"
Latvia: Sanctions on Russia needed for peace in Ukraine
US President Donald Trump said publicly that he was hoping for a "very big, beautiful agreement" that "might involve all of Europe."
Zelensky said he found the US approach "a bit strange."
Many of Europe's leaders speaking in Dublin referenced previous agreements with Russia that they believe Moscow has breached.

They include the 1975 Helsinki Accords, the 1990 Paris Charter, 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act and the one they consider most important: the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, which forbids Russia from using force against Ukraine unless in self-defense.
Financial support for Ukraine
The rancor over the seat at the peace talks is drawing focus away from arguably the bigger battle in the EU now ― how to fund Ukraine as the war continues.
Back in October, the European Commission identified a €70 billion hole in the EU’s funding it had promised for Ukraine’s economy.
Slovakia’s Prime Minister Robert Fico has opposed any further financial and military support for Ukraine.
But Germany's Merz warned he could block the EU's next seven-year budget unless member states agree to contribute to Ukraine's financing.
Merz accused of 'blackmail' over Ukraine funding

articles.title: Russian federation head Tretiak says it will seek compensation if barred from world juniors in Alberta
articles.summary: Russian hockey federation president Vladislav Tretiak is threatening to seek compensation from Canada and push for the relocation or cancellation of next month's world junior championship in Alberta…

image.caption: Russian hockey federation president Vladislav Tretiak, seen in 2024, says the federation will seek compensation from Canada and push for relocation of next month's world junior championship in Alberta if the country is barred. (Alexander Nemenov/AFP via Getty Images)

blocks.text: Hockey

Russian hockey federation president Vladislav Tretiak is threatening to seek compensation from Canada and push for the relocation or cancellation of next month's world junior championship in Alberta if Russia is barred from competing.
Tretiak: 'move the championship, not hold it at all or impose sanctions on Canada'

The warning comes after Ottawa confirmed Wednesday that Russian players would not be permitted to compete, even if they already hold valid Canadian visas, despite last month's Court of Arbitration for Sport ruling ordering Russia's reinstatement to international hockey.

Russia's state news agency TASS reported Thursday that Tretiak told a presidential sports council meeting Russia would also seek compensation from Germany, host of the 2027 men's world championship, if denied participation.
"There are rules: if a team does not take the ice, it receives a forfeit loss and sanctions are imposed," Tretiak told TASS in comments translated from Russian.
"The IIHF has a way out — either allow us to participate or, if we cannot enter Canada, move the championship, not hold it at all or impose sanctions on Canada."

Tretiak, a legendary Soviet goaltender and three-time Olympic gold medallist, also told TASS the Russian federation had asked the International Ice Hockey Federation's ethics council to investigate and punish national federations organizing boycotts of games against Russia.

items: Canadian government says Russian players with visas will still be barred from WJC

blocks.text: Russian President Vladimir Putin told the same sports council meeting that national federations were refusing matches against Russian teams under pressure from their governments, according to TASS, which did not identify the countries involved.
Several hockey federations, including Finland, Sweden, Czechia and Norway, have said their teams will refuse to face Russia.

The dispute follows an Oct. 30 ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport ordering the IIHF to allow Russian teams to participate in five international tournaments, beginning with the world juniors in Edmonton and Red Deer on Dec. 26.
Alex Ovechkin suggests fans want Russian players at World Juniors
Russia and Belarus have been banned from international hockey competition since Russia invaded Ukraine with Belarusian assistance in 2022.
Prime Minister Mark Carney said last week that Russian and Belarusian athletes would not be permitted to represent their countries in Canada as long as the war continues.
The federal government's earlier position allowed individual athletes to compete as neutrals, raising questions about whether a Russian team could participate under a neutral designation.
Secretary of State for Sport Adam van Koeverden clarified Monday that the exemption applied only to individual athletes, not national teams.

In a statement Wednesday, van Koeverden said Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada would assess Russian and Belarusian athletes and officials individually to prevent them from competing at the men's under-20 tournament in Alberta, even if they hold valid Canadian visas.

items: Canada's secretary of sport questions Russia competing as neutrals at Alberta world juniors
Norway says it has been bumped by the IIHF to allow Russia to compete at world juniors in Canada

blocks.text: There are Russian players with valid visas competing in the Canadian Hockey League, the umbrella organization for the country's three major junior hockey leagues.

Russian and Belarusian players were banned from the CHL's import draft from 2022-24 before being allowed back in. According to the CHL, Russia led this year's draft with 32 of the 114 players selected.
The controversy has also thrown Norway's participation into question.
Norway's hockey federation said Sunday the IIHF had informed it that Russia would be added to the world junior tournament at Norway's expense.
Norway qualified for the championship and has said it still hopes to compete.

The IIHF has not formally announced any changes to the tournament field, and its website continues to list Norway among the 10 participating teams. The federation did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the possibility of cancelling or relocating the tournament.
The world junior championship will conclude on Jan. 5.

articles.title: ‘Win-win’ deal with EU could be done, Andy Burnham says
articles.summary:
Prime minister says reset could be a deal ‘like the Brexit people thought they were voting for in 2016’

Andy Burnham has said he believes a “win-win” deal could be done with the EU that…
articles.byline: Jennifer Rankin, Jessica Elgot, Lisa O’Carroll and Pippa Crerar

blocks.text: Andy Burnham has said he believes a “win-win” deal could be done with the EU that could be “more like the Brexit that people thought they were voting for in 2016”.

The prime minister was meeting fellow leaders at the European Political Community summit in Dublin, ahead of a keenly anticipated EU-UK summit next week, where he hopes to bring Britain closer to Europe.

At the bilateral summit the EU and UK hope to sign deals on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme, but the question of tuition fees for European students remains a stumbling block.
He said: “I believe there is a good deal to be done that could be a win-win for Britain and Europe.
“The deal is not done, and there’ll be some long nights ahead in the next seven days,” Burnham said.

blocks.caption: Andy Burnham, left, and the president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, attend a bilateral meeting at the European Political Community summit in Dublin. Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/Pool PA/AP

blocks.text: He said the reset would be about whether we can “take a step back to closer working relationships with Europe”.
Burnham added: “We ended up with a far harder Brexit, I think, than people thought they were getting when they went to the polls.”
The EU has said the prized food and drink deal and emissions-trading agreement may not enter into force without a deal on tuition fees in which European students would pay domestic rates.

Burnham said it was a package deal, but would notbe drawn on whether he accepted the link. “I’m going to be fighting hard for these benefits for Britain in the next seven days … They will make a real difference. If I can do anything to address the cost of living crisis, I should be doing it.”
He has previously said the food and drink deal, which will ease Brexit red tape, will add 0.4% to British GDP.
Burnham is expected to make the EU reset the centrepiece of his white-tie speech at the lord mayor’s banquet on Monday night – though it will range widely across foreign policy challenges.

No 10 sources said the speech would be focused on the upcoming Brussels summit – and look ahead to the next stage in 2027 – rather than outline what a more permanent close relationship might look like.
Officials at the UK-EU summit will also discuss the agenda for the next round of the reset, expected to focus on a joint migration pact.
after newsletter promotion
It could also target collaboration on law enforcement and borders, visas for touring artists, and mutual recognition of qualifications.

Ministry of Justice officials are also trying to water down an EU ultimatum on halting the deportation of foreign national offenders. “This is the classic wheeze that the EU always pulls at the last minute of negotiations,” one Whitehall source said.

The next week is expected to be fraught with last-minute negotiations. Key will be access to Made in Europe, which has the potential to lock British firms out of continental supply chains and public contracts if no deal is done. Negotiations could be challenging despite the lure of the UK making a potential concession on tuition fees in exchange for inclusion in the Made in Europe legislation.
The EU has long said there cannot be a deal on Made in Europe at the summit, because it has yet to finalise its own position.
The joint communique for 2027 is expected to call for strengthening efforts between the UK and the most exposed member states to the small boats crisis in the Channel.
This will centre on both the EU’s Channel action plan, already in place since June this year, and a possible framework for a wider bespoke EU-UK migration plan.

The UK is believed to be pushing for access to the Eurodac database, which carriesthe fingerprints of asylum seekers, as well as to the Schengen Information System (SIS), which records details on fugitives, missing people and stolen goods. The UK was the third biggest user of SIS before it lost access through Brexit.

articles.title: Russian warship hit by Ukrainian drone in Gulf of Finland
articles.summary: The attack is thought to be the first time Ukrainian drones have attacked a Russian ship in an open stretch of the Baltic Sea.

blocks.text: Finnish officials have confirmed that a Russian warship was attacked in the Gulf of Finland on Wednesday, although little is known about the strike.
Ukraine's SBU security service said it targeted the ship Naro-Fominsk as part of a broader drone operation against Russia's Ust-Luga oil export depot on the Baltic coast.

The attack, thought to be the first time Ukrainian drones have attacked a Russian ship in an area of the Baltic Sea open to civilian maritime traffic, has raised questions about whether Ukraine could expand its strikes.
Helsinki has been one of Kyiv's closest European allies, and Finnish officials have described the incident as a direct result of Russia's continued full-scale war.
Finland's military has given few details of the incident, but it appears to have taken place in a narrow stretch some distance from the Finnish coast.
The country's Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen was adamant that the situation in the Baltic Sea remained stable and safe and that there was no threat of any kind to marine traffic.
Defence officials are understood to have stressed to Kyiv that the Gulf is a relatively narrow waterway used by oil tankers and civilian vessels, and is also home to subsea data cables.

Ukraine's SBU described the Russian ship as a Buyan-M type small corvette that carried Kalibr and Oniks cruise missiles. There were also unconfirmed reports of Russian combat helicopters being destroyed.

Martin Herem, the defence minister of Estonia, which borders the Gulf, told public broadcaster ERR that the ship was hit at about 05:30 (03:30 GMT) on Wednesday but did not say how it was attacked: "We know that smoke came from the ship afterwards. The ship itself went back towards St Petersburg."
The extent of casualties or damage sustained by the Russian navy ship remains unclear, and Moscow rarely gives such details.

"The Baltic Sea fleet has been untouched up to this point but there seemingly was a window of opportunity for Ukraine and they understandably tried to use it," said military analyst Emil Kastehelmi, co-founder of the Black Bird monitoring group.

Russian and Ukrainian vessels have been repeatedly targeted in the Black Sea since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, but even though the latest strike on a ship in the Baltic is unprecedented, Kastehelmi told the BBC he did not consider it a serious escalation.

Ukrainian drones are regularly launched into Russia from northern Ukraine. Several storage tanks at the Ust-Luga terminal are thought to have been hit overnight on Wednesday and fires at the port were visible over the border in Estonia.
Herem said Ukrainian drones attacked the Ust-Luga region from midnight until about 06:00, mostly flying close to the Estonian border but still in Russian airspace.
He added that one drone had entered Estonian airspace briefly from Latvia and then headed towards Russia.
Nato aircraft based in the Baltic states were in the air at the time, but Herem said it had not been considered safe for them to destroy the drones.

Ukrainian foreign ministry spokesman Heorhiy Tykhyy said late on Wednesday that Moscow's allegations that Kyiv had used the airspace of the Baltic states to attack Russia were "baseless", although he acknowledged "incidents might occur when Russia diverts drones from its airspace using electronic warfare".

articles.title: Jensen Huang has resigned, what's next for Nvidia?
articles.summary: The BBC's Samira Hussain reports from Wall Street on what the fall of the tech superstar means for the company and AI.

blocks.text: Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO of tech giant Nvidia, the company's board says, with chief financial officer Colette Kress appointed interim boss.
The company's shares have recovered some ground after plummeting more than 13% when US markets opened shortly after news of Huang's resignation.
The BBC's North America correspondent Samira Hussain explains what's next for the company.

articles.title: Will U.S. travel pick up after midterm 'blue wave'? Not so fast, say these Canadians
articles.summary: Travel from Canada to the U.S. dropped amid President Donald Trump's threats and trade war. While many Canadians view the Democratic Party's midterm election victory as an 'encouraging' sign, they…

image.caption: Cars wait to enter the U.S. from Windsor, Ont., at the Windsor-Detroit Tunnel on Feb. 27. While the midterm results have some Canadians more open to U.S. travel, others plan to wait until U.S. President Donald Trump is no longer in office. (Dax Melmer/CBC)

blocks.text: World

Travel from Canada to the U.S. dropped amid President Donald Trump's threats and trade war. While many Canadians view the Democratic Party's midterm election victory as an 'encouraging' sign, they say it's too soon to visit the U.S. again amid continued distrust.
Many Canadians have been boycotting U.S. travel amid Trump's tariffs and other threats
· CBC News
· Posted: Nov 12, 2026 2:24 PM EST | Last Updated: 36 minutes ago
John May had low expectations ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.
But he was glad to see the Democratic Party take control of both chambers of Congress in a Nov. 3 vote that many observers have described as a resounding rebuke of U.S. President Donald Trump.
"It's encouraging, isn't it? To see that there's finally some common sense coming around down there," said the 73-year-old from Manotick, Ont., an Ottawa suburb.

items: How will Republicans and Democrats move forward after midterms?
Americans in Canada hope midterm results will help mend ties between both countries

blocks.text: May, who stopped travelling to the United States last year amid Trump's repeated threats against Canada, said he and his wife Patti aren't ready to go south of the border again just yet though.
The couple had spent winters in Florida for more than a decade before May said the atmosphere turned "toxic" as Trump mocked Canadian leaders and pushed to turn Canada into the "51st state."
"We'd like to, but we're not feeling like we want to go back yet," May told CBC News.
"I think we've got to wait until they've got a different president down there and a whole different attitude," he said. "Things haven't changed enough. We'll need a couple more years, I think."
John and Patti May pose for a photo in Key West, Fla., in February 2024. (Submitted by John May)
Drop in travel
Many Canadians, including those with relatives or business interests south of the border, have continued to travel to the U.S. amid Trump's threats and the trade war with Canada.
But data shows travel to the U.S. has dropped alongside the strained relationship.
According to Statistics Canada, return border crossings from the U.S. fell by about 25 per cent in 2025 compared with the previous year.

items: Are you changing your holiday plans due to the cost of domestic airfare in Canada? Getting creative to find cheaper alternatives? Send an email to ask@cbc.ca.

blocks.text: There has been a slight increase in 2026: A total of 1.9 million return trips by car and air from the U.S. were reported in October, marking the seventh consecutive month of year-over-year growth and a three per cent increase from October 2025, Statistics Canada reported.
But when compared with October 2024, return trips by car were down 29 per cent while those by air were down 19.6 per cent.
Elbows up or down? Windsorites are mixed on returning to the U.S. post-midterms
Possible 'softening' of travel plans
It's too soon to say whether the midterms will lead to a major increase in Canadian travel south.
McKenzie McMillan, a travel consultant and co-owner of The Travel Group in Vancouver, said that, anecdotally, there may be some "softening" around U.S. travel.

"But it hasn't really translated at this point into new bookings, or a real change in the overall sentiment to avoid the United States," McMillan said. "We are still hearing overall that travellers are looking to alternative destinations for their winter travel and beyond."

Spokespersons for Air Canada and Porter Airlines also told CBC this week that it was too early to say whether the midterms have had an effect on travel. Air Transat said it did not have sufficient data to identify a trend.
What the U.S. midterm results could mean for border cities
But the midterms may help ease the negative feelings that some Canadians have had.

Marja Vermeer, a 67-year-old from Strathroy, Ont., said the vote results, coupled with messages over the past two years from Americans rejecting the Trump administration's attacks against Canada, make her more open to visiting the U.S.
"Especially to the states where they voted Democrat, I think they're ... a bit more comfortable and a bit more welcoming," she said.
Midterms provide 'great relief'
Jill Ellis-Worthington, 65, of London, Ont., also said the midterms made a recent trip to the U.S. more palatable.

Ellis-Worthington — who is originally from the U.S. but has been living in Canada since age 25 — said she went to her home country this month to deal with issues at a Texas property she owns. It was her first visit since 2024, and one she had put off for as long as possible.

items: Windsor residents not ready to return to U.S. despite Democratic midterm wins
How the Democrats' midterm wave shows a path back to the presidency

blocks.text: "There's just so much chaos and so much denial of everything that is America going on now with the government, so I just didn't want to support that in any way," she told CBC.
"I think there are a lot of people who feel great relief [after the midterms] and feel that there might be some light on the horizon."

Ellis-Worthington said Americans had been "nothing but friendly, gracious [and] hospitable" during her trip. But she acknowledged that some Canadians likely won't be going back soon, despite last week's vote. "And some won't ever go back, I don’t think."
The Peace Bridge U.S.-Canada border crossing is seen on March 20 in Buffalo, N.Y. (Yuki Iwamura/The Associated Press)
Distrust persists

Indeed, the new Congress doesn't take office until January, and many observers say the Trump administration's policies — including an immigration crackdown that has led to the detention of several Canadian citizens in recent months — continue to fuel distrust.
Mary Thurber, who lives in Lake Country in B.C.'s Okanagan Valley, said she has avoided going to the U.S. for several reasons.

"It's a combination of anger at their policies and disgust with some of the treatment of their own citizens, and frankly, a little bit of fear," said Thurber, 70. "And do I want to support the economy of ... an administration that is actively attacking my country?"
But she said visiting the U.S. is now "an active discussion" in her home after the midterms.

"My husband sometimes says, 'I know! Let's only go to the blue states,'" she said with a laugh. "And I'm like, 'Yeah but that doesn't quite deal with the fact that their president is still actively attacking us.'"
Thurber said she doesn't know when she might feel comfortable going back, adding she expects the Trump administration's policies to have a lasting impact. "That's a hard one," she said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jillian Kestler-D'Amours is a senior writer at CBC based in Montreal. You can reach her at jillian.kestler-d.amours@cbc.ca.
With files from Nisha Patel and Tess Ha

articles.title: Plane with mechanical problems makes 'successful' landing at St. John's International Airport
articles.summary: Emergency vehicles rushed to a PAL aircraft that landed at the St. John's International Airport around 4:10 p.m. NT.

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador·Breaking
Emergency vehicles rushed to a PAL aircraft that landed at the St. John's International Airport around 4:10 p.m. NT.
PAL Airlines plane appeared to be missing a wheel
Emergency crews on scene after plane lands in St. John's
A plane with mechanical problems made a "successful" landing in St. John's Thursday afternoon, according to police.
Emergency vehicles rushed to a PAL Airlines aircraft that landed at St. John's International Airport around 4:10 p.m. NT. on Thursday.

Prior to the plane landing, in an exchange between a PAL Airlines flight and air traffic control broadcast on the website LiveATC.net, a member of the flight crew indicated a plane had lost a wheel on take off from Happy Valley-Goose Bay.
A wheel appeared to be missing when a PAL plane flew over a CBC News crew Thursday evening.

The Royal Newfoundland Constabulary confirmed officers responded to a call at the airport Thursday afternoon due to an inbound flight with reported mechanical problems. After a "successful landing," officers left, a spokesperson said.
CBC News asked the airport authority for information and spokesperson Ryan Howell deferred all inquiries to the airline. PAL Airlines has not yet responded as of publication time.
Less than two weeks ago, CBC News reported on a PAL flight where a wheel fell off upon landing in Wabush.
More to come.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Maddie Ryan is a reporter with CBC News in St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador. Reach her at madison.ryan@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Pete Hegseth honors soldier who scolded him at Arlington cemetery
articles.summary: The soldier had reprimanded the US Defense Secretary and his group after they were heard talking and laughing at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. The site is one of the most solemn military memorials…

image.caption: The embattled defense secretary has been under fire over the Iran warImage: Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has awarded a soldier who reprimanded him and his entourage for laughing at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on Wednesday.
Hegseth posted photos on his X account on Thursday that show him giving the Joint Service Commendation Medal to Specialist Thomas Iglesias "for the execution of his duties."
"We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist," Hegseth said alongside the photos.
The Joint Service Commendation Medal is seen as one of the US military's top awards and is not usually given to junior enlisted service members.
What happened at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier?

In footage that was widely shared on social media, Iglesias was seen forcefully reprimanding Hegseth and a group that included his wife and some of his staffers, who were heard talking and laughing while taking photos on the steps in front of the tomb.
Iglesias shouted: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times!"

blocks.caption: Hegseth and his wife Jennifer had attended a ceremony to mark Veterans' Day before the incidentImage: Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Soon after the video emerged, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell praised Iglesias for "correctly and respectfully" reminding Hegseth and his party to "maintain decorum."
The public reprimand comes the same week that the under-fire defense secretary survived an impeachment attempt over his handling of the war with Iran.
US President Donald Trump pointed to the war as a major factor behind his Republican Party's stunning defeats in midterm elections last week.
In his first press conference in months on Tuesday, Hegseth slammed the impeachment attempt as a "farce, a stunt" and "sabotage."
US Defense Secretary Hegseth faces impeachment over Iran war
What is the importance of the site?
The tomb at Arlington National Cemetery outside Washington D.C. is considered of the most solemn military monuments in the US.
It is the burial site of US military personnel killed during World War I, World War II and the Korean War. It also features an empty site to honor missing soldiers from the Vietnam War.
Since 1948, the tomb has been guarded around the clock by a soldier from the US Army's 3rd Infantry Regiment, which is known as "The Old Guard," according to the cemetery's website.

articles.title: Nigeria: Axe-wielding men attack opposition campaign rally in Lagos
articles.summary: A group of men armed with axes, clubs and machetes have reportedly attacked an opposition rally in the run-up to presidential elections. Journalists were also attacked as victims pointed fingers at…

image.caption: Eyewitnesses say men armed with axes, clubs and machetes attacked supporters of opposition candidate Peter Obi on ThursdayImage: Sunday Alamba/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: A group of armed men rushed a campaign event in Nigeria on Thursday, attacking journalists and supporters of opposition candidate Peter Obi at a political rally two months before the country's January 16, 2027, presidential election.

Videos uploaded to social media captured the mid-morning incident, showing men armed with axes, clubs and machetes barging into an event center in Lagos, where they attacked supporters of Nigerian Democratic Congress (NDC) candidate Obi.
Supporters, who vowed they would not be intimidated, blamed the attack on the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC). APC spokesman Felix Morka rejected the claim, citing a lack of evidence.

The NDC has also accused the APC of being behind the forced cancellation of several of its campaign events, claiming the government of President Bola Tinubu is pressuring venue owners to turn them away.
Here, too, the government has denied the accusations.

blocks.caption: Opposition NDC supporters battled thugs in the street after chasing them out of a campaign event Image: Sunday Alamba/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Fighting spills into the street
Violence is a regular feature of Nigeria's elections and is often carried out by individuals colloquially referred to as "thugs."
Eyewitnesses on Thursday said the attackers, "came into the hall, [and] broke all the entrance doors and the glass walls."
"The NDC guys repelled them, chased them out of the hall into the road," one eyewitness added.

blocks.caption: Eyewitnesses said it took police more than an hour to arrive at the sceneImage: Sunday Alamba/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: After that, the two groups engaged in pitched street battles for over an hour before police arrived on the scene and began firing tear gas to disperse them.
Security officials on the scene said they had not been on site to protect participants when the violence broke out because they had not been notified of the event.
Journalist attacked, robbed
A local journalist attacked in the melee described being hit with an axe as well as being punched and kicked before thugs made off with all of his equipment.
"I tried to resist, so they started attacking me" said Sam Adebanjo of the online out TheCable.
"I eventually yielded and surrendered the devices when one of them kept shouting, 'Leave the camera — do you want them to kill you?'"
Peter Obi: 'I will not lose' — but can he deliver?
Oil-rich Nigeria, Africa's most populous country, ranked 112 out of 180 countries in the Reporters Without Borders 2026 World Press Freedom Index.

January's election will pit President Bola Tinubu, who is seeking his second term in office: against Obi, who placed third in the country's 2023 election; and Atiku Abubakar, who was runner-up in 2023.
Abubakar is facing legal challenges to his candidacy and accuses Tinubu's government of trying to push him out of the way with lawfare, a charge the APC also denies.

articles.title: Eddie's dead: What one monarch's ill-fated journey can teach us about migration patterns
articles.summary: In this issue of our environmental newsletter, we track the demise of a monarch named Eddie and find out what it says about monarch migration, map the threats faced by freshwater animals and find out…

blocks.text: Welcome to our weekly newsletter where we highlight environmental trends and solutions that are moving us to a more sustainable world.

Hey, it’s Bryce. I became monarch-obsessed as they boomed this summer on the Prairies. I documented scientists attaching radio trackers to the endangered butterflies. I continue to follow their migration to Mexico on the Project Monarch app — including the journey of one nicknamed Eddie.
This week:

items: Eddie's dead: What one monarch's ill-fated journey can teach us about migration patterns
The Big Picture: Mapping freshwater threats
Sewing is having a moment. Here’s why

blocks.text: Eddie's dead: What one monarch's ill-fated journey can teach us about migration patterns

A monarch butterfly, nicknamed Eddie by researchers, sports a new radio tracker and antenna on its back after being trapped, tagged and released at the Living Prairie Museum in Winnipeg on Aug. 26. It was the first time monarchs — 29 in total — have been tagged with such transmitters on the Canadian Prairies as part of a Canadian Wildlife Service project. (Bryce Hoye/CBC)
Lauran Burns had the highest of hopes for a butterfly she nicknamed Eddie.

He was the first of 29 endangered monarchs that she and scientists in Winnipeg outfitted with toothpick-sized solar powered radio trackers using eyelash glue, then set free to migrate to central Mexico.
But after a remarkable 1,200-kilometre flight, Eddie's signal went dark in early October — at the edge of a cul de sac near a cemetery southwest of Kansas City.
"Just giving one of the butterflies a name … I feel like we connected to Eddie more than the others," said Burns, conservation program manager at the Assiniboine Park Zoo in Winnipeg.
"[There's] a sad acceptance, I guess, that it's likely he's not going to make the full trip."

Data from Project Monarch and Environment and Climate Change Canada shows the migration path of two of the 29 butterflies tagged in Manitoba — including Eddie, who was southwest of Kansas City as of Thursday, and MB26011, who made it to Mexico on Tuesday. (CBC News Graphics)
Those that make the full trip converge by the millions at a mountaintop World Heritage Site of oyamel fir forests in central Mexico, where they rest until spring.
Far fewer have made the pilgrimage south in the past 15 years or so.

"About 15 to 20 years ago … there were so many, it was like every 10 feet, if you ran through the clover, it was like a dust of monarchs coming up," said Teddie Laframboise, who farms primarily hay in the south of Ottawa.
"It seems to have been going down and down, and I actually thought there was a little reboot this year, but nothing like before."

The species was red-listed as endangered in 2022 by the International Union for the Conservation of Nature. Habitat loss, pesticides and other threats are drivers of declines, but exactly how much each is responsible for isn't clear.
There are also mysteries around the spectacular and perilous monarch migration that scientists are beginning to disentangle, thanks to the tiny transmitters.

items: How eyelash glue is helping track monarch butterflies to Mexico
1st of 29 monarch butterflies tagged on Canadian Prairies reaches Mexico after perilous migration

blocks.text: The solar-powered backpacks transmit at the same frequency as Bluetooth, so as butterflies flutter along, their signals ping off radio telemetry towers and people's cellphones. Those signals are beamed to the Project Monarch app, where you can track and set alerts for any of the hundreds tagged across the U.S. and Canada this year.

The radio-tagging in Winnipeg this summer was the first time it's been done on the Prairies. It's part of a broader monitoring effort by Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC), University of Guelph, Assiniboine Park Zoo and others over the past couple years focused on identifying migration patterns and pathways.

As of Monday, at least 17 (60 per cent) of the Prairie monarchs' signals had gone dark, 10 had made it into Mexico (30 per cent) though not all had arrived yet to their overwintering grounds. Two were still en route.

For the monarchs that make it, Burns says the data could highlight important stopover spots where they rested or fuelled up on nectar. From there, scientists might be able to better push for protections for those habitats.
Equally as valuable is death data.

"You can start to look for trends — you know, are there areas [where] a lot of them stop emitting signals?" said Burns. "Maybe there's too big of a gap in the habitat they need or maybe they don't have that refuelling point to carry on."
1st monarch butterfly tagged on Canadian Prairies makes it to Mexico
The number of monarchs that don't make it from different regions will also reveal something important, said Greg Mitchell, a research scientist with Environment and Climate Change Canada in Ottawa.

"It's going to help us better understand where the pinch points are," said Mitchell. "The survival data is actually probably going to play a really big part in our understanding of the population dynamics."
Mitchell co-chairs the Trinational Monarch Conservation Partnership between Canada, the U.S. and Mexico.

Though ECCC has only been tracking monarchs for a couple of years and the data still hasn't been fully analyzed, Mitchell notes subtle details are emerging that point to inclement weather as a possible increasing threat factor.
He says last year there were drought conditions and intense wind events in the Kansas region, not all that far from where Eddie's signal last beeped.
"It happened a couple times where there were these stall-outs because of really strong winds in the opposite direction to which they're moving. We lost some," said Mitchell.
"That suggests to me … the weather that they're actually experiencing now might have changed through time with climate change, and so that's going to be really important to look into," he said.
"All this tagging is going to help us understand where maybe different populations of monarchs are more or less affected by climate change."
— Bryce Hoye
Old issues of What on Earth? are here. The CBC News climate page is here.

Check our podcast and radio show. In our latest episode: In the U.S. midterms, data centres and gas prices proved to be winning issues for Democrats. With the party set to control both chambers of Congress, we hear how energy concerns could usher in a new era of climate action — yes, even with Donald Trump still president.

What On Earth? drops new podcast episodes every Wednesday and Saturday. You can find them on your favourite podcast app or on demand at CBC Listen. The radio show airs Sundays at 11 a.m., 11:30 a.m. in Newfoundland and Labrador.

Check the CBC News Climate Dashboard for live updates on record-breaking weather and current conditions across the country. Set your location to find out how today's temperatures compare to historical trends.
(CBC)
Reader feedback
Last week, Bridget Stringer-Holden wrote about youth helping others understand how climate change affects brain health, partly as a way of dealing with climate anxiety.

Doug Sanden, who is from Alberta, wrote: "Regarding research on climate anxiety, it would be interesting to know if there is something equivalent for those worrying about losing fossil fuels — decarbonization anxiety. If so, that might explain some strange emotional reactions to economist-recommended government policies — such as carbon pricing — designed to reduce fossil fuel use. And it might give a focus to those seeking agency through action on the topic of climate change to reduce their own anxiety: helping reduce the anxiety of those worried about decarbonization, by explaining how they and others will transition and at what cost and benefit."

We also featured an article about ways to keep Halloween pumpkins out of the trash. Vivian Unger of Fredericton applauded the idea of feeding them to farm animals and shared her own solution: "I buy pie pumpkins and use them as jack-o'-lanterns. They're smaller, so there's not as much room for [facial] features. But it's doable. You can either carve really small features, or leave the nose out. I put the completed jack-o'-lantern on a plate in the window with a tea light in it. I also keep all the bits I cut out. Some of them can be incorporated into the design, for example by attaching them to the sides of the pumpkin with toothpicks, to make ears. The next day, I carve up the jack-o'-lantern and bake it. Delicious. It can be made into soup, pie or even paleo porridge (recipes available online)."
Got questions, comments or just want to share something? Write us at whatonearth@cbc.ca (and send photos there, too!)
The Big Picture: Mapping freshwater threats
(Submitted by Christophe Brabant et al.)

This colourful graphic reflects an inarguably dark message about the state of global freshwater biodiversity — but it could also light a way toward recovery. New research published in the journal Science illustrates the main threats by region that are driving declines of fish, amphibians, reptiles, dragonflies and water-borne mammals. Species within those five groups are among the one-quarter of all freshwater creatures on the planet that are facing extinction, according to the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).

A team led by McGill researchers analyzed more than 21,000 freshwater species on the IUCN's "red list" of threatened species. The resulting colour-coded visualization reveals intersecting ranges of species along with the most intense known threats they're facing at the regional level around the world — from dams and water diversion through parts of Western Canada, to agriculture on parts of the Prairies and in South America, to overharvesting in the north and parts of sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia.
The researchers hope the map helps conservationists tailor supports for specific groups of freshwater wildlife facing the most intense risks across the globe.
Hot and bothered: Provocative ideas from around the web

items: "Dunkelflaute" is a new German term to describe a weather pattern that poses problems for wind and solar generation. Euronews explains what that weather looks like, when it happens and what it means for the grid.
Climate change is altering the colours of the world around us. In a multimedia piece full of whimsical pen-and-watercolour-style illustrations, NPR shows us how the palette is shifting.

After torrential rainstorms linked to the super El Niño season, at least one famous rock formation in northwest New Mexico has been found in pieces. Here's what it used to look like — and what's left of it.

A U.S. survey by the Aspen Institute shows teens are very concerned about climate change, but are confused about the causes, consequences and solutions. Researcher Laura Schifter discusses what that means with Phoenix radio station KJZZ.

blocks.text: Sewing is having a moment. Here's why

A renewed interest in analogue hobbies and growing concern about the impacts of fast fashion are driving more Canadians to learn how to sew, says Sabine Weber, a professor of fashion at Seneca Polytechnic College in Toronto whose PhD research focused on sustainable fashion. (Jordi Calvera/Shutterstock)
Depending on the corner of the internet you inhabit, you may have noticed that the feeds are full of sewing enthusiasts.
Look up "thrift flips" on Instagram or TikTok and you'll find creators remaking second-hand garments into new ones or old quilts into hoodies and track suits.

On Pinterest, searches for "sewing ideas" are up 118 per cent year over year by its Canadian users, while those for "beginner sewing projects" rose 67 per cent, according to data the platform provided to CBC News.

Sewing hobbyists and the people who teach them say a number of factors — including renewed interest in analog hobbies and growing concern about the impacts of fast fashion — are driving more Canadians to pick up a needle and thread.

"A generation raised on fast fashion is rediscovering the value of making and repairing their own clothes," said Sabine Weber, a professor of fashion at Seneca Polytechnic in Toronto whose PhD research focused on sustainable fashion.
"And now they have discovered thrifting."

Referencing data from Trendex North America, a Canadian apparel market intelligence firm, Weber says the clothing resale market was forecast to grow from around $3.8 billion in 2022 to almost $6 billion in 2026.
Students from Seneca Polytechnic on a visit to the Textile Museum of Canada in Toronto. (Submitted by Sabine Weber)
That shift in shopping habits has prompted people to learn how to make small repairs to thrifted finds, and from there to try more ambitious upcycling projects, she says.
"And then you want to really … show your individuality and your self-expression by making your own clothes."
