In Victoria, Erin Kerr says she began in earnest to develop her sewing skills a few years ago. "I had a scrunchie brand called Hair of the Dog that ended up doing pretty well … but I was just kind of sewing rectangles over and over," Kerr told The Current.
Once she expanded her repertoire, Kerr began to offer sewing lessons to get more out of her studio space and bring in a little extra cash.
"We immediately had an email list of hundreds of people that were interested in learning to sew from us," she said.
What started as a weekend project has since morphed into the Sewing Club, a specialty shop and school that offers patterns, fabric, tools and a range of sewing workshops.
Embracing the analog
There's also the offline nature of the craft, says Weber.
"It's a very big contrast to all the typing we do and all the machines and phones and iPads and whatever."

Branislava Pavlovic started sewing in spring 2025 and one of her most prized projects is this jumpsuit made of vintage Toronto Blue Jays bedsheets, which she wears to games. (Submitted by Branislava Pavlovic)
As Branislava Pavlovic points out, "it's literally impossible to be on your phone and sew at the same time."
She took up sewing in the spring of 2025 with beginner classes at the Neon Needle in Toronto, and now works there as studio manager and instructor.

"We find that there's a lot of people who are in tech jobs, engineers and administrators, that just want to come and just do nothing like what they do all day, but actually do something for themselves and be creative."

Candice Alviz, who sews and designs patterns from her home studio in Burlington, Ont., says she thinks the increased interest coincides with a shift in people's understanding of the impacts of fast fashion. (Amanda Grant/CBC)
Ishmam Sarker says he was inspired by some of the sewing content he was seeing on Instagram and TikTok.
"I've always been into fashion … And then I guess the algorithm worked in my favour," Sarker said.
He followed a tutorial on how to make a tote bag and took on more ambitious projects from there.
Candice Alviz thinks the increased interest coincides with a shift in the way people look at fashion.
"Like fast fashion — for a while, people loved it," she said. "You could buy a T-shirt for $10 and it was amazing."
Whereas "people now, their eyes are opened to the fashion industry and how damaging it can be to the environment, and the labour [conditions] and, like, all of it."
Getting started
Those who are thinking of taking up sewing can check out an endless supply of tutorials online.
But brick-and-mortar studios where people can take in-person classes seem to be increasing in number.
Kerr recommends keeping expectations modest at the start.

"I would say don't get too emotionally attached to your first project, because it's probably going to look bad," she said. "So don't focus too much on the outcome. It's more the process and building your skills."
— Brandie Weikle

articles.title: Lewis Hamilton says ‘Israel’s genocide in Gaza is appalling’ after Rafah visit
articles.summary:
• F1 driver urges Israel to let aid into Gaza

  • Trip involved tour of facilities with aid workers

Formula One driver Lewis Hamilton said on Wednesday that Israel…

blocks.text: Formula One driver Lewis Hamilton said on Wednesday that Israel must allow aid ⁠trucks into Gaza, a day after he visited the Rafah border crossing in Egypt.

Hamilton, a seven-time ⁠world champion, arrived ⁠in ​El Arish on Tuesday, where he was briefed on how aid is prepared and coordinated before it ⁠is sent into Gaza, as he toured the Rafah crossing and the Egyptian Red Crescent’s aid warehouses.

He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire. A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.

“The past ⁠three years of Israel’s genocide in Gaza is appalling. It’s an ​injustice for people to ‌be denied their freedom, ‌their safety and their dignity. No human being should be treated ‌as though their life matters less,” the Ferrari driver wrote on Instagram.
Israel strongly denies accusations of genocide and says its military campaign in Gaza targets Hamas militants.
Hamilton described seeing food trucks lined up and ready to go at the border that were ‌regularly held up or faced major delays.

“I saw walls stretching for miles, built to keep them in. Standing there, outside what felt like an open-air prison, all I could think about was getting in to help,” he said in the post. “At the Rafah border, I saw food trucks lined up ready to go, but they’re regularly not allowed in or face major delays. The first driver in line that I spoke to had already been waiting over 12 hours. At the nearby logistics centre, I saw the hard work of the aid workers, but I also saw what gets rejected for crazy reasons. Sleeping bags, first aid kits, medical equipment, wheelchairs even footballs for kids.

“Israel needs to fulfil its obligations under the ceasefire and let the aid trucks in. I know so many people feel that same helplessness. That same need to do something rather than just watch. No excuse. I don’t want ⁠us to get used to their suffering. I don’t ​want us to ​look away.”
Allow Instagram content?

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.
Hamilton, 41, is an ​advocate for humanitarian causes. In 2021 he founded ​Mission 44, a ‌charity that supports ​young people ​and works to improve their access to education and employment.
“I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine,” Hamilton said last month. “I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage.”
At the crossing on Tuesday, Hamilton greeted aid workers with “Assalamu alaikum” a widely used Arabic greeting meaning “peace be upon you”. He shook hands and briefly spoke to workers and officials.

Hamilton is fourth in the drivers’ championship. Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli has won the title with three races to go. The Las Vegas Grand Prix is 21 November before the Qatar Grand Prix on 29 November and the season-ending Abu Dhabi Grand Prix on 6 December.

articles.title: Putin says Russia would target foreign troops deployed to Ukraine
articles.summary:
Hardline remarks come as Ukrainian military faces disruptions to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service

Vladimir Putin warned US negotiators that Russia would target any foreign troops…
articles.byline: Pjotr Sauer and Jennifer Rankin in Dublin

blocks.text: Vladimir Putin warned US negotiators that Russia would target any foreign troops deployed to Ukraine, in a series of hardline remarks that came as the Ukrainian military faced renewed disruptions to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service.

During the talks at the Kremlin with the US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff on Thursday, the Russian president refused to soften his territorial demands, insisting on full control over four Ukrainian regions that Moscow claims to have annexed.
He also ruled out accepting the deployment of foreign peacekeeping troops in Ukraine, describing such a move as a “continuation of war”.

Putin’s comments appeared to severely dampen hopes that a peace deal could be within reach, after Volodymyr Zelenskyy said there was a “window of opportunity” to reach an agreement before the end of 2026.

The latest trip to Moscow by Witkoff and Kushner, who have made numerous visits to Russia, was partly aimed at securing European participation in future negotiations, according to two people familiar with the talks.

Speaking after the meeting, Witkoff confirmed that European representatives would join the next round of talks. “They’re our partners, and it’s important for them to be involved,” he told reporters as he boarded a plane leaving Moscow.
The US envoys will now travel to Dublin, Ireland, where they will meet Zelenskyy and debrief him on the Moscow meeting.

Amid a flurry of diplomatic activity, including the recent talks in Abu Dhabi, the Kremlin appears to have succeeded in reframing negotiations over the war in Ukraine as part of a broader discussion about European security.
But Europe is wary of Russian attempts to focus discussions on a European security architecture, while Moscow continues to pound Ukraine with bombs and missiles.

The EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, told reporters: “We already have a European security architecture in place.” Kallas pointed to the cold war-era Helsinki accords and the Budapest memorandum, which guaranteed the territorial integrity of Ukraine. “The problem is that Russia is not keeping to those agreements, so right now the focus should be that Russia actually keeps to their obligations … and they don’t attack another country again.” Focusing on a European security architecture was a “distraction” without a ceasefire, she added.
Both Washington and Moscow have been urging European leaders to appoint a single representative to lead negotiations on their behalf.
“Once a representative is appointed, a chief negotiator authorised to speak on Europe’s behalf, there will be a four-way dialogue,” Putin said on Thursday.

EU leaders are due to discuss the issue of who speaks for Europe on Friday, but so far have declined to nominate one person to speak for the bloc. One EU official said the EU would be represented by its institutions when issues concerning the union were on the table, but played down any imminent appointment. They said: “Do I expect an agreement on a special representative? My answer is no, I don’t.”
Kallas suggested she – as the EU’s high representative for foreign and security policy – should represent the EU in talks, alongside António Costa, the president of the European Council.

More than 45 European leaders are meeting in Dublin for the European Political Community summit, a gathering that brings together nearly every country on the continent, apart from the leaders of Belarus and Russia.

The French president, Emmanuel Macron, played down the importance of having a single European negotiator, saying “the content determines the format”. “There is no more US support. So there [are] some mediations, fine,” he said, referring to the process led by Kushner and Witkoff. “But at the end of the day we will be the one to define and decide for our future security as Europeans.”

The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said it was first necessary to get Putin to the negotiating table before deciding on a European envoy. Merz said: “It’s not about individuals. What matters is that Putin is prepared to hold talks.”

Meanwhile, Zelenskyy accused Musk’s Starlink satellite service of damaging Ukraine’s ability to defend itself against Russian drone attacks, after Ukrainian military officials reported new restrictions on the system.

According to Zelenskyy, Starshield, a military version of Starlink funded by the Pentagon, has for several days been subject to speed limits of 100mph (161km/h) along the frontline and in Russian-occupied territory.
Similar restrictions last month prompted confusion over who had ordered them, with Musk and the Trump administration pointing fingers at each other before the service was partly restored.

The latest restrictions had made it harder for Ukrainian forces to intercept Russia’s increasingly sophisticated jet-powered drones, Zelenskyy said, accusing the service of “helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine”.
Kyiv has contacted Washington to seek an explanation for the disruption, which Zelenskyy said appeared to be deliberate rather than a technical fault.

articles.title: Can the EU make it harder to trick consumers online?
articles.summary: The EU wants to curb subscription traps, misleading sales tactics and features that keep people scrolling. What would the proposed Digital Fairness Act change, and does it go far enough?

image.caption: The Digital Fairness Act was proposed by the Commission and is set to better protect consumers onlineImage: James Arthur Gekiere/Belga/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: You sign up for a free trial to watch a series after work. A month later, you've forgotten about it. Then you find a charge for your new 12-month subscription on your bank statement. Sound familiar? You're not alone. Now the EU wants to stop that practice.

Under the European Commission's proposed Digital Fairness Act (DFA), a company would have to remind you before the free trial ends and get your explicit agreement before it can start charging you. The proposed law would also make it easier to cancel a subscription online and require reminders before certain contracts renew automatically.
The Commission presented the proposal on Wednesday. It wants to give consumers more control over how much time and money they spend online.
"We haven't seen that kind of reform in consumer protection in the last 20 years," Agustin Reyna, director general of the European Consumer Organisation (BEUC), told DW.
His organization pushed for stronger EU rules against manipulative online practices. He sees the proposal as a good starting point for tackling problems that frustrate consumers every day.

blocks.caption: EU Commissioner for the rule of law and consumer protection Michael McGrath has been pushing for the new regulationImage: Europäische Kommission

blocks.text: Ending doomscrolling and 'dark patterns'

The proposal also includes a ban on manipulative marketing tactics, so-called "dark patterns." A concrete example: You are trying to reserve a hotel room and the website claims that only three are left, a potentially false claim to pressure you into buying.

A concert ticket that gets more expensive while you're waiting in an online queue raises a different problem. The price could still go up in the process, but the seller would have to show the current price while you wait and tell you the maximum you could be asked to pay.
Online games that encourage users to spend their money to advance are also targeted. Children would no longer be able to pay to win or get to the next level of their online game.

Marketing and personalized ads would need to be clearly marked and restricted in the case of children. Consumers should get the option to switch off doomscrolling functions such as the autoplay of videos, showing one clip after the other. With these new rules, the EU wants to make apps and websites less addictive.

blocks.caption: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen promised that "Europe has the power to act: It is we who decide our rules, not big tech" (file photo from January 2026)Image: Omar Havana/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Consumer protection versus innovation?

For Christoph Busch, an academic with a focus on consumer law and digital services based at Osnabrück University in Germany, the option to opt out doesn't go far enough. He argues that a version in which consumers actively have to choose to opt into those functions would be more effective.
"But then there is always the question of proportionality," Busch said. "And I think here the European legislators are trying to balance different interests."

These competing interests are particularly visible in the gaming industry, where interest groups have warned that the proposed EU restrictions could hurt developers and leave players with fewer options to choose from.

Video Games Europe and the European Games Developer Federation called the proposal "unworkable, unjustified and disproportionate," arguing that a ban on selling children features that help them win or advance is worded so broadly that it "could cover almost any purchase in a game."
For Busch, this argument doesn't hold. "If your business model is based on addictive design features, then maybe your business model has to be reviewed," he said.

blocks.caption: The proposal still has to pass the Council and the European ParliamentImage: Alexey Vitvitsky/SNA/imago images

blocks.text: The risk of overregulation
Catalina Goanta, an associate professor of private law and technology at Utrecht University, emphasized in an interview with DW that "regulation can very easily slide into overregulation."

Even though she believes that the DFA is a solid and reasonable compromise, she argues that prohibiting dark patterns and doomscrolling altogether would be too prohibitive. Many of the issues consumers currently face could be resolved by enforcing existing regulation more effectively, she said.

She points to the fact that the EU has made a name for itself in the past by adding new rules and regulations that have made it more difficult to access the European market, especially for small online businesses.
BEUC director Agustin Reyna disagrees.
"Instead of having 27 different regulations to adhere to, companies will now only get one," Reyna said.
For him, this speaks for simplification, especially when the responsibility for compliance is shared between online influencers and the platforms they publish on.
According to the new legislation, the EU would have the possibility to impose fines of up to six percent of a company's global annual revenue should the company violate the law.
What happens next?

The European Parliament and the Council, which represents member state governments, still have to agree on the text and formally adopt it. All experts agree that in that process, changes are still very likely.

"It will be a difficult trialogue, especially in this climate of simplification and deregulation with a focus on strengthening European competitiveness," said Christoph Busch. In that climate, it is not easy to add consumer rights, he adds.

Agustin Reyna is more optimistic. "The parliament is a divided house, much more than in the past," he says. "But consumer protection is a subject that brings parties together because it brings tangible outcomes to people."

articles.title: Mercedes-Benz halts all further investment at German facilities
articles.summary: The announcement comes as the luxury German automaker faces increasing pressure from the works council and trade unions.

image.caption: Mercedes-Benz has long been a symbol for the German auto industryImage: Bernd Weißbrod/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Mercedes-Benz announced on Thursday that it was halting all further investment at its German sites for the time being.

"The executive board has jointly decided to halt all further investments in German sites," Mercedes board member Michael Schiebe said in a memo on the company's intranet that was seen by the AFP news agency.
The company is also weighing plant closures, the memo added.
The announcement comes as the luxury German automaker faces increasing pressure from the works council and the IG Metall trade union.
What else did Mercedes-Benz say?

Mercedes-Benz is "forced to examine, in concrete and detailed terms, which sites in Germany we can still afford to maintain," board of management member Britta Seeger said in an interview published on the company's intranet.
"We all want to avoid plant closures at all costs," she added. "Unfortunately, however, we must now pursue this option in more concrete terms."
Shiebe, the company's chief production officer, said the current cost structures meant it is not possible to invest in Germany.
German labour costs are sometimes five times higher than at plants in Eastern Europe, where administrative costs are also similarly much cheaper.
Schiebe had recently announced that two plants in Germany would have to close unless costs were reduced.

articles.title: Pentagon backs war memorial guard who reprimanded Hegseth's group
articles.summary: The guard told the defence secretary and his companions to maintain an atmosphere of "silence and respect" during a Veterans Day visit.

blocks.text: The Pentagon has given its backing to a US Army guard who reprimanded a group that included US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth at the Arlington National Cemetery.
A video of the Veterans Day observance event on Wednesday showed Hegseth, his wife, and senior advisers laughing and talking while posing for photos in front of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.
The footage showed the army sentinel on duty stepping towards Hegseth's group and shouting: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times."
Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement: "While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum."
"The Secretary and the entire Department have always honored - and will always honor - the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe."
On Thursday, he presented an award to the soldier who reprimanded his group.

Hegseth "welcomed the 3rd U.S. Infantry Regiment, the Old Guard to the Pentagon where he proudly awarded Specialist Thomas Iglesias the Joint Service Commendation Medal for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier on November 11, 2026," the Pentagon said in a statement.
In a post on X showing the soldier, Hesgeth said: "We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist."
The Arlington National Cemetery etiquette requests that visitors speak quietly and do not engage in disrespectful or disorderly conduct.
The tomb, which is one of the country's most sacred war memorials, marks the final resting place of an unknown soldier who was killed in World War I.
A service member from the 3rd Infantry Regiment stands watch over the tomb 24 hours a day and has done so since 1948.
It is not unusual for them to admonish visitors to the site, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News. They reportedly do so a few times a day.

articles.title: What have the talks with Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi achieved for Ukraine?
articles.summary: The first trilateral talks between Ukraine, the US and Russia in nine months have ended with an agreement on exchanging prisoners. Does this mark a genuine breakthrough and a step toward peace?

image.caption: Delegations from Russia and Ukraine held US-mediated talks in Abu DhabiImage: Altaf Qadri/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The two-day talks between delegations from Ukraine, the US and Russia in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11 ended without a ceasefire agreement.
The main outcome was an agreement on a prisoner exchange.

"We have agreed on the largest humanitarian release of prisoners, and tomorrow we will finalize the numbers," Jared Kushner announced after the talks. US envoys Kushner and Steve Witkoff arrived in Moscow on Thursday, where they are due to meet President Vladimir Putin.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had earlier suggested an exchange of "1,000 for 1,000" prisoners, or "1,500 for 1,500." Russia said a large-scale prisoner exchange with Ukraine could take place within the next two to three weeks.

Following the meetings, Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram that the parties had discussed security guarantees and that "the first step should be ending this war and ensuring Ukraine's security." He also stressed that Europe should be involved "at every stage of genuine diplomacy."
How significant is the prisoner swap?
Experts interviewed by DW agree that the main outcome of the talks is humanitarian.
"The agreement on a prisoner exchange is already a major step forward," says Artjom Bronzhukov of the Ukrainian think tank Polityka.

Pavlo Lakiychuk of the Ukrainian Center for Global Studies Strategy XXI also viewed it as a "very tangible result." He told DW that "getting our people back is already a major success. That is why it is worth continuing."
A real breakthrough, he added, would be the release of civilian detainees from territories occupied since 2014, particularly people from Crimea, who have been held in Russian prisons for years.
Russia, Ukraine exchange prisoners as talks end
Empty diplomacy without a real breakthrough?

Davyd Arakhamia, head of the ruling Servant of the People parliamentary faction and Ukraine's representative at the talks in Abu Dhabi, gave a positive assessment of the trilateral talks with the US and Russia, expressing hope that an agreement could be reached by the end of the year.

"I think the Russians came with extremely strict instructions, and it was difficult to ease the tone of the discussion. But the way the US representatives structured the talks with a view to the postwar situation in both countries opened up a dialogue, in my opinion, and allowed us to work together more productively," Arakhamia said at a joint press conference with US and Ukrainian representatives following the talks.
Iuliia Osmolovska of the Kyiv office of the international think tank GLOBSEC cautions against reading too much into the positive assessments of the talks from Washington and Kyiv.

"Diplomats taking part in negotiations will never say that everything went badly and that they have no expectations. Even when no results are achieved, they will still emphasize that the talks were constructive," she said. "For anyone familiar with diplomatic language, these are simply standard phrases."
Experts: chances for Russia-Ukraine ceasefire low as things currently stand

Osmolovska points to a joint assessment by 71 Ukrainian security and defense experts published by GLOBSEC in the summer. According to the assessment, the chances of a peace agreement or at least a ceasefire being reached this year or next stand at just 19%.

She blames this on the fact that neither side is "ready" for genuine negotiations. Russia, in particular, has yet to accept that its objectives cannot be achieved by military means. "What we are seeing now is more of a farce, an attempt by all sides to put a brave face on things and create the impression that something is moving forward," Osmolovska said.
Artjom Bronzhukov sees the talks as a way for Moscow to buy time.

"The visits by the Russian delegation, particularly under the leadership of Vladimir Medinsky, are nothing more than an attempt to stall and sell empty promises to the US administration in the form of grand agreements, in order to continue receiving so-called gestures of goodwill from Washington, such as the lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel," the political scientist says.

blocks.caption: Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, briefed journalists during the talks between Russia and UkraineImage: Altaf Qadri/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Redrawing borders to make Putin feel like a winner?

Ahead of the talks, several Western media outlets reported on new US proposals concerning disputed territories. The Economist, for example, reported on a proposal to redraw the administrative boundaries of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions. However, a member of the Ukrainian delegation stressed that there had "never been any discussion of concessions on territories occupied by Russia."
Washington made no official comment on the reports.

Kyrylo Budanov, a member of the negotiating delegation and head of the Ukrainian president's office, declined to say whether Russia had used the talks to demand that Ukrainian troops withdraw from the Donbas. Asked by journalists whether Moscow was still insisting that Ukraine pull out of the region, Budanov said the content of the negotiations would remain confidential until an agreement was reached.
"The issues discussed in the talks are matters for negotiation. The only thing that matters is the outcome. Once we achieve it, it will be made public," Budanov said.

The head of the Russian delegation, Vladimir Medinsky, took a different tone, declaring that "every inch of our land will be returned to Russia one way or another." He was responding to reports in European media that Ukraine was rejecting territorial concessions.
Putin demands large swaths of Ukrainian territory

In addition to the Crimean Peninsula, annexed in 2014, Russian President Vladimir Putin claims the four Ukrainian regions of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson in their entirety as Russian territory, even though Russia does not have full military control over them.
"Putin is not fighting over villages and ruined cowsheds in the Donbas. He is fighting for geopolitical influence and trying to exploit the collapse of the old world order," says Artjom Bronzhukov.

The expert from the Polityka think tank recalls that Ukraine was already asked in early 2026 to withdraw its troops from the part of the Donbas it controls and turn the area into a free economic zone. Such a zone "would very quickly become a Russian-controlled area," he warns.
Is Trump trying to end the war in Ukraine, or helping Putin win it?
Pavlo Lakiychuk questions the idea of changing administrative boundaries.

"Why would Putin stop there?" asks the expert from the Strategy XXI center. In his view, US negotiators are seeking to extract unilateral concessions from Ukraine "step by step" without demanding anything in return from Russia.

Iuliia Osmolovska describes the proposal as "very original," but says it would pose risks for Ukraine's leadership. Even if the Ukrainian delegation agreed to it, which Osmolovska doubts, the decision would have to be explained to the public, which, she says, is not ready to accept it.

The GLOBSEC expert points out that, following the last harsh winter, marked by shortages of electricity and heating, only 5% of Ukrainians were willing to make concessions to Russia in exchange for an end to attacks on the energy sector.
What next after Abu Dhabi?

Following the meeting between Jared Kushner, US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Vladimir Putin in Moscow, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he wants to "coordinate positions with the Americans once again." No further trilateral meetings have been announced so far.
Iuliia Osmolovska believes the parties will sooner or later have to admit that the negotiations have reached a dead end. She expects each side to return to military action.

Pavlo Lakiychuk, by contrast, believes the talks should continue, if only to secure the return of prisoners. He is also convinced that Europeans "will always be there," because the issue is not just the Russian-Ukrainian war but the security of the entire continent.
This article was originally published in Ukrainian.

articles.title: Hungary eases abortion restrictions in women's rights overhaul
articles.summary: The reforms mark a break the the conservative policies of former PM Viktor Orban. The controversial "heartbeat regulation" is to be scrapped and women are to be better protected against violence.

image.caption: Peter Magyar said the heartbeat regulation had not led to a decline in pregnanciesImage: Attila Kisbenedek/AFP

blocks.text: Hungary on Thursday said it would ease abortion rules and ratify an international treaty on violence against women.
Under the planned changes to the so-called "heartbeat regulation," women will no longer be forced to listen to the vital signs of the fetus before an abortion.
Women will also be able to get emergency contraceptive pills without prescription.
The changes proposed by the new government under Prime Minister Peter Magyar are a significant break with the conservative policies of his predecessor Viktor Orban.
The country also plans to ratify the Istanbul Convention, a treaty aimed at preventing violence against women and domestic violence.
Hungary to end controversial 'fetal heartbeat' policy

Hungarian law allows for most abortions to be performed up to 12 weeks, and up to 24 weeks in cases of severe developmental abnormalities. Until now, women were required to have a medical provider show them evidence of a definitive sign of fetal life, commonly understood as the so-called "fetal heartbeat," before deciding whether to have an abortion.
The controversial 2022 policy had received widespread criticism from doctors and women’s rights groups as being cruel and humiliating. It will now be scrapped.
The policy had not led to a decline in abortions and according to Magyar, had raised "serious bioethical questions."
The second major change is that emergency contraception will be available without prescription.

Further measures include changing the criminal code aimed at better protecting women, including making the misuse of intimate images a criminal offense and strengthening the treatment of victims of domestic violence during criminal proceedings.
What is the Istanbul Convention?

Hungary also plans to ratify an international treaty on the protection of women which most other EU members have long ratified. The Istanbul Convention came into force in 2014 and, among other things, requires rape to be criminalized based on the absence of freely given consent.
"We are making it clear that sexual acts can only ⁠take ​place with the voluntary consent of the other party," ​Magyar said.
The government of his predecessor Orban had opposed the treaty, arguing that it promoted what it described as "gender ideology."
"We are making a clear and accountable commitment to putting an end to the era of inaction," Magyar said in a Facebook video.
Among the EU’s other members, only Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Lithuania and Slovakia have not yet ratified the convention.

The Istanbul Convention is a treaty by the Council of Europe, an international organization that promotes human rights and the rule of law across Europe and includes more countries than the member of the EU.

articles.title: The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal
articles.summary: Within days, Huang's status as a seemingly untouchable figure leading the global tech race has crumbled.

blocks.text: Jensen Huang, known for sporting a black leather jacket to shareholder events, appeared to have it all. He was courted by leaders in both Washington and Beijing, worshipped by investors and seen as a loyal family man. But a rockstar approach to his personal life has ultimately led to his resignation.
The 63-year-old has been married since 1985, long before the foundation of Nvidia, the company that propelled him to tech stardom.

He is known as a workaholic and a demanding manager, with high standards for those who worked for him, which included his own children, promoted within the company. But he has seen his personal reputation go into free fall this week, undone by romantic entanglements, that throw doubt on his focus and his judgement.

On Thursday he resigned following back-to-back revelations of two affairs. News of the first - a relationship with a businesswoman, alleged to be a Chinese spy - ricocheted around the world, raising eyebrows among investors. It was followed on Wednesday by reports that the tech boss had also had an affair with an Nvidia colleague.
His departure creates uncertainty in the global stock market, which was already knocked-off balance in recent weeks. Nvidia is a linchpin in the US's race for technology leadership with China.
Huang may not be a household name on the same level as Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg.

But his role in the tech industry, especially in relation to the explosion of artificial intelligence in the last three years, may prove more consequential. Nvidia dominates the market for the microchips, which are used to power the new technology.
The company, which is still valued at nearly $4 trillion despite recent events, is at the centre of the AI race between the US and China, the world's tech and economic powerhouses.
Huang has had access to the seats of political power on an unrivalled scale, being courted by both US President Donald Trump and China's President XI Jinping.

His remarkable rise to the top of his profession has led to him being dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech" and seen him amass an estimated fortune of $145bn (£109bn), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

Despite always donning his trademark all-black outfits and playful approach to investor presentations, Huang has worked for years to present himself as a family man, someone who exemplified the American Dream.

Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang and his family moved to the west coast of the US when he was nine years old. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.
It was at college where he met his wife, Lori Mills. The pair were lab partners and married in 1985, eight years before Huang founded Nvidia.
They have two children, Madison and Spencer, who now both work at their father's firm.
He worked at US chip firm AMD before co-founding Nvidia. Known as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan, he has a reputation for having incredibly high standards for his staff.

The company became a key provider of computer chips and circuits used for gaming before it expanded in direction and entered the world of AI. It now creates the key processing chips used to power the growing technology.
Huang has hailed AI as a "new industrial revolution" that is on par with the advent of electricity.

"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on the Jensen Huang, told the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.
The Nvidia co-founder has a famously close relationship with Trump. At a recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Huang and Musk.
It was no surprise that Huang was at the top table. Companies using Nvidia's chips include Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Tesla, OpenAI and Anthropic.
In essence, Huang's customer base includes the biggest firms on the planet and they are spending plenty on Nvidia's products.
This intertwining of companies means that the negative impact being felt by Nvidia, on the stock market for example, could perhaps have wider implications on other companies and the wider economy.
Witt told the BBC that Jensen Huang had gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, and that it was "very important to him".

"He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways," he added. "The fallout of this would be bad for anyone's family. But for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad."
After the revelations of the first affair, Huang admitted to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting their family.
Trump, as well as other leaders in the AI tech industry, had backed Huang to continue in his role at Nvidia. The president described him as "honourable".

articles.title: UK court convicts 2 Iranian men of spying on journalists
articles.summary: A London court has found two Iranian citizens guilty of surveilling reporters for a Persian-language television station critical of Iran's goverment. One was also convicted of planning a violent…

image.caption: The trial opened at Woolwich Crown Court in London on October 5 this yearImage: Kin Cheung/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Two Iranian men were found guilty of spying in dissident journalists in Britain on behalf of Iran's Revolutionary Guard on Thursday.

British counterterrorism police said the case reflected intensifying hostile Iranian activity in the country, an issue that recently made headlines amid the security scare at the RAF Fairford airbase that's a major operational site in Europe for the US Air Force.
The men, both in their 40s, were arrested last year, with Iran repeatedly rejecting the allegations against them.
What did the court rule?

The Woolwich Crown Court in London convicted one of the Iranian citizens not just of spying on journalists working for the Persian-language dissident TV channel Iran International, but of plotting a violent attack against one or more of them.
The second individual had also faced charges of plotting an attack but was only convicted of spying on the reporters.
One of the convicted defendants said he was acting under duress after his family was threatened, and the other said he did not know that his actions were assisting Iranian intelligence.
A third defendant, a 57-year-old Iranian man, was acquitted of all charges.

blocks.caption: Sentencing in the case is expected at the 'Old Bailey' in London on December 17Image: Kin Cheung/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The men were accused of engaging in conduct likely to assist the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Iran's multi-discipline military force that's seen as closer to the country's religious leadership and more influential than its regular armed forces.

The UK formally designated the IRGC as a threat to national security in July, meaning that supporting or assisting the organization can carry penalties of up to 14 years in prison as part of new rules on national security and state threats.
Sentencing in this case is still pending and is scheduled for mid-December.

"This was a calculated operation to spy on those critical of the Iranian regime," said Frank Ferguson, chief prosecutor for the Crown Prosecution Service's special crime and counter-terrorism division.
The two men were accused of visiting addresses linked to their targets, taking photos and videos, and using platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online
"Thankfully, the defendants were stopped before any attack could take place," prosecutor Ferguson said.
Senior ‌National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing Vicki Evans said that the IRGC or "middlemen" for Iranian intelligence were directing the plot.
Iran's government had repeatedly denied the allegations, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi saying he was "disturbed" by the trio's arrests last May.
UK releases air base plot suspects
Not the first plot targeting Iran International
There have been four cases targeting the Persian language television channel Iran International since late 2023.
In July, two Romanian men were jailed for stabbing a journalist outside his home in 2024.

A spokesman for the broadcaster's parent company, Volant Media, said in a statement that Thursday's verdicts "don't make the lives of our journalists any safer so long as the Islamic Republic of Iran continues its campaign of death threats and violence against them."
Iran International reported that a British barrister was also one of the targets.
What other alleged signs of Iranian hostile activity in the UK are there?
British law enforcement has been warning of an uptick of hostile Iranian activity in recent years, particularly since the US military operations against Tehran began earlier this year.

Most notably, the UK has accused Iran of being behind a suspected plot targeting the RAF Fairford base in September, after which US President Donald Trump withdrew some long-range bombers from the site.
Three men were indicted in the US in relation that plot this week, while two others currently face charges in the UK.

But beyond this, the head of Britain's MI5 domestic intelligence agency Ken MacCullum said in October that Iran-linked operations had led to more than 50 arrests in the last year. He also said known cases of so-called state threats had more than quadrupled in a decade.
Counter-terrorism police chief Evans said she expected this trend to continue.
France this week also accused Iran of being behind a cyberattack targeting refrigeration units at hundreds of supermarkets in October, although Iran denied any involvement.

European governments are on heightened alert for so-called hybrid warfare tactics, from Russia as well as Iran, amid the geopolitical tensions of recent years. New technologies like low-cost drones and AI are also threatening to make such activities cheaper, harder to trace, and potentially more effective.

articles.title: Jensen Huang: Spy row, affairs leave Nvidia without its rockstar CEO
articles.summary: Jensen Huang, who built Nvidia into the world’s dominant AI chipmaker, is stepping down as CEO over extramarital affairs. DW examines how losing its figurehead will affect the firm and the US-China…

image.caption: Jensen Huang started Nvidia in 1993, aged 30Image: Lisi Niesner/REUTERS

blocks.text: 1. What do we know about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure?
Nvidia's board met late Wednesday to decide on CEO Jensen Huang's future as reports emerged of other extramarital affairs — this time with employees.
In a statement issued on Thursday, the world's most valuable chip supplier said Huang was resigning as president, CEO and board member, effective immediately.
The firm added that current Vice President and Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Colette Kress would become interim CEO.
Under Nvidia's bylaws, Huang can be removed "with or without cause" by a majority vote of its 11 directors.
The New York Times first reported that the 63-year-old Huang had an affair with a senior Nvidia executive who reported directly to him.
Later Thursday, Reuters news agency alleged an intimate relationship between Huang and a second employee, citing unidentified sources.
Those revelations emerged just three days after Huang admitted a relationship with a Chinese woman, whom United States intelligence agencies believe was spying for China.

The woman, Alice Huang — no relation — is a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm that runs artificial intelligence (AI) data centers across Southeast Asia and is a major client of Nvidia.
The US government is investigating the startup on suspicion that it secretly sent some of its Nvidia chips to China, violating Washington's curbs on high-end semiconductors.
Those advanced Nvidia processors ‌are ​used to train and run the large AI models behind chatbots and other generative AI products.
Megaspeed denies the allegations and on Thursday pledged to cooperate with US investigators. Huang, the alleged spy, has been barred from entering Singapore and Taiwan — a key chipmaking island.
While Nvidia's board backed its CEO after the first scandal emerged, market watchers believe the second caused too much reputational damage to one of the world's top three companies by market value.

blocks.caption: Nvidia is the hardware backbone of the global AI raceImage: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS

blocks.text: 2. Who could replace Huang as Nvidia CEO?
According to The Wall Street Journal, Huang doesn't believe in formal succession planning, so with little notice, Nvidia appointed CFO Kress as interim CEO.
Bloomberg reported Wednesday that Nvidia’s board is working with advisers to identify potential permanent successors.

Kress, other senior Nvidia executives and members of Huang's own family have been mooted as replacements. The family members include his daughter Madison, a senior director of product marketing, and his son Spencer, who currently works in the firm's robotics division.
Rumors also abound over a longer-term solution. On India's CNBC-TV18, Jeffrey Sonnenfeld from the Yale School of Management floated former Apple CEO Tim Cook and ex-Google CEO Eric Schmidt.
US President Donald Trump also backed Cook on social media, writing: "A Legend replaces a Legend."
Anthropic seeks $1.3 trillion valuation amid AI bubble fears
3. What will be the impact of Huang's departure on Nvidia?

The scandals have certainly hit Nvidia's market value. Since the first extramarital affair emerged on Sunday, the chipmaker's market capitalization has fallen by well over $600 billion to $4.2 trillion.
Nvidia shares were down more than 9% in premarket trading Thursday, after dropping by 10% earlier this week. Some analysts expect the stock price to struggle in the short term.

Nvidia stock hit all-time highs just a month ago as US technology giants continued to announce billions in spending on AI infrastructure. Still, Nvidia's stock hit all-time highs only a month ago, as US technology giants kept announcing billions in spending on AI infrastructure.
Demand for Nvidia's advanced chips is so high, however, that many market analysts expect little impact on near-term sales.

"While Jensen [Huang] is the heart and lungs of the Nvidia story…the company and its leading-edge GPU technology will go on and [his departure] does not change the entrenched position Nvidia has in the AI Revolution chip arms race," said Dan Ives, a partner, senior managing director and tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, a US-based merchant bank
Analysts see the biggest long-term risk in strategy and execution. After all, Huang was the leader who picked which ideas Nvidia should bet heavily on and got the whole company behind them.
His sudden exit is also seen as highly disruptive to the chip designer's strong relationships with AI hyperscalers, Taiwanese chip producer TSMC and foreign governments — especially China.
Huang was Nvidia's main lobbyist on US chip export rules and persuaded US President Donald Trump to ease some curbs on China last year.

blocks.caption: NVIDIA's systemic position as an AI leader will help the post-Huang eraImage: Jens Kalaene/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: 4. How dangerous is it for firms like Nvidia to rely on so-called rockstar CEOs?
Huang is often called a rockstar CEO for his leather jackets instead of suits.
Like Elon Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, he was also seen as a key-person risk as Nvidia’s public image, strategic direction and technical decisions became closely tied to him.
Huang steered the company for more than three decades and was also respected for his hands-on involvement in product architecture and engineering decisions.
He also insisted on a flat management structure, with around 60 executives reporting directly to him.
Huang has run the company so tightly around his own technical judgment and product decisions that investors may have little sense of how it would function without him.

At the same time, Nvidia is no longer the startup Huang founded in 1993. The company has built deep expertise in chip design and software, creating a durable moat that helps protect its huge profits, which topped $120.1 billion last year.
Some analysts argue that its central role in the AI hardware buildout makes it less dependent on Huang’s day-to-day input.
5. How will Huang's departure affect the US-China AI war?
China is quickly playing catch-up with the US in the global race for AI dominance.

While Chinese AI models have lagged behind the likes of ChatGPT and Claude, recent updates from DeepSeek, Alibaba and Moonshot have closed much of the gap on benchmark tests and often beat US rivals on cost and speed.
Beijing is also investing heavily in domestic chips and data centers to reduce reliance on US hardware.
The US has curbed exports to China of Nvidia's most advanced AI chips.
However, this move has only slowed the pace of China's AI ambitions.

Reuters reported Thursday that Chinese AI firms are now trying to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity at data centers outside China, amid fears the US could further tighten restrictions on advanced chips.
Also Thursday, Beijing accused the US of using the Nvidia spying claims as a pretext to impose a technological "blockade" on China.
The issue is likely to dominate talks next week between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the APEC gathering in Shenzhen in southern China.
Nvidia investigates CEO after reports of affair with Chinese spy
Editor's note: This article was first published on November 12, 2026 and was updated a day later with further developments.

articles.title: Shelter-in-place advisory issued for B.C.'s Pemberton Valley, parts of Squamish as flooding closes roads
articles.summary: Shelter-in-place advisories have been issued in the Pemberton Valley and parts of the District of Squamish as flooding threatens local properties and roads. Líl̓wat Nation expanded an evacuation…

image.caption: Water runs through a field in the Pemberton Meadows area on Thursday. (Erica Van Loon)

blocks.text: British Columbia

Shelter-in-place advisories have been issued in the Pemberton Valley and parts of the District of Squamish as flooding threatens local properties and roads. Líl̓wat Nation expanded an evacuation order for its community Thursday morning.
Evacuation orders also issued for part of Pemberton, Líl̓wat Nation
Shelter-in-place advisories have been issued in the Pemberton Valley and parts of the District of Squamish as flooding threatens local properties and roads.
Residents are told to stay where they are, unless they are covered by an evacuation order. Those under order are told to leave immediately.
The order areas include parts of Líl̓wat Nation and part of the village of Pemberton.
Líl̓wat Nation expanded an evacuation order for its community Thursday morning. It said flooding was occurring along the Green River, which is experiencing "exceptionally high flows."
"The Lillooet River is forecast to continue rising for several more hours. The Birkenhead is flowing near record levels," the order reads.

The Líl̓wat Nation has EXPANDED the Evacuation Order from Kwetsa7 along the Lillooet River corridor to Lillooet Lake due to flooding. Flood waters are a threat to life & safety. Go to Úll̓us Community Complex. If water blocks your route, do not attempt to cross. Move to a safe location on higher ground & call for assistance. For immediate danger or rescue call 911. More info: https://t.co/zGyQznHOE9 #BCFlood #BC—EmergencyInfoBC
The nation says sections of Lillooet Lake Road had about six inches to one foot of water flowing over it.
People are urged not to walk or drive through floodwater.
The nation has a muster point and reception centre open at Úll̓us Community Complex.
Rivers, streams running high in Sea-to-Sky region after days of heavy rain
In Pemberton, an evacuation order covers the Pemberton Regional Airport, the B.C. Wildfire Service base, golf course facilities, an animal shelter and a small number of residential properties.
A reception centre is open at the Pemberton and District Community Centre.
The entire village is under evacuation alert, as well as properties within the Electoral Area C portion of the Pemberton Valley.
The valley is also covered by a shelter-in-place advisory.
The Squamish-Lillooet Regional District (SLRD) says sections of Pemberton Meadows Road and Highway 99 are impassable.

Canada Post issued a red delivery service alert due to the flooding impacting Pemberton. It said in a statement that all mail and parcels destined for the village will be held at a Canada Post facility until postal services can resume.

items: Series of storms leaves B.C. woman with tree stuck on her house for days

blocks.text: In the District of Squamish, a shelter-in-place advisory covers the Paradise Valley, Sunwolf Lodge and Cheekye Ranch area due to flooding downstream of the Cheakamus Dam (Daisy Lake).
Squamish Valley Road was closed at the Pilchuck Bailey Bridge due to flooding concerns on Thursday. (Troy Charles/CBC)
The district said Paradise Valley Road is closed at the Paradise Valley Bailey Bridge and Squamish Valley Road is closed at the Pilchuck Bailey Bridge.
"River levels are expected to peak today and begin to drop as rainfall from the storm works its way through the river system," it said in a morning update.
More rain on the weekend
Squamish Mayor Sean Easton said the district is used to big storms and heavy rainfall, and is preparing for another weather system on the weekend.

"We're trying to respond in this moment, but then also trying to look at it and make sure that we're ready for the next storm moving through," he said. "It's unclear what that storm looks like, as far as amounts at this time."
He added the district's emergency operations centre is monitoring the situation.
Squamish Mayor Sean Easton said the Sea-to-Sky community is bracing for more storms on the weekend. (Mike Zimmer/CBC)

Pemberton Valley and parts of the South Coast are under a flood warning, with the River Forecast Centre saying river levels there "have been rising rapidly since late Tuesday night" and are expected to continue to rise into Thursday.
The centre has also issued flood warnings for the Kingcome River and Vancouver Island.
High streamflow advisories are in place for southern Vancouver Island, the Fraser Valley, Fraser Canyon and Chilcotin.
Environment Canada has rainfall warnings in effect for east, inland and west Vancouver Island, as well as parts of the Sunshine Coast.
With files from Troy Charles

articles.title: Before Scott Colom, these two men were the last black US senators in Mississippi
articles.summary: The Democratic candidate won in a southern state that had not seated a black senator since 1874.

blocks.text: A significant factor in Colom's victory was his success in mobilising young people and the state's large black population, who are expected to have turned out in high numbers.
In a victory speech, Colom referenced how Revels, who was a minister and served as a chaplain during the Civil War, gained support for his Senate campaign through his words.
"That's an example of the power of prayer, and through our history, there are so many people that lifted this state up through the power of prayer in very dark times," Colom said.
Prior to the result being called, the BBC spoke to students at Jackson State University, a historically black college in Mississippi. Many of them had voted for the first time and backed Colom.
"I really feel like a change is what we need," 18-year-old Jamyria Dunn said.
"I've had some amazing days in my life," she continued, "but seeing Mississippi, this state in particular, turn blue, would really bring a light to my heart that people just would not understand."

articles.title: NAZA: how and where to watch the Guardian’s acclaimed Gaza documentary
articles.summary:
Film features testimony from 24 Israeli officials involved in surveillance and remote killing of Palestinian civilians

• NAZA is in cinemas worldwide and will screen for free on the…

blocks.text: Where can I watch the film?
NAZA will be released in full on the Guardian’s website for free in early December. Sign up here to be notified of the exact streaming date and to be sent a link to the film when it is live.

NAZA has been shown by cinemas in 47 countries and seen by more than 1.5 million people since its release last month, making it one of the most-watched documentary films with a theatrical release in 2026. The film has been offered to a number of distributors and cinemas in Israel but has not been screened there yet.
You can watch a trailer here.

blocks.caption: Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, the directors of NAZA, take questions after its UK premiere at the Ritzy cinema in south London. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian

blocks.text: What is NAZA about?

NAZA is a documentary featuring testimony from 24 Israeli military intelligence officers and soldiers involved in the surveillance and remote killing of Palestinian civilians during the war in Gaza. The film’s title comes from an Israeli military acronym used euphemistically to refer to civilians expected to be killed in a military attack.

The interviewees detail the methods used by the Israeli military in Gaza, including AI-based systems built to identify large numbers of potential Hamas operatives, who were then bombed in their homes at night, in the knowledge that the attacks would also kill their families.

Interviews were filmed at night on rooftops in Tel Aviv, on the condition of anonymity, because of the risks involved in speaking publicly. The appearance and voices of participants in the film have been digitally altered to disguise their identities.
Who is behind the film?

The film was directed by the Oscar-winning Israeli directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor and produced by the Guardian. It builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian magazine +972, the Hebrew-language news outlet Local Call and the Guardian newspaper between 2023 and 2025.

Abraham and Szor were two of the four co-directors – with the Palestinians Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal – of No Other Land, which documents the destruction of Masafer Yatta, a village in the occupied West Bank targeted by Israeli forces. It won the Oscar for best documentary in 2025.
NAZA was co-produced by James Wilson and executive-produced by Jonathan Glazer, the team behind the Oscar-winning film The Zone of Interest.

blocks.caption: NAZA features interviews with Israeli officials who explain the targeting of presumed Hamas operatives. Photograph: NAZA/The Guardian

blocks.text: How has it been received?

NAZA has received widespread critical acclaim and is selling out in cinemas across the world. The New York Times says it is “tough to watch and impossible to ignore”, while New York Magazine describes it as “one of the most important films of our time”. In a five-star review, the Financial Times says that “journalism and film-making brilliantly entwine”. British Vogue calls NAZA a “brilliant and harrowing film”.

The film won the special jury prize at the Venice film festival in September, where its premiere had a 25-minute ovation – a festival record. In November, it won the best political documentary from the Critics Choice Association.
Why has there been an Israeli backlash?

The film, its directors and their confidential sources have faced fierce attacks from the Israeli government and military. The prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has ordered the attorney general and the head of the Shin Bet security service to reveal the identities of sources interviewed and prosecute them for causing “harm to Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.

Netanyahu also threatened to strip Abraham and Szor of their citizenship, accusing them of treason. The Israeli military’s chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, said the military would “not allow soldiers to be made targets through lies and blood libels” and would use “every tool at our disposal” against the film.

Far-right groups have vowed to hound the film-makers on their return to Israel and picketed Szor’s family home. Some of the messages included explicit calls for violence, with one protester demanding the “death penalty for traitors”.

The Israeli military claimed there were “substantial errors” in the film and that it had relied on sources who had only a partial picture of the target approval process. It said that while AI was used to help identify targets in Gaza, final decisions on strikes, and the risk of civilian casualties, were signed off by officers.
In response, the team behind the film have revealed they spoke to more than 100 sources with knowledge of the military systems used in the war.
What is NAZA: The Real Story?

The Israeli government is promoting an online film project, called NAZA: The Real Story, which mimics the style of the genuine NAZA film and is hosted on a website called nazadocumentary.com. It is not the real NAZA documentary and has been misleading some viewers.

Initially, the rival film’s website falsely presented itself as a promotional page for NAZA itself, naming Abraham and Szor as the directors, and listing film festivals where the documentary was to be screened. The site now appears as a platform for the rival film, which has been promoted by Israeli embassies.

Ariel Averbuch, an Israeli attorney and army reservist who co-created NAZA: The Real Story, describes it as an “offensive move” to shift the world’s focus from allegations about the Israeli military’s killing of civilians.
Szor and Abraham have addressed the backlash to their documentary. “Our country is doing so much to hide these systems,” Szor said.

articles.title: Two men found guilty over Iranian attempts to ‘eliminate’ UK-based journalists
articles.summary:
Mostafa Sepahvand and Farhad Javadi Manesh carried out surveillance in an effort to inflict violence on three people

Two men of Iranian origin who were hired through social media as part of…

blocks.text: Two men of Iranian origin who were hired through social media as part of a plan to “eliminate” journalists in the UK have been found guilty of engaging in conduct likely to assist Tehran’s intelligence services.
Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, and Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, carried out surveillance and reconnaissance between August 2024 and March last year in an attempt to inflict violence on “subjects” in the UK.

These subjects included two journalists for the London-based Persian broadcaster Iran International, Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini, and a founder member of UK Lawyers for Israel, Jonathan Turner.

The defendants visited addresses linked to their targets, took photos and videos and used platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online. They appear to be part of a growing new tactic used by hostile states in which “proxies” are hired to work for foreign security forces, with often little idea who they are targeting or why.

Last month the Norwegian teenager Johannes Natland, 19, was jailed for life after he agreed to carry out a hit in Huddersfield for the Foxtrot Network, a Swedish organised crime group backed by the Iranian regime.
The Iranian men came to the UK illegally between 2016 and 2022 – Sepahvand in the back of a lorry and Manesh in a small boat.

Sepahvand used the AI platform ChatGPT to find the home address of Mojtaba Pourmohsen who worked for London-based Persian language broadcaster Iran International. He hoped to earn £150,000 to carry out a violent attack and help to “finish off” Pourmohsen.
Sepahvand chatted on WhatsApp to his handler, an IRGC commander called Amin, as he spied on Pourmohsen in December 2024, Woolwich crown court heard.
Amin wrote: “These are new pictures of the guy/bloke.”
Sepahvand replied: “I’ll go tomorrow.”
Referring to a picture, Amin said: “And that dot is their office?”
Sepahvand said: “Love you brother, I’ll go there tomorrow.”
The pair also discussed surveillance of Iranian satirist Kambiz Hosseini, who eventually had to leave home because of the threats made against him.

Bill Emlyn Jones KC, prosecuting, said the Islamic Republic of Iran and its rulers do not and cannot tolerate dissent. “One organisation critical to the regime, and therefore very much in its sights, is Iran International, a news organisation which has come under particular attack because of its explicit support for opposition groups and its editorial stance, which is anti-Islamic Republic of Iran.
“Eliminating hostile, critical or dissident actors overseas is a staple policy of the Islamic Republic. Together, the defendants were engaged in what is very obviously a form of spying,” Jones said.

Hosseini, 51, had to leave home and stop work as a standup comedian as a result of the threats he received. He was sent a message with a picture of his car saying the next time he started the engine it would blow up. Hosseini’s family in Iran also received threats, and his family had to leave the country.
The court heard Sepahvand had been convicted of theft in Iran and was drawn into the plan to “eliminate” dissidents in the hope of reducing his criminal record.
after newsletter promotion
He told his Iranian handlers he was prepared to escalate from surveillance to violence, the court heard.

He hoped to receive a final payment of £150,000 for “finishing the job”, a reference to killing one of the journalists, the court was told. “If the person [the target] is inside, they pay the £150,000, and I’ll finish him off,” said Sepahvand in a voice note.
Sepahvand claimed his family were being threatened and he never intended to go through with the hit. He also denied plotting to kill Jonathan Turner of UK Lawyers for Israel.
Manesh claimed he took a picture of the Iran International site because it was “a beautiful building” and did not know they were working with the Iranian intelligence services.

Earlier this year, Roman Lavrynovych, 22, and Stanislav Carpiuc, 27, were jailed at the Old Bailey for seven and two years respectively for arson attacks on property connected to Keir Starmer. An anonymous Russian-speaking figure named El Money had recruited Lavrynovych and Carpiuc on Telegram.

Last year, six Britons were jailed for their parts in a Russian-ordered arson attack on a London warehouse providing aid to Ukraine. The ringleader, Dylan Earl, was recruited by the Wagner group, a mercenary organisation that acts on behalf of the Russian state.

Sepahvand was convicted by the jury of assisting a foreign intelligence service and preparatory conduct. Manesh was convicted of assisting a foreign intelligence service, but cleared of preparatory conduct.
Shapoor Noori, 57, of Ealing, was cleared by the jury of assisting a foreign intelligence service and preparatory conduct.
Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb remanded Sepahvand and Manesh ahead of sentencing at the Old Bailey on 17 December.

articles.title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza cleared of using AI to write prize-winning story
articles.summary:
After a month-long investigation it was concluded that Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which won the £10,000 Caine prize, was ‘human-written’

Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has…
articles.byline: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg and agencies

blocks.text: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation.
Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October.

Five days later, the Atlantic published an article titled: “Yet another literary prize winner seems to be AI,” in which author and journalist Vauhini Vara said AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated.

Caine prize chair Ellah Wakatama said in a statement: “From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human-written. We now look forward to awarding and celebrating Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza … before the end of the year.”
She said: “When concerns were raised, we have a duty as an organisation to look at them carefully and fairly,” adding that the prize had taken a “human-centred” approach to its investigation.

“Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel and The Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published,” Wakatama said. “It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author.”

Kundizeza, who had strongly denied using generative AI to write the story, said he was “relieved” that the allegations had been dismissed after the investigation. “It was not necessary in the first place, I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey,” he said.
Vara’s article prompted outrage online, with many claiming that Black writers, and Africans in particular, were being unfairly singled out by allegations they were using AI.
Associated Press contributed to this report
